questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: Medical termination of pregnancy is governed by specific legal and medical regulations. Under certain defined conditions, termination is permitted up to 24 weeks of gestation. In which scenario is medical termination of pregnancy legally allowed up to 24 weeks?
questions.explanation: Under the Medical Termination of Pregnancy (MTP) Amendment Act 2021 in India, the gestational limit for termination was increased from 20 to 24 weeks for specific categories of women. These categories include survivors of sexual assault, rape, or incest, as well as minors, women whose marital status changed during pregnancy (widowhood or divorce), and women with physical disabilities or mental illness. For rape victims, this extension acknowledges the extreme trauma and potential delays in recognizing or reporting the pregnancy. While fetal malformations (Option A) also allow for termination, they are often permitted even beyond 24 weeks if a medical board confirms substantial abnormalities. Contraception failure (Option C) is generally only a valid ground up to 20 weeks for married women or those in stable relationships. Minor status (Option B) is a valid category for the 24-week extension, but in the context of most standard medical examinations, "rape victim" is the classic textbook example for this specific legal threshold
questions.learning: Under the Medical Termination of Pregnancy (MTP) Amendment Act 2021 in India, the gestational limit for termination was increased from 20 to 24 weeks for specific categories of women.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A patient presents with thick nasal discharge and headache. Examination reveals hypertrophy of the inferior turbinate with a mulberry appearance. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Hypertrophic rhinitis

This clinical vignette is suggestive of hypertrophic rhinitis.

It is characterized by the thickening of the mucosa, submucosa, seromucous glands, periosteum, and bone.

Recurrent nasal infections, chronic sinusitis, chronic irritation of nasal mucosa due to smoking, prolonged use of nasal drops, vasomotor and allergic rhinitis, and industrial irritants are some of the causes of hypertrophic rhinitis.

Clinical features are thick and sticky nasal discharge, headache, and transient anosmia. Examination reveals hypertrophy of the turbinates with underlying fibrosis. Mulberry hypertrophy is seen in hypertrophic rhinitis. Maximum changes are seen in the inferior turbinate.

Treatment includes cryosurgery of turbinates, linear cauterisation, submucosal diathermy, partial or total turbinectomy and lasers.

Pearl PF1339: Clinical Features of Atrophic Rhinitis

* More common in females

* Usually starts at puberty

* It is a bilateral condition

* Symptoms:

* Foul smell from the nose

* Nasal obstruction in spite of roomy chambers due to large crusts filling nasal cavity

* Epistaxis on removing of the crusts

* Anosmia due to degeneration of nerve elements (merciful anosmia)

* Signs:

* Greenish or greyish black dry crusts covering the turbinates and septum

* After removal of crusts, nasal cavities appear roomy with atrophy of turbinates

* Nasal mucosa appears pale

Pearl PF1084: Antrochoanal Polyp

* Main etiological factors: Infection and allergy

* Usually affects children

* Site of origin: Mucosa of the maxillary antrum

* Clinical features:

* Usually single and unilateral

* Unilateral nasal obstruction which becomes bilateral when it grows posteriorly and obstructs opposite choana

* Mucoid nasal discharge

* Hyponasal voice

* Findings:

* Grows posteriorly and usually missed on anterior rhinoscopy

* Posterior rhinoscopy: Globular mass filling the choana or nasopharynx

* Investigation of choice: Nasal endoscopy. Shows nasal polyps that are pale, gelatinous and pedunculated

* Treatment of choice: FESS
questions.learning: Hypertrophic rhinitis — This clinical vignette is suggestive of hypertrophic rhinitis. It is characterized by the thickening of the mucosa, submucosa, seromucous glands, periosteum, and bone.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: A middle-aged female patient presented with slowly progressive motor weakness, nuchal rigidity, and difficulty in swallowing and carrying out day-to-day activities. A provisional diagnosis of multiple sclerosis is suspected. Which of the following cells are affected in multiple sclerosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Oligodendrocytes

Oligodendrocytes are affected in multiple sclerosis.

In multiple sclerosis, there is patchy destruction of myelin in the central nervous system and the axons are demyelinated. This causes loss of conduction or delayed conduction in the demyelinated axons. Oligodendrocytes and Schwann cells are involved in the formation of myelin. Hence, they are affected by multiple sclerosis.

Other options

Option A: Microglia are a part of the immune system. Microglia are scavenger cells that aid in the removal of cellular debris formed due to various diseases. They originate from macrophages outside of the nervous system and are unrelated to the neural cell types.

Option C: There are three types of macroglia - astrocytes, oligodendrocytes, and Schwann cells. Astrocytes are found throughout the brain and they induce capillaries to form the blood-brain barrier. The astrocytes may be fibrous or protoplasmic.

Option D: Ependymal cells line the ventricular system. They are in contact with the cerebrospinal fluid and play a role in fluid homeostasis.
questions.learning: Oligodendrocytes Oligodendrocytes are affected in multiple sclerosis. In multiple sclerosis, there is patchy destruction of myelin in the central nervous system and the axons are demyelinated.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which nerve damage would most likely cause sensory loss over the dorsum of the foot and the medial four toes, along with impaired eversion of the foot?
questions.explanation: The symptoms described pinpoint a lesion of the superficial peroneal nerve. This nerve provides motor innervation to the peroneus longus and peroneus brevis muscles, which are the primary evertors of the foot; hence, injury causes eversion difficulty. Sensorial, it supplies the majority of the dorsum of the foot and the dorsal aspects of the medial four toes, excluding the first web space. The deep peroneal nerve (Option A) supplies the first web space and the extensors responsible for dorsiflexion; its injury results in foot drop. The common peroneal nerve (Option C) is the parent trunk; a lesion here would cause both foot drop and eversion loss. The posterior tibial nerve (Option D) supplies the calf muscles and the sole of the foot, which are unrelated to these specific dorsal symptoms. Therefore, the isolated loss of eversion and specific dorsal sensation confirms superficial peroneal nerve damage
questions.learning: The symptoms described pinpoint a lesion of the superficial peroneal nerve. This nerve provides motor innervation to the peroneus longus and peroneus brevis muscles, which are the primary evertors of the foot; hence, injury causes eversion difficulty.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Urate crystals are described as having the following shape:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Long and needle-like

Monosodium urate (MSU) crystals are the diagnostic hallmark of gout. On polarized light microscopy, they appear as long, slender, needle-shaped crystals showing strong negative birefringence. In contrast, calcium pyrophosphate dihydrate (CPPD) crystals seen in pseudogout are rhomboid-shaped and exhibit weak positive birefringence.

Why are the other options incorrect?

• A. Short and stout: Not the characteristic morphology of urate crystals.
• C. Small and triangular: Not seen in crystal-induced arthropathies.
• D. Large and rhomboid: Rhomboid crystals are characteristic of CPPD deposition disease (pseudogout), not gout.
questions.learning: Long and needle-like Monosodium urate (MSU) crystals are the diagnostic hallmark of gout. On polarized light microscopy, they appear as long, slender, needle-shaped crystals showing strong negative birefringence.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 3-month-old child presents with photophobia and watering. Which of the following cannot be the cause?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Congenital nasolacrimal duct obstruction

In infants, photophobia + watering (epiphora) suggests corneal irritation or raised intraocular pressure, not just a drainage problem.

• Congenital nasolacrimal duct obstruction (CNLDO) causes:

• Watering and discharge
• NO photophobia
• Cornea remains clear → hence not a cause here

Conditions that DO cause photophobia + watering:

• Congenital glaucoma:

• Triad: Epiphora + Photophobia + Blepharospasm
• Due to corneal edema and raised IOP

• Congenital entropion / distichiasis:

• Misdirected lashes rub cornea → corneal irritation
• Leads to photophobia and tearing

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.topic: General Physiology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: Which of the following is correct about the recruitment of fast fatiguable motor unit?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Recruited last

Motor units are recruited according to the Henneman size principle, which states that motor neurons are activated from smallest to largest depending on the force required.

Recruitment order:

1.      Slow (Type I) motor units – small neurons, fatigue-resistant, used for low-force, sustained activities.

2.      Fast fatigue-resistant (Type IIa) – moderate force and endurance.

3.      Fast fatigable (Type IIb/IIx) – large neurons producing high force but fatigue quickly.

Therefore, fast fatigable motor units are recruited last, only during high-intensity or powerful muscle contractions.
questions.learning: Recruited last Motor units are recruited according to the Henneman size principle, which states that motor neurons are activated from smallest to largest depending on the force required.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which among the following is not a Hyperestrogenic condition?
questions.explanation: Hyperestrogenism refers to excessive levels of estrogen in the body, which can drive various gynecological pathologies. Adipose tissue is a significant site for the peripheral aromatization of androgens into estrogens; therefore, individuals with high BMI (obesity) are often in a hyperestrogenic state. Conversely, a Low BMI is associated with reduced estrogen production and is not a hyperestrogenic condition; in extreme cases, it can lead to hypoestrogenism and amenorrhea. Ovarian cancer (Option A), particularly granulosa cell tumors, can secrete high levels of estrogen. Endometriosis (Option B) is an estrogen-dependent inflammatory disease that thrives in a high-estrogen environment. Tamoxifen (Option D), while an estrogen antagonist in the breast, acts as a partial agonist in the endometrium, creating a localized hyperestrogenic effect that can lead to hyperplasia. Understanding these metabolic and pharmacological links is crucial for managing reproductive health, as chronic estrogen excess is a major risk factor for endometrial carcinoma and other hormone-sensitive malignancies

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 6-year-old girl came to your clinic with refractive power of +1D in right eye and -2D in left eye. Fundus examination reveals normal acuity and retinal findings. What is the correct diagnosis? D - dioptre
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Anisometropia

The history of defective vision and 2 different refractive errors of the eyes suggests a diagnosis of anisometropia.

Anisometropia occurs when the total refraction of both eyes are unequal. A difference of 1D in the two eyes causes a 2% difference in the size of retinal images formed. A difference up to 2.5D is well-tolerated, but beyond 4D cannot be tolerated. Anisometropia can occur as a combination of emmetropia, myopia, hypermetropia, and astigmatism.

It is diagnosed after retinoscopic examination and autorefractometry.

Treatment includes the usage of spectacles (it can be tolerated up to a maximum difference of 4D), contact lenses, intraocular lenses (for uniocular aphakia), refractive corneal surgery, or refractive lens exchange methods (used in high degree anisometropia).

Other options:

Option B: Myopia (Short-sightedness): The parallel rays of light coming from infinity are focused in front of the retina when accommodation is at rest.

Option C: Hypermetropia(Long-sightedness): The parallel rays of light coming from infinity are focused behind the retina when accommodation is at rest.

Option D: Amblyopia or 'lazy eye' is a developmental defect of spatial visual processing that occurs in the central visual pathways of the eye.

Pearl PF1369: Causes of Myopia

Myopia

Etiology

Axial myopia

(Most common)

Increase in the anteroposterior length of the eyeball.

Curvatural myopia

Increased curvature of the cornea, lens, or both

Positional myopia

Anterior placement of the crystalline lens in the eye

Index myopia

Increase in the refractive index of crystalline lens

Nocturnal myopia

Due to spherical aberration and accomodation
questions.learning: Anisometropia — The history of defective vision and 2 different refractive errors of the eyes suggests a diagnosis of anisometropia. Anisometropia occurs when the total refraction of both eyes are unequal.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 45-year-old alcoholic with a history of binge drinking presents with an episode of vomiting bright red blood. His vitals are stable. What is the probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Mallory Weiss Tear

The most probable diagnosis for the above-mentioned clinical presentation is Mallory Weiss tear .

Mallory Weiss Syndrome is due to a longitudinal tear in mucosa or submucosa of the gastroesophageal junction. It is a common cause of upper gastrointestinal bleeding due to the presence of longitudinal superficial mucosal lacerations (Mallory-Weiss tears). The left gastric artery is the most common vessel to bleed.

It mainly occurs in patients with repetitive forceful retching and vomiting and is associated with heavy alcohol intake. The presence of portal hypertension with oesophagal varices and hiatal hernia may aggravate the condition. The investigation of choice is endoscopy.

Management of Mallory Weiss tear is conservative, as it usually is self-limiting. Endoscopic electrocoagulation or sclerosant therapy is done in some cases. Angiographic embolization or high gastrotomy is necessary only in rare cases that don't respond to conservative management.

Boerhaave syndrome is characterized by a tear in the lower third of the oesophagus which occurs when a person vomits against a closed glottis, causing a leak into the mediastinum, pleural cavity and peritoneum. Here all layers are involved.

The patients initially present with severe chest pain, tachypnea, and shock. Clinical features include Mackler's triad

* Retching

* Chest pain

* Subcutaneous emphysema

This catastrophic event produces severe mediastinitis(deranged vitals tachypnea, tachycardia, fever, and hypotension) and generally requires surgical intervention.
questions.learning: Mallory Weiss Tear — The most probable diagnosis for the above-mentioned clinical presentation is Mallory Weiss tear . Mallory Weiss Syndrome is due to a longitudinal tear in mucosa or submucosa of the gastroesophageal junction.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 30-year-old woman, one week after delivering a healthy full-term baby, presents to the obstetrics and gynecology clinic with complaints of a pale brownish vaginal discharge that has a fishy odor. What is the nature of this discharge?
questions.explanation: The vaginal discharge seen during the first few weeks postpartum is called lochia. Based on the timing (one week ago) and appearance (pale brownish or pinkish), the discharge is classified as Lochia Serosa, which characteristically occurs between days 5 and 9 of the puerperium. It is composed of wound exudate and mucus and often has a fishy smell. Regarding the distractors, Lochia Rubra (Option A) is red, contains blood, and is seen only in the first 1–4 days. Lochia Alba (Option C) is pale white or yellowish and is seen after the 10th day. Leukorrhea (Option D) is a profuse white discharge usually associated with vaginitis or subinvolution rather than normal postpartum recovery. Thus, the specific one-week timing and brownish color definitively identify the discharge as lochia serosa

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Which type of radiation is produced using the principle of linear accelerators?
questions.explanation: Linear accelerators (LINACs) are the most common devices used for external beam radiation therapy. They work by accelerating electrons to near light speed and striking a heavy metal target (like tungsten), which results in the production of high-energy X-rays (photons). LINACs can also be configured to deliver electron beams directly. Protons (Option A) are produced in cyclotrons or synchrotrons for specialized proton beam therapy. Gamma rays (Option C) are emitted by the decay of radioactive isotopes like Cobalt-60. Neutrons (Option D) are produced in nuclear reactors or specialized neutron generators. LINACs are favored because they allow for highly precise conformal therapy (like IMRT), targeting the tumor with high-dose X-rays while sparing adjacent healthy organs. Unlike cobalt units, they do not require a radioactive source, making them safer to house and maintain in clinical settings. The ability to vary the X-ray energy allows for the treatment of both superficial and deep-seated tumors

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which of the following is not a marker for gastrointestinal stromal tumors?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. NRG-1

NRG-1 (Neuregulin-1) is not a marker for gastrointestinal stromal tumors (GISTs).

GIST are the most common mesenchymal tumor of the abdomen, the stomach being the most common site. They arise from the interstitial cells of Cajal, the pacemaker cells of the GIT. GIST is seen in the 5th to 6th decade of life and has an equal preponderance among males and females. Most patients present with haematemesis, melena, or vague abdominal pain. The most common indications for surgery include bleeding and obstruction.

The GIST may occur in a sporadic form or as part of familial syndromes. In sporadic GIST, the most common mutations seen are gain-of-function mutation in KIT (75-80%) and PDGFRA mutation (8%). Microscopically, GIST has elongated spindle cells or plumper epithelioid cells, or a mixed pattern.

The below image shows the microscopy of GIST composed of bundles, or fascicles, of spindle-shaped tumor cells.

Succinate dehydrogenase (SDH)-deficient GIST is a subset of wild-type GIST seen with Carney triad or Carney-Stratakis syndrome.

Imatinib can be used to treat GIST with mutations in KIT or PDGFRA. Succinate dehydrogenase (SDH) - deficient GIST is imatinib-resistant, so sunitinib, sorafenib, or regorafenib can be used instead.

During surgical resection of GIST, care must be taken to prevent capsule rupture, which causes seeding of nearby tissues leading to relapse in 100% of the cases. If capsule rupture occurs, adjuvant therapy with imatinib is indicated regardless of tumor extent.

Other options:

Option A: KIT (CD117): This is the most well-known marker for GISTs. About 85% of GISTs show mutations in the KIT gene, leading to the expression of the KIT protein on the cell surface. KIT is a receptor tyrosine kinase, and its activation is a key driver in the pathogenesis of GISTs.

Option B: SDH (Succinate Dehydrogenase): SDH mutations are associated with a subset of GISTs, particularly those that are KIT and PDGFRA wild-type. Loss of SDH function is characteristic of this subgroup, and SDH deficiency can be demonstrated through immunohistochemistry.

Option C: PDGFRA (Platelet-Derived Growth Factor Receptor Alpha): Mutations in the PDGFRA gene account for approximately 5-10% of GISTs. Similar to KIT, PDGFRA is a receptor tyrosine kinase, and mutations in this gene can lead to the development of GISTs.
questions.learning: NRG-1 NRG-1 (Neuregulin-1) is not a marker for gastrointestinal stromal tumors (GISTs). GIST are the most common mesenchymal tumor of the abdomen, the stomach being the most common site.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: During recovery from anesthesia, a patient started experiencing hallucinations and vivid dreams. Which inducing agent is most likely responsible?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Ketamine

Hallucinations and vivid dreams during recovery from anesthesia are a manifestation of an emergence reaction following the administration of ketamine.

The incidence of psychic emergence reactions ranges from 3% to 100% and is usually associated with excitement, confusion, euphoria, and fear. The symptoms usually appear in the first hour of emergence and subside within several hours.
questions.learning: Ketamine Hallucinations and vivid dreams during recovery from anesthesia are a manifestation of an emergence reaction following the administration of ketamine.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which factor promotes gastrointestinal motility (peristalsis), characterized by coordinated, sequential smooth muscle contractions that move food along the digestive tract beginning at the esophagus?
options: Presence of fatty food in the stomach
Presence of tryptophan in the stomach
Presence of acid in the stomach
questions.explanation: Peristalsis is the rhythmic, wave-like contraction of intestinal smooth muscle that propels contents forward. The most potent physiological stimulus for initiating and enhancing this movement is the distension of the stomach or intestinal wall (Option B). When food enters the gut, it stretches the wall, stimulating mechanoreceptors that activate the myenteric plexus. This leads to the contraction of circular muscles behind the bolus and relaxation ahead of it, known as the "Law of the Intestine". In contrast, the presence of fatty food (Option A) or acid (Option D) in the duodenum actually inhibits gastric emptying and slows down motility to allow for adequate neutralization and digestion. Tryptophan (Option C) does not have a direct excitatory effect on peristaltic waves. Therefore, mechanical distension is the primary factor that triggers the neuro-muscular reflex required for propulsion
questions.learning: Peristalsis is the rhythmic, wave-like contraction of intestinal smooth muscle that propels contents forward. The most potent physiological stimulus for initiating and enhancing this movement is the distension of the stomach or intestinal wall (Option B).

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Pick the correct statement regarding the Sanchol cholera vaccine
options: Bivalent vaccine given in 2 liquid doses orally to children >=1 year of age
Bivalent given in single dose orally to children >1 years of age
Monovalent given in 2 liquid doses orally with a bicarbonate buffer
Monovalent given in a single dose orally with a bicarbonate buffer
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Bivalent vaccine given in 2 liquid doses orally to children >=1 year of age

The Sanchol cholera vaccine is a bivalent vaccine given in 2 liquid doses orally to children >=1 year of age.

The Sanchol cholera vaccine is a bivalent oral cholera vaccine (OCV) that targets both Vibrio cholerae O1 and Vibrio cholerae O139 serogroups, which are the primary causes of cholera outbreaks. It is designed to provide immunity by stimulating the production of antibodies in the intestines, the site of infection.

Key Features of the Sanchol Vaccine:
Bivalent Nature: The vaccine protects against two strains of the cholera bacterium: O1, which is responsible for most global cholera cases, and O139 which is seen in South Asia.

Dosing Schedule: The Sanchol vaccine is administered in two oral doses. The doses are given 14 days apart for children aged 1 year and above as well as adults. This two-dose regimen is essential for achieving effective immunity. The vaccine is provided in liquid form, making it easy to administer. It does not require any special preparation, such as mixing with a bicarbonate buffer, which is needed for some older cholera vaccines.

Age Recommendation: The vaccine is recommended for individuals aged 1 year and older. It is particularly useful in endemic regions or during outbreaks to prevent the spread of the disease.

Efficacy and Duration: Sanchol has been shown to provide significant protection against cholera for up to 3-5 years after vaccination, although booster doses may be required in areas with ongoing transmission.

The vaccine is widely used in mass vaccination campaigns, especially in areas prone to cholera outbreaks, such as refugee camps or regions with poor sanitation. It has been a critical tool in reducing the incidence of cholera in many endemic areas.
questions.learning: Bivalent vaccine given in 2 liquid doses orally to children >=1 year of age The Sanchol cholera vaccine is a bivalent vaccine given in 2 liquid doses orally to children >=1 year of age.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following develops from the dorsal mesogastrium?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Spleen

The spleen develops from the mesoderm in the dorsal mesogastrium.

The mesenchymal cells in the dorsal mesogastrium form small lobular masses of splenic tissue called spleniculi. Later, these lobules fuse to form a single mass of spleen. The capsule, septa, and connective tissue framework, including reticular fibers, develop from mesoderm. The mesenchymal cells also differentiate into lymphoblasts and other blood-forming cells.

When the spleen develops, the dorsal mesogastrium gets divided into an anterior segment called gastrosplenic ligament that extends from the spleen to stomach, and a posterior part called the lienorenal ligament that extends from the spleen to the left kidney.
questions.learning: Spleen — The spleen develops from the mesoderm in the dorsal mesogastrium. The mesenchymal cells in the dorsal mesogastrium form small lobular masses of splenic tissue called spleniculi.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: Where would you place the pulse oximeter to measure pre-ductal oxygen saturation in an infant who was born 3 minutes ago?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Right upper limb

The right upper limb is the best area to check pre-ductal oxygen saturation in a newborn infant as it receives blood supply primarily from the right brachial artery, which arises from the aorta before the ductus arteriosus.

In routine neonatal screening for critical congenital heart diseases (CCHD), saturation probes are placed on the right upper limb (pre-ductal) and the right lower limb (post-ductal) respectively.

If the difference between pre-ductal and post-ductal saturation is more than five percent, it confirms the presence of hypoxemia. Any reading showing an SpO2 <90% or greater than a three percent difference between the right hand and right foot for three successive readings separated by an hour each would suggest the presence of a congenital cardiac disease.

Screening is done to identify critical conditions before they present symptomatically, and before the neonate leaves the hospital post-delivery. This would allow for early and effective treatment of an underlying disease.

Critical congenital heart diseases include coarctation of the aorta, double outlet right ventricle, Ebstein anomaly, hypoplastic left heart syndrome, interrupted aortic arch, pulmonary atresia, single ventricle, tetralogy of Fallot (TOF), total anomalous pulmonary venous return (TAPVC), d-transposition of the great arteries (TGA), tricuspid atresia, and truncus arteriosus.
questions.learning: Right upper limb — The right upper limb is the best area to check pre-ductal oxygen saturation in a newborn infant as it receives blood supply primarily from the right brachial artery, which arises from the aorta before the ductus arteriosus.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following is the most common type of renal stones?
questions.explanation: In the global population, calcium oxalate stones are the most frequently encountered type of renal calculi, accounting for approximately 75–80% of all cases . These stones are typically radiopaque on X-ray and can form in both acidic and alkaline urine. Triple phosphate stones (Option C), also called struvite or staghorn calculi, are associated with chronic urinary tract infections caused by urease-producing bacteria like Proteus. Uric acid stones (Option D) are unique because they are radiolucent and are often seen in patients with gout or high purine diets. Cystine stones (Option B) are rare and result from a specific genetic defect in amino acid transport. Identifying the chemical composition of the stone is vital for metabolic evaluation and preventing recurrence through dietary modifications and pharmacological therapy. Therefore, based on broad epidemiological data, calcium oxalate is the definitive "most common" type of stone. Patients are often advised to maintain high fluid intake to reduce the concentration of stone-forming salts
questions.learning: In the global population, calcium oxalate stones are the most frequently encountered type of renal calculi, accounting for approximately 75–80% of all cases .

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 5-year-old boy presents with intense itching of the eyes, photophobia, and a sticky ocular discharge. Ophthalmic examination reveals characteristic findings. Based on these symptoms and examination results, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Vernal Keratoconjunctivitis (VKC), or "Spring Catarrh," is a recurrent, bilateral allergic inflammation of the conjunctiva. It typically affects young boys in hot, dry climates. The hallmark symptom is intense itching, often accompanied by photophobia and a characteristic ropy, sticky discharge. Clinical signs include giant papillae on the superior tarsal conjunctiva ("cobblestone" appearance) or white dots at the limbus (Horner-Trantas dots). Option A (Trachoma) is an infectious scarring disease with follicles. Option C (Phlyctenular conjunctivitis) is a hypersensitivity reaction presenting with localized nodules near the limbus. Option D (Xerophthalmia) is due to Vitamin A deficiency and presents with extreme dryness and Bitot's spots. VKC is a combined Type I and Type IV hypersensitivity reaction. Treatment involves cold compresses, mast cell stabilizers, antihistamines, and occasionally topical steroids. Severe cases can lead to "shield ulcers" on the cornea, which can permanently impair vision
questions.learning: Vernal Keratoconjunctivitis (VKC), or "Spring Catarrh," is a recurrent, bilateral allergic inflammation of the conjunctiva. It typically affects young boys in hot, dry climates.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A patient with a history of breast cancer underwent tele cobalt-60 radiotherapy. She now presents with respiratory distress, and imaging shows bilateral perihilar ground glass opacities. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Radiation pneumonitis

A patient with a history of breast cancer who previously received Tele cobalt-60 radiotherapy now presents with respiratory distress. Imaging shows bilateral perihilar ground glass opacities, suggesting a likely diagnosis of radiation pneumonitis.

Radiation pneumonitis is an inflammatory reaction in the lungs that occurs as a result of radiation therapy, commonly seen in patients treated for breast cancer, lung cancer, or lymphomas. It typically develops within weeks to months after radiation exposure and presents with symptoms such as cough, fever, chest pain, and progressive shortness of breath. The condition arises due to damage to the alveolar and capillary structures, leading to increased vascular permeability, inflammatory infiltration, and pulmonary oedema. Imaging findings, particularly on CT scans, may show areas of ground-glass opacities, consolidation, or haziness, often in the radiation field.

If left untreated, radiation pneumonitis can progress to pulmonary fibrosis, causing long-term respiratory complications. Management involves corticosteroids to reduce inflammation and supportive care, including oxygen therapy if needed.

Prevention strategies include limiting the radiation dose, using advanced radiotherapy techniques to minimize lung exposure, and closely monitoring high-risk patients. Early recognition and intervention are crucial to improving outcomes and preventing long-term lung damage in affected individuals.
questions.learning: Radiation pneumonitis — A patient with a history of breast cancer who previously received Tele cobalt-60 radiotherapy now presents with respiratory distress.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: What is occipitomental view with open mouth also known as?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Water's view

Occipitomental view is called Water's view. Water's view with an open mouth is known as Pierre's view. Among the given options, Water's view is the best answer.

In Water's view, the patient’s head is positioned such that the nose and the chin touch the film while the X-rays are projected from backward. The mouth is usually kept open, which allows visualizing the sphenoid sinus.

Structures seen in Water’s view are:

• Maxillary sinuses (seen best)
• Frontal sinuses
• Sphenoid sinus (if the film is taken with an open mouth)
• Zygoma
• Zygomatic arch
• Nasal bone
• Frontal process of the maxilla
• Superior orbital fissure
• Infratemporal fossa

Other options:

Option B: Towne's view is an angled anteroposterior radiograph of the skull. Structures seen are the petrous part of the pyramids, arcuate eminence, superior semicircular canal, mastoid antrum, internal auditory canal, tympanic cavity, cochlea, and external auditory canal. This view is taken for acoustic neuroma and apical petrositis.

Option C: Law's view is a lateral oblique X-ray view of the mastoid. Structures seen are the external auditory canal, mastoid air cells, tegmen, lateral sinus plate, and temporomandibular joint.

Option D: Stenver's view is an X-ray view of the skull where the long axis of the petrous bone is parallel to the film. Structures seen are the entire petrous pyramid, arcuate eminence, internal auditory meatus, labyrinth with its vestibule, cochlea, and mastoid antrum.
questions.learning: Water's view Occipitomental view is called Water's view. Water's view with an open mouth is known as Pierre's view.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Consider the following statements with respect to endometrial cycle: 1. The basal zone is uninfluenced by any hormone. 2. Saw-toothed glandular epithelium is seen in secretory phase. 3. Stratum compactum contains mainly the glands and less stroma. 4. Pseudostratification is seen in proliferative phase of menstrual cycle. Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1, 2 and 4

1. Basal zone is uninfluenced by hormones — Correct

• The stratum basale is relatively unaffected by cyclical hormonal changes and remains after menstruation.
• It serves as the source for regeneration of the functional layer.

2. Saw-toothed glandular epithelium is seen in secretory phase — Correct

• Under progesterone influence, endometrial glands become tortuous/coiled (“saw-toothed”) and begin secreting glycogen.

3. Stratum compactum contains mainly glands and less stroma — Incorrect

• The stratum compactum contains densely packed stromal cells and relatively fewer glands.
• The stratum spongiosum contains more prominent, dilated glands.

4. Pseudostratification is seen in proliferative phase — Correct

• During the estrogen-driven proliferative phase, the endometrial glands are relatively straight and show pseudostratified columnar epithelium.
questions.learning: Basal zone is uninfluenced by hormones — Correct • — The stratum basale is relatively unaffected by cyclical hormonal changes and remains after menstruation. • It serves as the source for regeneration of the functional layer.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text:
Match the following in relation to fingerprint changes.

1) Incomplete atrophy of ridges
a) Radiation

2) Loss of pattern with ridge atrophy
b) Scleroderma

3) Altered ridges
c) Celiac disease

4) Permanent loss of fingerprints
d) Acromegaly

5) Distance between ridges changed but pattern retained
e) Dermatitis
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 1-e, 2-c, 3-b, 4-a, 5-d

The correctly matched option is 1-e, 2-c, 3-b, 4-a, 5-d.

1. Incomplete atrophy of ridges
e. Dermatitis

2. Loss of pattern with ridge atrophy
c. Celiac disease

3. Altered ridges
b. Scleroderma

4. Permanent loss of fingerprints
a. Radiation

5. Distance between ridges changed but pattern retained
d. Acromegaly

The study of ridge patterns in the skin is Dactylography/ Galton-Henry system/ Dermatoglyphics. Fingerprints are the impressions of patterns produced by the papillary or epidermal ridges present on the fingertips.

Some changes in fingerprints include:

• Moderate epidermal ridge atrophy and loss of pattern in celiac disease
• Incomplete atrophy of the ridges in dermatitis
• Ridge alteration occurs in eczema, acanthosis nigricans, scleroderma, and dry or atrophic skin
• Permanent impairment of the fingerprint pattern occurs in leprosy, electric injury, and after exposure to radiation
• Distance between the ridges is changed but the pattern is not altered in infantile paralysis, rickets, and acromegaly

Classification of fingerprint ridges:

• Loops: radial or ulnar
• Whorls: concentric, spiral, double spiral, or almond-shaped
• Arches: plain, tented, exceptional
• Composite: They are a combination of 2 or more types

The fingerprint patterns are not inherited and cannot be used to prove paternity. The fingerprint pattern differs even between identical twins.

Edgeoscopy is the study of edges of friction ridges which normally show seven characteristic features. Ridgeology is the study of friction ridges which are composed of the edges of ridge units that vary in size, shape, and alignment.
questions.learning: 1-e, 2-c, 3-b, 4-a, 5-d The correctly matched option is 1-e, 2-c, 3-b, 4-a, 5-d. Loss of pattern with ridge atrophy c.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A woman presents a few weeks after delivery with complaints of fever and bloody discharge from the nipple. On examination, a diffuse lump is palpated beneath the areola. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The patient’s presentation—fever, bloody or purulent nipple discharge, and a diffuse lump occurring a few weeks postpartum—is highly suggestive of lactational mastitis. This condition is usually caused by milk stasis followed by bacterial infection, most commonly by Staphylococcus aureus. Regarding the distractors, a galactocele (Option A) is a milk-retention cyst that presents as a painless, non-tender lump without fever or bloody discharge. Mondor disease (Option C) is a superficial thrombophlebitis of the breast veins, which presents as a palpable, cord-like structure rather than a diffuse inflammatory mass. Fibrocystic disease (Option D) causes cyclic pain and nodularity in response to menstruation and is not typically associated with the postpartum period or acute infection. Management of mastitis involves frequent breastfeeding and appropriate antibiotics to prevent the formation of a breast abscess
questions.learning: The patient’s presentation—fever, bloody or purulent nipple discharge, and a diffuse lump occurring a few weeks postpartum—is highly suggestive of lactational mastitis.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: Identify the injury in the image below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Abrasion

The given image shows an abrasion.

An abrasion is the most superficial of injuries. It does not penetrate the full thickness of the epidermis.

A pure abrasion does not bleed, as blood vessels are confined to the dermis. However, the dermal papillae are corrugated in nature. Thus, many abrasions enter the dermis and bleeding commonly occurs.
questions.learning: Abrasion — The given image shows an abrasion. An abrasion is the most superficial of injuries.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Through which of the following marked sites does SARS-COVID 19 spread to the brain?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. A

The given image shows various skull foramina's. Infection through the cribriform plate and olfactory bulb (A) and dissemination through trans-synaptic transfer are some of the mechanisms proposed for the SARS-COV2 virus to reach the brain.

Encephalitis, demyelination, neuropathy, and stroke are the neurological sequelae to severe COVID-19 infection. The neurological invasion of the virus on the medullary cardiorespiratory center can lead to refractory respiratory failure in patients infected with COVID-19.

The pathogenesis implicated is explained in the image attached below.

options: VWD type 3 has severely low levels of VWF

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A 2-month-old infant presents with poor feeding, vomiting, and lethargy. Laboratory investigations reveal hyperammonemia along with increased urinary orotic acid levels. Which enzyme deficiency is most likely responsible for this condition?
questions.explanation: Hyperammonemia combined with elevated urinary orotic acid is diagnostic of Ornithine Transcarbamylase (OTC) deficiency, also known as Type 2 Hyperammonemia. This X-linked disorder prevents the conversion of carbamoyl phosphate and ornithine into citrulline within the mitochondria. The resulting buildup of carbamoyl phosphate shunts into the pyrimidine synthesis pathway, leading to high orotic acid levels. Carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I (CPS1) deficiency (Option A) causes hyperammonemia but with normal orotic acid levels because the cycle is blocked before that point. Orotidine 5'-phosphate decarboxylase deficiency (Option C) results in orotic aciduria and anemia, but ammonia levels remain normal. Argininosuccinate lyase deficiency (Option D) causes hyperammonemia with elevated citrulline/argininosuccinate rather than orotic acid. Thus, OTC deficiency is the only condition matching this metabolic profile
questions.learning: Hyperammonemia combined with elevated urinary orotic acid is diagnostic of Ornithine Transcarbamylase (OTC) deficiency, also known as Type 2 Hyperammonemia.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A child presents with telecanthus, hypertelorism, an antimongoloid slant of the eyes, and associated congenital cardiac defects. Which chromosomal abnormality is most likely responsible for this presentation?
questions.explanation: The child’s clinical features—telecanthus (increased distance between inner canthi), hypertelorism (widely spaced eyes), antimongoloid slant, and cardiac defects—are highly characteristic of DiGeorge syndrome (or Velocardiofacial syndrome). This condition is caused by a chromosomal microdeletion at the 22q11.2 locus. Regarding the distractors, translocations (Option A) involve the rearrangement of parts between non-homologous chromosomes and are common in leukemias. Inversions (Option B) are structural rearrangements within a single chromosome. Trisomy (Option D), such as Down syndrome (Trisomy 21), presents with a mongoloid (upward) slant rather than an antimongoloid one. Because the described cluster of facial and cardiac anomalies is the classic phenotype for the 22q11.2 deletion, a microdeletion is the correct genetic mechanism
questions.learning: The child’s clinical features—telecanthus (increased distance between inner canthi), hypertelorism (widely spaced eyes), antimongoloid slant, and cardiac defects—are highly characteristic of DiGeorge syndrome (or Velocardiofacial syndrome).

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Consider the following statements: Statement-1: In fetal growth restriction, there is always oligohydramnios. Statement-2: In fetal growth restriction, there is placental insufficiency leading to redistribution of blood flow to fetal brain shunting it from fetal kidney. Which one of the following is correct?
options: Both Statement-1 and Statement-2 are true and Statement-2 is the correct explanation for Statement-1.
Both Statement-1 and Statement-2 are true and Statement-2 is not the correct explanation for Statement-1.
Statement-1 is true but Statement-2 is false.
Statement-2 is true but Statement-1 is false.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Statement-2 is true but Statement-1 is false.

Fetal Growth Restriction (FGR) is commonly caused by uteroplacental insufficiency, resulting in chronic fetal hypoxia. The fetus adapts by redistributing blood flow (“brain-sparing effect”) to vital organs such as the brain, heart, and adrenal glands, at the expense of the kidneys, gastrointestinal tract, and peripheral tissues.

Why are the statements correct/incorrect?

• Statement-1. In fetal growth restriction there is always oligohydramnios: False. Oligohydramnios is common but not universal. It is mainly seen in placental insufficiency-related (late-onset/asymmetric) FGR, whereas some cases (e.g., constitutionally small fetus or certain early-onset FGR) may have normal amniotic fluid volume.
• Statement-2. In fetal growth restriction there is placental insufficiency leading to redistribution of blood flow to the fetal brain, shunting it from the fetal kidney: True. Reduced renal perfusion decreases fetal urine production, which can result in oligohydramnios.
questions.learning: Statement-2 is true but Statement-1 is false. Fetal Growth Restriction (FGR) is commonly caused by uteroplacental insufficiency, resulting in chronic fetal hypoxia.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Which of the following is not a component of the classical triad of Melkersson–Rosenthal syndrome?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Proptosis

Melkersson–Rosenthal syndrome is a rare neuro-mucocutaneous disorder characterized by the classical triad of recurrent orofacial edema, recurrent facial nerve (LMN) palsy, and fissured tongue (lingua plicata). The diagnosis is clinical, although not all three features are present in every patient.

• Proptosis is not a component of the classical triad of Melkersson–Rosenthal syndrome.

Why not the other options?

• B. Orofacial edema ✓: Recurrent, painless swelling of the lips (especially the upper lip) is the most common manifestation.
• C. Fissured tongue ✓: Also known as lingua plicata or scrotal tongue.
• D. Recurrent facial paralysis ✓: Typically a recurrent lower motor neuron facial nerve palsy, resembling Bell’s palsy.
questions.learning: Proptosis Melkersson–Rosenthal syndrome is a rare neuro-mucocutaneous disorder characterized by the classical triad of recurrent orofacial edema, recurrent facial nerve (LMN) palsy, and fissured tongue (lingua plicata).

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: What is the mechanism of action of doxycycline?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Protein synthesis inhibitor

Doxycycline is a tetracycline that acts by inhibiting protein synthesis.

Protein Synthesis Inhibitors:

Antibacterial drugs which bind to the 30s subunit of the 70s ribosome are given below:

* Tetracyclines

* Aminoglycosides

Antibacterial drugs which bind to the 50s subunit of 70s ribosome are given below:

* Macrolides

* Clindamycin

* Streptogramins

* Chloramphenicol

Other options:

Options A: Cefotetan and oxacillin are beta-lactam antibiotics that act by inhibiting cell wall synthesis.

Option C: Ciprofloxacin is a fluoroquinolone that acts by inhibiting DNA gyrase.

Option D: Tavaborole inhibits fungal leucyl-tRNA synthetase, thereby inhibiting fungal protein synthesis and finally resulting in fungal cell death.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 52-year-old woman presents with abnormal vaginal bleeding and pelvic pain. Pelvic examination reveals a friable mass on the cervix, and biopsy confirms carcinoma of the cervix. As she is planned for chemotherapy as part of her treatment, which chemotherapeutic drug is most commonly used in the management of cervical cancer?
questions.explanation: In the management of carcinoma cervix, particularly when combined with radiotherapy (chemoradiation) for locally advanced disease, Cisplatin is the most commonly used and foundational chemotherapeutic agent. Cisplatin acts as a potent radiosensitizer, enhancing the effectiveness of radiation therapy in destroying malignant cells. While Paclitaxel (Option A) and Topotecan (Option D) are effective agents used in combination for recurrent or metastatic cervical cancer, Cisplatin remains the gold standard for primary curative treatment. Cyclophosphamide (Option B) is an alkylating agent more frequently used in breast cancer or lymphomas. The standard regimen involves weekly infusions of Cisplatin during the course of external beam radiotherapy. Management must also include monitoring for cisplatin-related toxicities, such as nephrotoxicity and ototoxicity. Platinum-based therapy has significantly improved the survival outcomes for patients with cervical malignancy, which remains a leading cause of female cancer mortality in developing nations due to late presentation
questions.learning: In the management of carcinoma cervix, particularly when combined with radiotherapy (chemoradiation) for locally advanced disease, Cisplatin is the most commonly used and foundational chemotherapeutic agent.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: After examining the left eye shown in the image, what is the most appropriate course of management?
questions.explanation: The clinical image shows a total opaque cornea (corneal scarring or leukoma), likely resulting from the patient's previous eye injury a year ago. This opacity prevents light from reaching the retina, causing total vision loss. The most appropriate management strategy to restore vision is a keratoplasty (corneal transplant), which involves replacing the diseased cornea with a healthy donor cornea. Keratotomy (Option B) is an outdated refractive procedure involving incisions in the cornea. LASIK (Option C) is used for correcting minor refractive errors in a clear cornea and is ineffective for total opacity. DCR (Option D) is a surgery for the tear drainage system and has no impact on corneal clarity. If the posterior segment (retina and optic nerve) is healthy, keratoplasty offers the patient a chance to regain functional vision. Therefore, given the visual evidence of a scarred, opaque cornea, keratoplasty is the definitive therapeutic intervention
questions.learning: The clinical image shows a total opaque cornea (corneal scarring or leukoma), likely resulting from the patient's previous eye injury a year ago. This opacity prevents light from reaching the retina, causing total vision loss.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: What is the type of cartilage present in the histology section given below?
questions.explanation: The histology section shows a homogeneous, glassy (translucent) basophilic matrix with chondrocytes housed in lacunae, often arranged in small isogenous groups. This appearance is characteristic of hyaline cartilage, the most common cartilage type in the body, found in costal cartilages and tracheal rings. Elastic cartilage (Option B) would show a dense network of dark-staining elastic fibers within the matrix, providing flexibility to structures like the auricle. Fibrocartilage (Option D) contains heavy bundles of Type I collagen and fewer chondrocytes, often arranged in rows, and lacks a perichondrium; it is found in intervertebral discs. While articular cartilage (Option C) is a form of hyaline cartilage, it is a specific anatomical designation for cartilage covering joint surfaces; the general tissue type shown is hyaline. Therefore, based on the classic "glassy" matrix and cellular arrangement, hyaline cartilage is the correct histological diagnosis
questions.learning: The histology section shows a homogeneous, glassy (translucent) basophilic matrix with chondrocytes housed in lacunae, often arranged in small isogenous groups.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A 27-year-old male complains of lethargy and weakness while climbing stairs or walking a mile. He is 6 feet tall with a history of previous thromboembolic events and low intellectual. His plasma vitamin profile revealed low levels of folic acid, vitamin B12, and vitamin B6. He was eventually prescribed vitamin B supplements, but there was no improvement. Which of the following is the most likely cause?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Homocysteinemia

The given clinical scenario of a patient with lethargy, marfanoid habitus, intellectual disability and a history of thromboembolic events, along with plasma levels showing low folic acid, B12, and B6, and no improvement after vitamin supplementation, is highly suggestive of Homocystinemia due to classic homocystinuria. Administration of large doses of pyridoxine (vitamin B6) restores the activity of the deficient enzyme in only half of all cases of homocystinuria.

Classic homocystinuria is an inherited inborn error of methionine metabolism caused by a deficiency of the enzyme cystathionine beta-synthetase leading to accumulation of plasma homocysteine. There are two clinical variants: B6 (pyridoxine)-responsive homocystinuria and B6-non-responsive homocystinuria. It is an autosomal recessive condition.

Clinical features:

* Affected children are initially asymptomatic.

* Ectopia lentis (subluxation of the lens) is seen first, after 3 years of age.

* Intellectual disability and psychiatric and behavioral disorders.

* Thromboembolic episodes.

* Skeletal abnormalities resembling those of Marfan syndrome: They are tall and thin with elongated limbs and arachnodactyly (slender fingers).

Elevations of both methionine and homocysteine in body fluids are the diagnostic laboratory findings. The diagnosis is established by molecular analysis of cystathionine β-synthase (CBS) or by assay of the enzyme in cultured fibroblasts, phytohemagglutinin-stimulated lymphocytes, or liver biopsy specimens. Treatment includes restriction of methionine intake and supplementation with cysteine, betaine, vitamins B6, B12, and folate.

Other options:

Option B: Decreased activity of methionine synthase in vitamin B12 deficiency results in the accumulation of methyltetrahydrofolate, which cannot be used, resulting in a folate trap. The folate cycle acts as the link between the functions of folate and vitamin B12, and a deficiency of vitamin B12 can cause a functional deficiency of folate. Hence, vitamin B supplementation should have improved the symptoms.

Option C: Orotic aciduria is characterised by megaloblastic anaemia and a build-up of orotic acid in the urine. The symptoms of lethargy and weakness would be present, but the primary cause is not a vitamin deficiency, and the clinical picture would be more complex, including developmental delays and failure to thrive.

Option D: Marfan syndrome's symptoms primarily affect the skeleton (tall stature, long limbs), eyes, and cardiovascular system (aortic dilation).

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: The Nobel Prize for Physiology and Medicine in 2025 was given for:
options: Discovery of genomes of extinct hominins
Discovery of tissue mRNA and its role in post-transcriptional modification
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Peripheral immune tolerance

The 2025 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine was awarded to Mary E. Brunkow, Fred Ramsdell, and Shimon Sakaguchi for their discoveries concerning peripheral immune tolerance, specifically regulatory T cells that prevent the immune system from attacking the body’s own tissues. This work on immune regulation won the Nobel Prize in Medicine in 2025.

Regulatory T cells (Tregs)

Phenotype:

• CD4⁺ CD25⁺ FOXP3⁺
• Express CTLA-4, IL-2 receptor (high affinity)

Origin:

• Thymic (natural Tregs)
• Peripheral (induced Tregs)

Core function → Peripheral immune tolerance

They suppress autoreactive T cells that escape central tolerance.

Mechanisms of suppression:

1. Cytokine-mediated inhibition

• IL-10, TGF-β

2. Cell–cell contact

• CTLA-4 → inhibits APC costimulation (↓ CD80/86)

3. IL-2 consumption

• “Cytokine sink” → deprives effector T cells

4. Direct suppression of APCs

IPEX syndrome

Full form:

Immune dysregulation, Polyendocrinopathy, Enteropathy, X-linked

Cause:

• Mutation in FOXP3 gene
• → Defective / absent Tregs
• → Loss of peripheral tolerance

Clinical features (classic triad):

1. Severe early-onset diarrhea (autoimmune enteropathy)
2. Type 1 diabetes mellitus
3. Eczema / dermatitis

Other associations:

• Thyroiditis
• Hemolytic anemia
• Thrombocytopenia
• Elevated IgE, eosinophilia

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Identify the drugs marked as A, B, and C.
options: A - Aspirin, B - Eptifibatide, C - Vorapaxar
A - Aspirin, B - Eptifibatide, C - Prasugrel
A - Aspirin, B - Prasugrel, C - Eptifibatide
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. A - Aspirin, B - Eptifibatide, C - Vorapaxar

The drugs marked A, B and C are aspirin, eptifibatide, and vorapaxar, respectively.

Aspirin causes inhibition of cyclooxygenase-1 (COX-1), which would inhibit the formation of thromboxane A2. Thromboxane A2 is an inducer of platelet aggregation and is a potent vasoconstrictor. Hence, inhibition of its formation is responsible for antiplatelet action.

Aspirin is a non-competitive, irreversible inhibitor of the cyclooxygenase (COX) enzyme. It is a nonselective COX inhibitor and inhibits both COX-1 and COX-2.

Abciximab, tirofiban, and eptifibatide act by blocking Gp IIb/IIIa receptors. They are mainly used during percutaneous coronary intervention for acute coronary syndrome. They carry a high risk of bleeding and can cause thrombocytopenia.

Vorapaxar primarily inhibits platelet aggregation caused by thrombin. PAR-1 activation by thrombin contributes to platelet aggregation. Vorapaxar is a competitive antagonist of protease-activated receptor-1 (PAR-1). Vorapaxar is indicated in combination with aspirin and/or clopidogrel to reduce thromboembolic events in patients with MI or peripheral vascular disease.

Prasugrel is an irreversible P2Y12 inhibitor and lasts for the entire lifetime of a platelet.

Prasugrel is a prodrug that is used in patients with acute coronary syndrome who have undergone percutaneous coronary intervention. It reduces the rate of thrombotic cardiovascular events in such patients.
questions.learning: A - Aspirin, B - Eptifibatide, C - Vorapaxar — The drugs marked A, B and C are aspirin, eptifibatide, and vorapaxar, respectively. Aspirin causes inhibition of cyclooxygenase-1 (COX-1), which would inhibit the formation of thromboxane A2.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: An 8-year-old child presented with sudden onset of high-grade fever, seizures, and loss of consciousness. On examination, the child had anaemia, hypoglycemia, and no neurological deficits. What is the probable diagnosis
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Cerebral malaria

This scenario depicts a case of cerebral malaria due to a severe complicated falciparum infection.

Severe complicated malaria is caused by Plasmodium falciparum and is characterized by jaundice, severe anaemia, respiratory distress, bleeding manifestation, cardiovascular collapse, renal failure and cerebral malaria.

Cerebral malaria is diagnosed in the case of P. falciparum parasitemia with altered consciousness. Common features include seizures and hypoglycemia. Retinal haemorrhages, neurological findings like hemiplegia, absent or exaggerated deep tendon reflexes, and a positive Babinski sign can also be seen.

All patients with severe malaria should be treated with intravenous or intramuscular artesunate for at least 24 hours.

Meningitis has fever accompanied by lethargy, irritability, signs of meningeal irritation like the Kernig sign-flexion of the hip 90 degrees with subsequent pain with extension of the leg, and Brudzinski sign-involuntary flexion of the knees and hips after passive flexion of the neck while supine. Increased ICP is suggested by headache, emesis, bulging fontanel or widening of the sutures, oculomotor (anisocoria, ptosis) or abducens nerve paralysis, hypertension with bradycardia, apnea or hyperventilation, stupor, coma, or signs of herniation. A lumbar puncture is essential to obtain CSF for Gram stain and culture, which is the most important step in the diagnosis of meningitis.

questions.text: Laparoscopic tubal sterilization can be done after:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 6 weeks of delivery

Laparoscopic tubal sterilization is generally performed as an interval sterilization, i.e., after the uterus and reproductive organs have returned closer to their normal non-pregnant state.

• Immediate postpartum sterilization → usually performed by mini-laparotomy, not laparoscopy.
• Laparoscopic interval sterilization → typically performed after 6 weeks postpartum.

Therefore, the correct answer is D. 6 weeks of delivery.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Identify the structure labeled in the cross- section image of the trachea displayed below.
questions.explanation: The cross-section of the trachea reveals a tube held open by C-shaped hyaline cartilage rings. The posterior "gap" between the open ends of these cartilage rings is bridged by a band of smooth muscle known as the Trachealis muscle. In the provided image, the arrow specifically points to this posterior muscular band. The Tracheal cartilage (Option B) forms the rigid anterior and lateral framework shown as the outer gray ring. Submucosal glands (Option C) are located deep to the epithelium but would appear as small glandular structures rather than a distinct posterior muscle band. The perichondrium (Option D) is the thin layer of dense connective tissue that surrounds the cartilage itself. The trachealis muscle is functionally important as it allows the esophagus (located directly posterior) to expand during swallowing and can contract to narrow the tracheal lumen to increase airflow velocity during coughing. Therefore, based on its location and structure, it is definitively the trachealis muscle

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 28-year-old woman presented to your OPD with complaints of non-foul-smelling curdy white vaginal discharge accompanied by itching and burning. Microscopic examination revealed gram-positive budding yeast and pseudohyphae. What is the causative organism in this case?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Candida albicans

In the given clinical scenario, symptoms of non-foul smelling curdy white vaginal discharge and budding yeast cells and pseudohyphae on microscopy are suggestive of vulvovaginal candidiasis caused by Candida albicans.

Candida species are yeast-like fungi, which normally inhabit the skin and mucosa. Vulvovaginal candidiasis occurs in conditions that decrease the normal genital microbiota(e.g., long-term antibiotic use), allowing the yeasts to proliferate and produce symptoms.

Candida albicans is an ovoid or spherical budding cell, which produces pseudohyphae both in tissues and in culture. Unlike other species of candida, yeast cells of Candida albicans will begin to form germ tubes after incubation in serum maintained at 37°C for about 90 minutes. This is known as the Reynolds-Braude phenomenon.

The clinical symptoms of vulvovaginal candidiasis include curdy white vaginal discharge, dysuria, and intense itching with vaginal pH <4.5.

Diagnosis includes:

* Wet smear with 10% KOH solution- shows budding yeast cells and pseudohyphae as seen in the image below:

* Gram staining - Gram-positive budding cells with pseudohyphae

* Sabouraud agar culture - Creamy white smooth colonies with yeasty odour.

* Corn meal agar culture - Candida albicans form chlamydospores.

* CHROMagar - Candida albicans colonies appear green.

Treatment involves oral fluconazole 150 mg single dose or local intravaginal application of antifungal agents such as imidazole miconazole, clotrimazole, vaginal pessaries or creams used for 3-6 days is effective.
questions.learning: Candida albicans — In the given clinical scenario, symptoms of non-foul smelling curdy white vaginal discharge and budding yeast cells and pseudohyphae on microscopy are suggestive of vulvovaginal candidiasis caused by Candida albicans.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: What is the indication of this procedure?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Keratoconus

The given image shows the placement of Intacs, which is done for keratoconus.

Keratoconus or conical cornea is a non-inflammatory condition of the axial cornea. Central or paracentral thinning of the cornea and apical protrusion of the anterior cornea are pathognomonic. This is attributed to mucopolysaccharide and collagen tissue synthesis defects.

Clinical features of the condition include defective vision, which develops due to progressive myopia and irregular astigmatism. Light sensitivity and ocular irritation may also be present. Complications include acute hydrops due to rupture of Descemet's membrane.

Slit-lamp examination reveals Fleischer's ring at the base of the cone formed. Deep, vertical stromal striae (Vogt lines) that disappear on external pressure are characteristic. Retinoscopy shows a yawning reflex.

The image below shows Munson's sign i.e. bulging of the lower lid on looking down.

The severity of the condition is graded based on keratometry. Corneal topography is a diagnostic modality with the highest sensitivity for early cases.

Intacs or intracorneal ring segments are useful in moderate cases, due to their flattening effect. Rigid gas permeable contact lenses, corneal collagen cross-linking with riboflavin, and keratoplasty are the other treatment modalities.

Other options:

Option B - Vogt's limbal girdle is a degenerative corneal disease that is more commonly seen in women aged ≥40 years. A white crescentic limbal band can be seen at 9 and/or 3 'o'clock position, more frequently on the nasal side. In type I, a swiss-cheese hole pattern with a clear zone separating it from the scleral margin can be observed. Type II is more common and lacks a clear zone and holes.

Option C - Keratoglobus is a familial disorder, marked by thinning and hemispherical protrusion of the entire cornea. It can be congenital or acquired. Globular protrusion is seen here, in contrast to the conical ectasia seen in keratoconus. Intrastromal ring segments and cross-linking can be used for management.

Option D - Corneal dystrophy is used to describe a group of non-inflammatory conditions, with bilateral opacification of the cornea with no vascularisation. These are divided into epithelial, Bowman layer, stromal, Descemet membrane, and endothelial dystrophies. Most conditions have genetic abnormalities.
questions.learning: Keratoconus — The given image shows the placement of Intacs, which is done for keratoconus. Keratoconus or conical cornea is a non-inflammatory condition of the axial cornea.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Administering benzathine penicillin to a patient with rheumatic heart disease represents which level of prevention?
questions.explanation: Prevention levels are defined by when the intervention occurs in the disease's natural history. Secondary prevention focuses on early diagnosis and prompt treatment to prevent disease recurrence or complications. In a patient who already has Rheumatic Heart Disease (RHD), administering benzathine penicillin is a form of secondary prophylaxis. The goal is to prevent a recurrent Group A Streptococcal infection, which would trigger further immunological damage to the heart valves. Primary prevention (Option B) would be treating an initial streptococcal sore throat in a healthy child to prevent the first onset of rheumatic fever. Primordial prevention (Option A) involves avoiding the emergence of risk factors, like improving living conditions to reduce overcrowding. Tertiary prevention (Option D) involves rehabilitative efforts or surgery, like valve replacement, after permanent disability has occurred. Since the patient already has a diagnosed morbid condition (RHD), the intervention fits the definition of secondary prevention
questions.learning: Prevention levels are defined by when the intervention occurs in the disease's natural history. Secondary prevention focuses on early diagnosis and prompt treatment to prevent disease recurrence or complications.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Renal Electrolytes · Acid Base Electrolyte Disturbances
questions.text: A man goes trekking at a high altitude. Due to the physiological response to decreased atmospheric oxygen tension, which of the following primary acid–base disturbances is most likely to develop in this individual?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Respiratory alkalosis

At high altitude, reduced atmospheric oxygen tension causes hypoxemia, which stimulates peripheral chemoreceptors. At High Altitude

| Parameter | Change

| --------- | ------

| pH | ↑ (alkalosis)

| pCO₂ | ↓

| HCO₃⁻ | Initially normal → later ↓ (renal compensation)

This leads to hyperventilation, resulting in excessive CO₂ washout.

The primary acid–base disturbance is therefore respiratory alkalosis.

| Phase | Mechanism | ABG

| ----- | --------- | ---

| Acute (hours) | Hyperventilation | Respiratory alkalosis

| Chronic (days) | Kidney excretes HCO₃⁻ | Compensated alkalosis

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following does not indicate a syndromic approach treating sexually transmitted infection in males?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Lower abdominal pain

The syndromic approach for STI management in males is based on presenting symptom complexes such as urethral discharge, genital ulcer disease, and inguinal swelling (bubo).

Lower abdominal pain is a syndrome used for females, not males. It usually indicates Pelvic Inflammatory Disease (PID).

Lower abdominal pain is a key syndrome in female STIs, often indicating pelvic inflammatory disease, and is not part of male STI syndromic management.

Syndromic management prioritizes immediate treatment without laboratory confirmation to prevent complications and transmission.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: A student consumed an unknown substance and came with shock and pulmonary edema. The silver nitrate breath test is positive. What is the antidote?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. MgSO4

The patient presents with clinical features suggestive of Aluminium phosphide (ALP) poisoning. Magnesium sulphate is given in ALP poisoning to correct hypomagnesemia, arrhythmias and reduce organ toxicity.

Aluminium phosphide (ALP) is a solid fumigant pesticide, insecticide and rodenticide. ALP has a garlicky odour. Phosphine is a toxic agent. It acts by inhibiting the electron transport resulting from preferential inhibition of cytochrome oxidase. Aluminium phosphite and Aluminium hypophosphite are non-toxic agents. Phosphine is a systemic poison and affects all organs of the body. The presence of HCl in the stomach accelerates this reaction.

Signs and Symptoms include irritation of mucous membranes and acute respiratory distress in mild toxicity. Moderate toxicity produces ataxia, numbness, tremors, muscular incoordination and paralysis. Severe toxicity produces ARDS, cardiac arrhythmias, congestive heart failure, pulmonary oedema, convulsions and coma. Cardiogenic shock is the most common cause of death and is associated with higher mortality(35%- 100%)

There is no specific antidote. Gastric lavage should not be done with warm water as on coming in contact with water, aluminium phosphide releases phosphine and increases the concentration of toxic agent phosphine, so it is done with potassium permanganate and activated charcoal. Magnesium sulphate is used to correct hypomagnesemia, arrhythmias and reduces organ toxicity. Supportive measures to treat acidosis, shock and hemodialysis can be done.

On post-mortem examination, a garlic-like odour is present at the mouth, nostrils and in the gastric contents. Silver nitrate paper test is done to detect phosphine which turns the paper black.

Silver nitrate paper test: This test is used to detect aluminium phosphide poisoning.

• Aluminium phosphide (ALP)is used as a pesticide, insecticide, and rodenticide.
• When ALP comes in contact with moisture, it releases an active component called phosphine.
• When the silver nitrate-impregnated filter paper, comes in contact with phosphine the paper turns black in colour.
• The test is done in two methods:
a. Gastric aspirate: 5 mL of gastric aspirate and 15 mL of water are put in a flask and the mouth of the flask is covered with silver nitrate-impregnated filter paper. The flask is heated at 50°C for 15 to 20 minutes. If the filter paper turns black, it indicates the presence of phosphine.
b. Breath: The patient is asked to breathe in and out through a face mask which is impregnated with silver nitrate. If the face mask turns black, it indicates the presence of phosphine. The breath test is positive only if the patient ingests more than 6 grams of aluminium phosphide.
questions.learning: MgSO4 — The patient presents with clinical features suggestive of Aluminium phosphide (ALP) poisoning. Magnesium sulphate is given in ALP poisoning to correct hypomagnesemia, arrhythmias and reduce organ toxicity.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A 45-year-old patient presents with characteristic facial changes marked by thickened, coarse, and deeply furrowed skin over the cheeks, forehead, and nose. The patient also complains of numbness and weakness in the limbs. Cutaneous examination reveals hypopigmented and erythematous patches with areas of sensory loss. The facial appearance described as “leonine facies” is classically associated with which medical condition?
questions.explanation: The term "Leonine facies" (lion-like face) is a classic clinical description for the facial appearance in advanced Lepromatous Leprosy. It results from the diffuse infiltration of the facial skin with lepra bacilli, leading to coarsening, thickening, and deep furrowing of the skin, often accompanied by the loss of eyebrows (madarosis). The patient's associated symptoms of anesthetic skin patches and peripheral nerve involvement (numbness and weakness) confirm the diagnosis of Hansen's disease. Acromegaly (Option A) involves coarsening of facial features due to bone growth but lacks the specific skin furrows and anesthetic patches. Myasthenia gravis (Option B) involves muscle weakness (ptosis) but no primary skin changes. Bell’s palsy (Option D) is an isolated facial nerve paralysis. Lepromatous leprosy is the multibacillary form of the disease seen in patients with low cell-mediated immunity. Management involves a two-year course of Multi-Drug Therapy (MDT) with rifampicin, dapsone, and clofazimine. Recognizing leonine facies is a fundamental task in identifying late-stage leprosy in endemic regions
