questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient comes with a blood pressure of 160/100 mmHg and left-sided facial paralysis and weakness for 8 hours. Her CT is shown below. What would be your next step?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Observation and monitoring

This patient with sudden onset hemiparesis and a normal CT could have a transient ischemic attack or an ischemic stroke. The next step for this patient would be observation and monitoring.

Non-contrast CT(NCCT) is the imaging modality of choice in patients with acute stroke. CT may appear normal for the first few hours and the infarct may not appear until 24-48 hours. Diffusion-weighted MRI(DWMRI) is more sensitive to detecting early brain infarction.

Initial treatment of acute ischemic stroke includes maintaining the patient's airway, breathing, and circulation. Complications such as hyperglycemia, hypoglycemia, or fever should be treated if present.

Thrombolysis with alteplase is the first-line therapy for acute ischemic stroke and should be initiated within 4.5 hours of symptom onset. Since this patient arrived 8 hours later which is outside of window period, the appropriate management would be observation and monitoring. Endovascular mechanical thrombectomy is done in patients who do not respond to thrombolytic therapy or in whom thrombolysis is contraindicated. Oral aspirin is recommended for the acute treatment of ischemic stroke.

Labetalol, nicardipine, and clevidipine are the first-line anti-hypertensive agents used in the acute phase of stroke. If the patient is to receive thrombolytic therapy, maintain BP ≤185/110mmHg. If not, BP should not be treated acutely unless it is more than 220/120 mmHg. BP should be lowered cautiously by only 15% in the first 24 hours in order to preserve perfusion to the ischemic penumbra.
questions.learning: Observation and monitoring — This patient with sudden onset hemiparesis and a normal CT could have a transient ischemic attack or an ischemic stroke. The next step for this patient would be observation and monitoring.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following best helps assess the quality of healthcare provided?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Ishikawa diagram/ Fish bone diagram

Ishikawa diagram or else better known as the fishbone diagram helps sketch out problems that affect healthcare in a community and thus uses those as pointers to better address them in the community.

The Ishikawa diagram, often known as the fishbone diagram, is employed by teams aiming to comprehend the numerous potential factors that contribute to a quality of care issue. This tool enables teams to concentrate their development endeavours on these identified causes. The utilization of this tool is applicable across several phases of the quality improvement framework, with its primary application commonly observed within the context of root cause analysis.

The fishbone graphic bears a resemblance to the skeletal structure of a fish. To depict the diagram about a quality of care issue, the problem (effect) is encapsulated within a box positioned on the extreme right of the diagram. A vertical line, referred to as the centre line or spine, is then positioned to the left of the box where the problem is documented. Subsequently, diagonal lines resembling fish bones are sketched emanating from the central line, also known as the spine. The diagonal lines depicted in the diagram signify distinct categorizations of the underlying factors contributing to the issue. Supplementary branches may also be delineated from the primary skeletal structure to symbolize underlying factors leading to the causes.

The groupings are typically structured into categories, commonly known as the five Ps (patients/clients, providers, policies, processes and procedures, and place/equipment), the six Ms (machine, method, materials, measurement, man, and Mother Nature), and the four Ss (surroundings, suppliers, systems, and skills). Nevertheless, the groupings need to be tailored to the organization and problem being investigated. The responsibility for ensuring this specificity lies with the quality improvement team. Once the categories have been delineated, the quality improvement team proceeds to partake in a brainstorming session to identify causes that are specific to each respective grouping. The aforementioned procedure persists until the team reaches a point where they are unable to ascertain any further underlying factors.

Other options:

Option A: Logistic regression may be used in some situations where we are not interested in a numerical outcome (like risk, etc) but we want a nominal or categorical one (like death/survival, developing a disease/not developing a disease). Here, the relationship between the variables will not be a linear one as the outcome from survival to death in relationship with the risk factor can change suddenly. Thus these outcomes are represented by 0 and 1.

Option B: A bar graph is a pictorial way of presenting a set of numbers, the magnitudes of which are proportional to the length of the bars in the graph. It can be simple, multiple, or component bar graphs and enable values to be compared visually. They are used to compare a single variable value between several groups.

Option C: A scatter plot is a statistical map used to study the correlation between two given variables. In scatter plots or scatter diagrams, the pattern made by plotted points along the two axes indicates the possible relationship. If the dots cluster along a straight line, then the relationship is linear. If there is no cluster, then there might be no relationship. Below is an example of a scatter diagram without a linear relation.

GI secretions are not static liquids. They get modified along ducts and segments like a river changing chemistry as it flows.

Saliva is the only GI fluid that becomes hypotonic

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 3-year-old child presents with profuse diarrhea and vomiting, along with deeply sunken eyes and complete absence of urine output. On examination, the child is severely dehydrated, lethargic, tachypneic, and hypotensive with a blood pressure of 80/60 mmHg. In this clinical scenario of severe dehydration with shock, which intravenous fluid should be administered for management?
questions.explanation: The child presents with severe dehydration and hypovolemic shock, indicated by lethargy, hypotension (80/60 mmHg), tachypnea, sunken eyes, and anuria. This is a life-threatening condition requiring immediate intravenous fluid resuscitation. In pediatric diarrheal dehydration, Ringer lactate (RL) is the preferred fluid because it is a balanced crystalloid solution containing electrolytes such as sodium, potassium, calcium, and chloride. Importantly, the lactate component is metabolized to bicarbonate, helping to correct metabolic acidosis, which commonly occurs due to severe diarrhea. The addition of 5% dextrose is beneficial in children to prevent hypoglycemia and provide energy, especially when oral intake is compromised. Why other options are wrong: (A) ORS → Not suitable in shock or severe dehydration (C) Normal saline → Effective but may cause hyperchloremic acidosis; less physiological than RL (D) Dextrose → Does not restore intravascular volume
questions.learning: The child presents with severe dehydration and hypovolemic shock, indicated by lethargy, hypotension (80/60 mmHg), tachypnea, sunken eyes, and anuria.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following cerclage procedures would be done in a nonpregnant female through a transabdominal approach?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Laparoscopic cerclage

The cerclage procedure performed on nonpregnant females through a transabdominal approach is laparoscopic cerclage. Abdominal cerclage is conducted through either laparotomy or laparoscopy and is recommended in cases where the cervix is hypoplastic or in instances of prior failed vaginal cerclage.

Cerclage is usually done for cervical incompetence, defined as the inability to maintain pregnancy till term due to a functional or structural defect of the cervix. Cervical incompetence is diagnosed by clinical examination and ultrasonography showing the presence of short cervix (<25 mm) with or without funneling of internal os.

Prophylactic cerclage is done around 14 weeks of pregnancy or 2 weeks earlier than the previous fetal loss. Rescue or emergency cerclage is done anytime within 24 weeks of gestation. It should only be done when there is bulging of membranes through the dilated cervix.

Commonly used types of cervical cerclage during pregnancy:

• McDonald's procedure - non-absorbable (mersilene) material placed as a purse-string suture at the level of the internal os
• Modified Shirodkar's procedure - non-absorbable (mersilene) tape passed subcutaneously through a transverse anterior incision and tied posteriorly

Removal of cerclage should be done by 37 weeks of gestation. It can be removed earlier in case of preterm labor or if signs of abortion are seen.

Other options:

Option A: Lash and Lash cerclage is the first described treatment for cervical incompetence, involving the placement of stitches in the cervix through the transvaginal approach. It is now replaced by procedures such as McDonald's and Shirodkar's.

Option B: Benson und Durfee cerclage is the technique of placement of cervical cerclage through a transabdominal approach by a laparotomy. It is preferred in pregnant females when the vaginal approach is either not possible or very difficult.

Option C: Wurms cerclage is a type of cerclage used in pregnancy where monofilament material (Prolene) is used to place two higher circumferential sutures through the cervix without the need for bladder dissection.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: The patient is admitted with low urine output, and lab reports show BUN: 140 mg/dL, serum creatinine: 8.0 mg/dL, and 2+ protein on urine dipstick. Which of the following is most useful for distinguishing acute kidney injury (AKI) from chronic kidney disease (CKD)? BUN-Blood urea nitrogen
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Creatinine clearance

In a patient admitted with low urine output, BUN of 140 mg/dL, serum creatinine of 8.0 mg/dL, and 2+ protein on urine dipstick, the most useful criterion for differentiating acute kidney injury (AKI) from chronic kidney disease (CKD) is creatinine clearance.

Acute kidney injury (AKI) is defined as an increase in serum creatinine by 1.5 times of baseline value over 7 days.

Acute kidney injury is defined as an abrupt (within hours) decrease in kidney function, which encompasses both injury (structural damage) and impairment (loss of function). It is characterized by abrupt deterioration in kidney function, manifested by an increase in serum creatinine level with or without reduced urine output.

AKI is defined as any of the following:

* Increase in serum creatinine to ≥1.5 times baseline (50% higher), which is known or presumed to have occurred within the prior 7 days.

* Increase in serum creatinine by ≥0.3 mg/dL from baseline within 48 hours.

* Urine volume of <0.5 ml/kg/h for 6 hours.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: What is the most commonly affected organ in an air blast due to shockwave?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Lung

Lungs are considered to be severely damaged organs in the air due to variations in density between the alveolar walls and the contained air.

A blast causes the most damage at an interface between tissues in contact with the atmosphere, which is why the lung usually suffers the most severe damage.

Blast injury is a complex type of physical trauma resulting from direct or indirect exposure to an explosion. Primary blast injuries result from the rapid overpressure or shock waves produced by an explosion. These injuries result from the dramatic changes in barometric pressure projecting outwards from the point of detonation. They predominantly cause damage to air-filled hollow organs of the body from rapid pressure change (barotrauma). This includes the middle ear, lungs, and GIT.

The most sensitive and most frequently injured hollow organs are the tympanic membranes > lungs.

Blast damage to the lungs is the most common cause of life-threatening injury following an explosion.

Solid organs are the most resistant to blast injuries as the parenchymal disruption requires very high levels of overpressure. The liver is the least vulnerable to blast wave (primary blast) injury.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: A patient with severe Maxillofacial trauma after a road traffic accident presented with SpO2 80% at room air. In a situation where the patient cannot be intubated and cannot be ventilated (CICV), what is the next most appropriate immediate step in management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Perform cricothyroidotomy

In the above clinical scenario of an RTA patient with severe maxillofacial trauma, where endotracheal intubation (Cannot Intubate, Cannot Ventilate) has failed to secure the airway, an alternate airway in the form of a surgical airway is indicated. Thus, performing a needle cricothyroidotomy is the next best step in the management of this patient.

This should be followed by percutaneous transtracheal oxygenation to provide temporary ventilation. In conditions that obstruct the airway, like edema of the glottis, laryngeal fracture, or severe oropharyngeal hemorrhage, a surgical airway is indicated.

Needle cricothyroidotomy involves inserting a needle through the cricothyroid membrane to provide short-term ventilation till a definitive airway can be achieved. A Y-connector is attached, and oxygenation is provided at 15 L/min.

Surgical cricothyroidotomy involves inserting an endotracheal or tracheostomy tube after making a transverse incision over the cricothyroid membrane. An emergency surgical airway is preferred over tracheostomy as it is easier to perform, is associated with less bleeding, and can be done quickly.

Other options:

Option A: Nasopharyngeal intubation is contraindicated in cases of severe maxillofacial trauma because of risk of basilar skull fracture (risk of injury to brain by putting the tube) and distorted anatomy making it unsafe or impossible to perform.

Option B: Supraglottic airway devices are used in difficult airway management but in case of severe macillofacial trauma, it is not preferred as it cannot bypass the distorted anatomy or complete obstruction of upper airway.

Option D: Administer Succinylcholine and Retry Intubation in a case of a patient that cannot be intubated and cannot be ventilated (CICV) is very dangerous and ineffective as repeating might do more harm by increasing airway trauma, edema and worsened oxygenation.
questions.learning: Perform cricothyroidotomy — In the above clinical scenario of an RTA patient with severe maxillofacial trauma, where endotracheal intubation (Cannot Intubate, Cannot Ventilate) has failed to secure the airway, an alternate airway in the form of a surgical…

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A farmer presents with a wart-like lesion on the foot, and the diagnosis is supported by the histopathological image provided. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Chromoblastomycosis is a chronic subcutaneous fungal infection typically seen in farmers or laborers who sustain minor injuries while working barefoot. The infection presents as slow-growing, wart-like (verrucous) or cauliflower-like plaques. The pathognomonic diagnostic finding on histopathology is the presence of sclerotic bodies (also known as Medlar bodies or 'copper-penny' bodies). These are thick-walled, dark brown pigmented fungal cells that divide by septation rather than budding. Sporotrichosis (Option A) would show a characteristic lymphocutaneous spread pattern. Mycetoma (Option B) presents with a triad of swelling, sinuses, and discharge of granules. Phaeohyphomycosis (Option D) involves pigmented fungi but presents as abscesses or cysts without the specific Medlar bodies. Therefore, based on the verrucous lesion and the provided histopathology showing copper-penny bodies, chromoblastomycosis is the definitive diagnosis
questions.learning: Chromoblastomycosis is a chronic subcutaneous fungal infection typically seen in farmers or laborers who sustain minor injuries while working barefoot.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A neurologist evaluates a patient with rapidly progressive dementia, myoclonus, and periodic sharp-wave complexes on EEG. MRI shows hyperintensity in the caudate nucleus and putamen, raising suspicion for Creutzfeldt–Jakob disease (CJD). Which of the following best describes the causative agent?
options: An infectious protein lacking nucleic acid
A hybrid infectious particle composed of bacterial and viral components
An infectious agent containing abundant DNA responsible for replication
An organism that can be propagated on routine cell-free culture media
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. An infectious protein lacking nucleic acid

Prions are proteinaceous infectious particles composed of an abnormal isoform (PrPS) of the normal cellular prion protein (PrPC).

Key characteristics:

• No DNA or RNA
• Infectious despite lacking nucleic acid
• Propagate by inducing misfolding of normal prion proteins
• Resistant to heat, proteases, formalin, UV radiation, and standard sterilization methods
• Cause transmissible spongiform encephalopathies (TSEs)

Major Prion Diseases:

• Creutzfeldt–Jakob disease (CJD)
• Variant CJD
• Kuru
• Gerstmann–Sträussler–Scheinker syndrome
• Fatal familial insomnia
• Bovine spongiform encephalopathy ("Mad cow disease")
questions.learning: An infectious protein lacking nucleic acid Prions are proteinaceous infectious particles composed of an abnormal isoform (PrPS) of the normal cellular prion protein (PrPC).

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: 1-year-old boy is brought to the clinic for mass in the neck. The parents noticed a small area of nontender swelling in the neck a month ago. Over the last few days, it has enlarged and become painful, and the patient has a fever. Examination shows a mobile, tender, fluctuant, and warm mass approximately 2 cm in diameter that is located at the right mandibular angle. There is purulent drainage from the skin surface just anterior to the right sternocleidomastoid muscle. This patient's clinical findings are most likely due to which of the following embryologic processes?
options: Failed descent of a pharyngeal pouch structure
Failed neural crest migration into a pharyngeal arch
Inadequate fusion of the mandibular prominences
Incomplete obliteration of a pharyngeal groove
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Incomplete obliteration of a pharyngeal groove

A branchial cleft (pharyngeal groove) cyst or fistula occurs due to failure of obliteration of the second pharyngeal cleft during embryologic development. These lesions commonly present in children or young adults as a lateral neck swelling along the anterior border of the sternocleidomastoid muscle. Typical features:

• Located anterior to the sternocleidomastoid muscle
• Mobile, fluctuant neck mass
• May become painful, infected, and drain purulent material
• Often appears near the mandibular angle

Normally, the second pharyngeal arch overgrows the third and fourth arches, forming the cervical sinus, which later obliterates.

Failure of this obliteration leads to branchial cleft cysts, sinuses, or fistulas.
questions.learning: Incomplete obliteration of a pharyngeal groove — A branchial cleft (pharyngeal groove) cyst or fistula occurs due to failure of obliteration of the second pharyngeal cleft during embryologic development.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A 38-year-old man with depressive symptoms is concerned about sexual dysfunction as a side effect of treatment. Which antidepressant would be most appropriate given this concern?
questions.explanation: Sexual dysfunction is a very common and distressing side effect of most standard antidepressants, particularly SSRIs and SNRIs. For a patient prioritizing the avoidance of these side effects, Bupropion is the recommended choice. Bupropion is an atypical antidepressant that works by inhibiting the reuptake of Norepinephrine and Dopamine (NDRI). Unlike SSRIs, it has no significant effect on the serotonin system, which is the primary pathway responsible for antidepressant-induced sexual dysfunction. In fact, bupropion is often used as an adjunct to reverse SSRI-induced sexual issues. Escitalopram (Option B) and Fluoxetine (Option D) are SSRIs, and Venlafaxine (Option C) is an SNRI; all three have high rates of sexual side effects like decreased libido or delayed orgasm. Bupropion is also useful for smoking cessation and weight loss but is strictly contraindicated in patients with a history of seizures or eating disorders. This "sexual-sparing" property makes it a valuable alternative for maintaining treatment adherence in young, sexually active patients
questions.learning: Sexual dysfunction is a very common and distressing side effect of most standard antidepressants, particularly SSRIs and SNRIs. For a patient prioritizing the avoidance of these side effects, Bupropion is the recommended choice.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: In a patient with severe maxillofacial trauma following a road traffic accident, which airway management technique is most appropriate as the initial step?
questions.explanation: In severe maxillofacial trauma, the airway is often compromised due to bleeding, edema, fractured bones, and distorted anatomy. In such situations, tracheostomy is the safest and most appropriate initial airway management, as it bypasses the upper airway entirely. This avoids the risk of failed intubation and prevents further injury. It provides a definitive airway quickly, especially when conventional routes are difficult or dangerous. Why other options are incorrect: (B) Orotracheal intubation: Although usually first-line, it may be difficult or impossible here due to distorted anatomy and can worsen injuries or dislodge clots. (C) Nasotracheal intubation:Contraindicated in maxillofacial trauma, especially with possible basilar skull fracture, as the tube may enter the cranial cavity. (D) Oxygen therapy: Provides only supportive care and does not secure the airway, which is critical in severe trauma
questions.learning: In severe maxillofacial trauma, the airway is often compromised due to bleeding, edema, fractured bones, and distorted anatomy. In such situations, tracheostomy is the safest and most appropriate initial airway management, as it bypasses the upper airway…

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Four weeks after cataract surgery, a patient presents with pain, decreased vision, and redness in the eye. Examination reveals cells in the anterior chamber and vitreous haze. Identify the diagnosis and the associated microorganism:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Endophthalmitis; Staph epidermidis

Postoperative endophthalmitis is an acute, sight-threatening intraocular infection occurring after procedures like cataract surgery, presenting with pain, decreased vision, redness, anterior chamber reaction, and vitreous haze.

• Most common organism for early endophtalmitis (<6 weeks) : Staphylococcus epidermidis (normal conjunctival flora); P.acnes >6 weeks
• Infection involves both anterior chamber and vitreous → differentiates from sterile inflammation

Clinical differentiation:

• Endophthalmitis:

• Painful
• Severe vision loss
• Vitreous involvement (haze)

• TASS (toxic anterior segment syndrome):

• Sterile, painless
• Limited to anterior segment only

Why not other options:

• Posterior capsular opacification: Painless, late complication
• Sympathetic ophthalmia: Bilateral autoimmune condition
questions.learning: Endophthalmitis; Staph epidermidis Postoperative endophthalmitis is an acute, sight-threatening intraocular infection occurring after procedures like cataract surgery, presenting with pain, decreased vision, redness, anterior chamber reaction, and vitreous…

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Doxycycline is a commonly used antibiotic. How does it function in the body?
questions.explanation: Doxycycline belongs to the tetracycline class of antibiotics. Its primary mechanism of action is acting as a protein synthesis inhibitor. It functions by binding reversibly to the 30S ribosomal subunit of the bacteria. This binding prevents the attachment of aminoacyl-tRNA to the mRNA-ribosome complex, effectively halting the addition of new amino acids to the growing polypeptide chain. Option A describes beta-lactams and vancomycin. Option C describes fluoroquinolones. Option D describes mupirocin. Doxycycline's ability to inhibit protein synthesis is bacteriostatic and effective against a wide range of gram-positive, gram-negative, and atypical organisms (like Rickettsia and Chlamydia). Because it specifically targets the prokaryotic 30S ribosome, it is a definitive example of a translation inhibitor
questions.learning: Doxycycline belongs to the tetracycline class of antibiotics. Its primary mechanism of action is acting as a protein synthesis inhibitor.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Researchers analyzed past records of 46 mothers who delivered infants with congenital anomalies and found that 41 had been exposed to thalidomide during early pregnancy. Based on this approach, what type of epidemiological study was conducted?
questions.explanation: In this study, researchers analyzed past records of 46 mothers, identifying their exposure to thalidomide during early pregnancy and then examining outcomes (congenital anomalies). Although it looks backward, the key feature is that researchers traced from exposure → outcome using historical records, which defines a retrospective cohort study. The cohort was defined by thalidomide exposure and outcomes were assessed from existing past records, making it retrospective in nature. Why other options are wrong: (A) Prospective cohort study is incorrect because prospective cohort studies follow participants forward in time from exposure to outcome. Here data was collected from existing past records, not followed prospectively. (C) Case-control study is incorrect because case-control studies select participants based on outcome first, then look back at exposure. Here selection was based on exposure to thalidomide, not on presence of congenital anomalies as the starting point. (D) Descriptive study is incorrect because descriptive studies only describe disease distribution without analyzing specific exposure-outcome relationships or testing etiological hypotheses
questions.learning: In this study, researchers analyzed past records of 46 mothers, identifying their exposure to thalidomide during early pregnancy and then examining outcomes (congenital anomalies).

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which hormone is produced from the layer marked in the given image?
questions.explanation: The marked region in the image represents the adrenal medulla, which is the inner part of the adrenal gland. Histologically, it appears darker and more vascular compared to the cortex and contains chromaffin cells arranged in clusters. These cells are responsible for secreting catecholamines, mainly epinephrine (adrenaline) and norepinephrine. Epinephrine plays a major role in the “fight or flight” response, increasing heart rate, blood pressure, and blood glucose levels during stress. Why other options are incorrect: (A) Androgen: Produced in the zona reticularis of the adrenal cortex, not in the medulla. (B) Cortisol: A glucocorticoid secreted by the zona fasciculata of the cortex. (C) Corticosterone: A mineralocorticoid precursor produced mainly in the zona glomerulosa of the cortex. Since the marked layer is medulla, the hormone produced is epinephrine
questions.learning: The marked region in the image represents the adrenal medulla, which is the inner part of the adrenal gland. Histologically, it appears darker and more vascular compared to the cortex and contains chromaffin cells arranged in clusters.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Causes for expanding blind spot are all except __________
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Hypoplasia of optic disc

Optic disc hypoplasia does not cause enlargement of the blind spot.

The physiological blind spot is an area of absolute scotoma in the visual field, seen in the region of optic disc. It is due to the absence of photoreceptors (rods and cones) in that region. Enlarged blind spot is seen in primary open-angle glaucoma (POAG) (Option A), papilledema (Option C), medullated nerve fibers (Option D), optic disc drusen, coloboma of optic disc and
myopic disc with a crescent.

Optic nerve hypoplasia is the most common congenital optic disc anomaly. There is underdevelopment of the optic disc in the disease and it typically presents with a small disc that is surrounded by a yellowish pigmented ring, called the 'double ring sign'.

Option A: In primary open-angle glaucoma(POAG), the optic disc enlargement is seen secondary to increased intra-ocular pressure (IOP) in the eye.

Option C: Papilledema is a passive disc swelling seen with raised intracranial pressure. The blind spot is enlarged due to the edema of the optic disc.

Option D: Medullated or opaque nerve fibers are the abnormal myelination of nerve fibers of the retina. Normally, optic nerve myelination stops at the level of lamina cribrosa. If the myelination continues beyond the optic disc it leads to the expansion of the blind spot.  On ophthalmoscopic examination, these are seen as a whitish patch with feathery margins.
questions.learning: Hypoplasia of optic disc Optic disc hypoplasia does not cause enlargement of the blind spot. The physiological blind spot is an area of absolute scotoma in the visual field, seen in the region of optic disc.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Corticospinal tract crosses at ?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Lower medulla

The corticospinal tract crosses over at lower medulla.

Corticospinal fibres have the following course as shown below:

Cerbral cortex → Corona radiata → Posterior limb of the internal capsule → Crus cerebri of cerebral peduncles → Ventral part of the pons → Pyramids of medulla oblongata (most fibers decussate here) → Anterior and lateral white columns of the spinal cord (as anterior and lateral corticospinal tracts, respectively)

Note:

Most fibers (80% fibers) decussate (cross) in the medullary pyramids in the lower medulla and descend in the lateral white matter of the spinal cord to form the lateral corticospinal tract. They control the movements of the contralateral limbs.

The remaining 20% make up the ventral corticospinal tract. These fibers remain uncrossed until reaching the spinal cord where axons terminate bilaterally on spinal interneurons antecedent to motor neurons. These fibers control the movements of the axial musculature.
questions.learning: Lower medulla — The corticospinal tract crosses over at lower medulla. Corticospinal fibres have the following course as shown below: Cerbral cortex → Corona radiata → Posterior limb of the internal capsule → Crus cerebri of cerebral peduncles → Ventral…

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 16-year-old patient has pellagra-like skin eruptions that appear every spring and have recurred for the past 5 years. Laboratory tests show normal 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid (5- HIAA) levels, elevated aminoaciduria, and normal urinary indole levels. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Hartnup disorder is an autosomal recessive metabolic condition characterized by a defect in the transport of neutral amino acids, particularly tryptophan, in the intestines and kidneys. Since tryptophan is a precursor for niacin (Vitamin B3), its deficiency results in pellagra-like skin eruptions that are often photosensitive and worsen in the spring. The key laboratory finding is "high aminoaciduria" (neutral amino acids in urine) without high indole levels. Carcinoid tumor (Option A) can cause pellagra-like symptoms by "diverting" tryptophan to serotonin, but it would show elevated urinary 5-HIAA levels. Nutritional pellagra (Option B) is caused by a dietary lack of niacin but would not show the specific pattern of renal aminoaciduria seen here. Essential fructosuria (Option D) is a benign metabolic defect in fructose metabolism unrelated to skin findings. Treatment involves a high-protein diet and oral nicotinamide supplementation
questions.learning: Hartnup disorder is an autosomal recessive metabolic condition characterized by a defect in the transport of neutral amino acids, particularly tryptophan, in the intestines and kidneys.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: What is the drug used for estrogen dependant breast cancer?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Tamoxifen

Tamoxifen is a selective estrogen receptor modulator (SERM) that is mainly used for estrogen receptor-positive breast cancers in pre-menopausal women.

It exhibits selective agonistic and antagonistic activity for ER receptors (ERα and ERβ):

• Agonist activity at the uterus, bone, liver, and pituitary
• Antagonist activity in breast and blood vessels

Uses:

• Part of the primary treatment regimen for estrogen receptor-positive (ER+) breast cancers in pre-menopausal women
• Adjuvant therapy after breast conservative surgery to prevent a recurrence
• Tamoxifen also is effective (a 40%–50% reduction in tumor incidence) in preventing ER+ breast cancer in women at increased risk.

Adverse effects:

• Vasomotor symptoms (hot flashes) and sweating
• Endometrial cancer
• Increased risk of thromboembolic events
• Fatty liver disease
questions.learning: Tamoxifen Tamoxifen is a selective estrogen receptor modulator (SERM) that is mainly used for estrogen receptor-positive breast cancers in pre-menopausal women.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: The procedure performed with the help of instrument given below is?
questions.explanation: The instrument shown is a specialized cannula or suction curette used for uterine aspiration, such as a Pipelle or Manual Vacuum Aspiration (MVA) tool. This device is primarily used for endometrial sampling (Option D), allowing clinicians to obtain a tissue biopsy from the uterine lining in an office setting. This is essential for investigating postmenopausal bleeding or suspected hyperplasia. Hysterosalpingography (Option A) is a radiologic procedure using contrast media to visualize the fallopian tubes. Dilatation and curettage (D&C, Option B) is a more invasive surgical procedure involving mechanical dilation and metal curettes. Cervical sampling (Option C), like a Pap smear or colposcopic biopsy, targets the cervix using different tools like brushes or punch forceps. While MVA can be used for therapeutic evacuation, its diagnostic role is endometrial sampling. The minimally invasive nature of the pictured tool makes it the gold standard for initial endometrial evaluation
questions.learning: The instrument shown is a specialized cannula or suction curette used for uterine aspiration, such as a Pipelle or Manual Vacuum Aspiration (MVA) tool.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A patient presents to the OPD with the visual field defect shown in the image. Based on this visual field pattern, what is the most likely site of the lesion?
questions.explanation: The visual field plot shows a classic Bitemporal Hemianopia, which is the loss of the temporal (outer) visual fields in both the right and left eyes. This specific pattern of vision loss is the hallmark of a lesion at the optic chiasm. In the chiasm, the nerve fibers from the nasal retinas (which carry information from the temporal visual fields) cross over to the contralateral side. A compressive lesion here, most commonly a pituitary adenoma, craniopharyngioma, or meningioma, disrupts these decussating fibers while sparing the uncrossed temporal retinal fibers. A lesion of the optic tract (Option B) or optic radiations (Option D) would result in a contralateral homonymous hemianopia (loss of the same side of the visual field in both eyes). A lesion in the occipital cortex (Option C) typically causes a homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing. Therefore, the unique "tunnel vision" or loss of peripheral vision on both sides is localizing specifically to the midline optic chiasma, necessitating neuroimaging of the sellar region
questions.learning: The visual field plot shows a classic Bitemporal Hemianopia, which is the loss of the temporal (outer) visual fields in both the right and left eyes. This specific pattern of vision loss is the hallmark of a lesion at the optic chiasm.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: A 20-year-old man is brought for psychiatric evaluation due to intellectual disability, with an IQ of 45. He has a long face, large ears, and macroorchidism, along with a cardiac murmur on examination and a paternal family history of intellectual impairment. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The clinical combination of intellectual disability, a long face with large ears, and macro-orchidism (large testes) is pathognomonic for Fragile X syndrome (Option C) . This is the most common inherited cause of intellectual disability and is caused by a CGG triplet repeat expansion in the FMR1 gene. The "cardiac murmur" mentioned likely represents mitral valve prolapse, which is common in these patients. William syndrome (Option D) features a "pixie-like" face, hypercalcemia, and great social skills ("cocktail party personality"). Rett syndrome (Option B) is an X-linked disorder seen almost exclusively in females, characterized by loss of hand skills and purposeful movements. Cushing's syndrome (Option A) involves cortisol excess with different physical findings like a buffalo hump and striae. Because the classic triad of facial features, macro-orchidism, and moderate intellectual disability is present, Fragile X is the definitive diagnosis
questions.learning: The clinical combination of intellectual disability, a long face with large ears, and macro-orchidism (large testes) is pathognomonic for Fragile X syndrome (Option C) .

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: An 18-year-old girl presented with seizures and her radiological image is as given below. Knowing that the MR spectroscopy of the lesion showed elevated choline, alanine, and lactate, what is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Neurocysticercosis

The given radiological image and history of seizures suggests a diagnosis of neurocysticercosis.

Neurocysticercosis presents with seizures, hydrocephalus, raised ICP, and may even cause signs of chronic meningitis. The given image shows multilobulated cystic lesions (with scolex) in the subarachnoid space, typical parenchymal brain calcifications are suggestive of neurocysticercosis caused by T. solium (Cysticercosis cellulose).

• Cyst with a dot sign: seen in both MRI and CT and the dot represents the eccentrically placed scolex of the parasite.

MR Spectroscopy features of neurocysticercosis include elevated lactate, alanine, succinate, and choline levels and reduced levels of N -acetyl aspartate and creatine. Escobar's pathological stages describe 4 stages - vesicular, colloidal vesicular, granular nodular, and nodular calcified.

Other options

• Solid or ring enhancement is typical in the post-contrast images of tuberculoma. A central focus of calcification with a ring of peripheral enhancement (the "target sign") is also described in tuberculosis but is not specific to it.
• Cerebral toxoplasmosis appears as multiple hypodense regions predominantly in the basal ganglia and at the corticomedullary junction. It can be associated with ring enhancing lesions as well.
• Cryptococcosis is usually associated with normal scans but may show cerebral atrophy, hydrocephalus or mass lesions as well.
questions.learning: Neurocysticercosis — The given radiological image and history of seizures suggests a diagnosis of neurocysticercosis. Neurocysticercosis presents with seizures, hydrocephalus, raised ICP, and may even cause signs of chronic meningitis.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: A 23-year-old man with hypertension presents at the hospital. His blood pressure upon examination is 150/90, and he is afebrile. Further evaluation reveals normal serum renin levels, leading to a diagnosis of Conn's syndrome. All of the following conditions would be seen in Conn's syndrome except?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Metabolic acidosis

Conn's syndrome presents with Metabolic alkalosis.

Patients with Conn's syndrome have primary hyperaldosteronism which results in a modest increase in plasma sodium, usually less than 4-6 mEq/L over the normal range, hypokalemia (due to increased K+excretion), hypertension (due to slight increase in ECF volume), metabolic alkalosis because increased hydrogen ions are secreted in the urine.

Excess secretion of aldosterone causes only a modest increase in plasma sodium. When sodium gets reabsorbed, water also accompanies it, resulting in plasma sodium remaining fairly normal.

Primary hyperaldosteronism is due to autonomous overproduction of aldosterone with resultant suppression of RAAS. It can occur due to adrenal hyperplasia, adenoma, or carcinoma. It is associated with the following features:

* Hypertension (most common)

* Hypokalemia

* Metabolic alkalosis

* Polyuria (due to ANP)

* Polydipsia (due to polyuria)

* Muscle weakness

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following techniques is based on behavioral sciences?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Management by objective

Management by objective is based on behavioral sciences.

Management methods used in health programmes are either quantitative or based on behavioral sciences.

Methods based on behavioral sciences include:

• Organizational design
• Personnel management
• Communication
• Information systems
• Management by objectives (MBO)

Quantitative methods include:

• Cost-benefit analysis
• Cost-effective analysis
• Cost–accounting
• Input-output analysis
• Model
• Systems analysis
• Network analysis - includes programme evaluation and review technique (PERT) and critical path method (CPM)
• Planning–programming–budgeting system (PPBS)
• Work sampling
• Decision making
questions.learning: Management by objective Management by objective is based on behavioral sciences. Management methods used in health programmes are either quantitative or based on behavioral sciences.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Among the following options, what is the cause of sensorineural hearing loss?
questions.explanation: Hearing loss is divided into conductive and sensorineural types. Sensorineural hearing loss (SNHL) results from damage to the inner ear (cochlea) or the auditory nerve. Labyrinthitis (Option A) is an inflammation of the inner ear that affects both the vestibular and auditory systems, typically resulting in vertigo and SNHL. Otosclerosis (Option B) is a bone remodeling disorder of the middle ear that primarily causes conductive hearing loss (CHL) by fixing the stapes footplate, although it can have a sensorineural component in later stages. Ear wax (Option C) and Chronic Suppurative Otitis Media (Option D) are classic causes of conductive hearing loss because they physically obstruct the sound transmission pathway through the external or middle ear. Therefore, labyrinthitis is the specific condition listed that primarily impacts the neural sensory structures of the inner ear
questions.learning: Hearing loss is divided into conductive and sensorineural types. Sensorineural hearing loss (SNHL) results from damage to the inner ear (cochlea) or the auditory nerve.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text:
A 75-year-old man with prostate carcinoma presents to you with a PSA of 9 ng/mL with a small tumor focus. His Gleason score is 6. What will be your most likely management?

PSA- Prostate-specific antigen
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Active surveillance

The given clinical vignette of a 75-year-old man, with a low PSA (<10 ng/ml), Gleason score of 6, and a small tumor focus point to a diagnosis of low-risk prostatic carcinoma. The most likely management for this patient would be active surveillance only.

Active surveillance is done when there is:

• Gleason score of 6
• Early-stage disease (T1c)
• Small volume disease on biopsy
• Low PSA (< 10 ng/ml)

Active surveillance protocols include a digital rectal examination and PSA monitoring every 3 to 6 months, with TRUS-guided prostate biopsies every 1 to 3 years.

Gleason grading system evaluates the abnormalities in the glandular architecture of the prostate. It is based on a scale of 1 to 5, with 1 being the most differentiated grade and 5 being the least differentiated. The grades are added to give the Gleason score.

The classification and management of carcinoma prostate are outlined below:

Grade
Treatment

Low Risk

Radical prostatectomy (<70 years),

Active surveillance (>70 years)

Intermediate Risk

Radical prostatectomy and/or Radical radiotherapy(EBRT) (<70 years)

Active surveillance +/- TURP and hormone therapy (>70 years)

High Risk

Early androgen ablation + Radiotherapy + Surgical treatment (< 70 years)

Metastatic disease

Systemic chemotherapy with palliative treatment ( <70 years)

Androgen ablation therapy and palliative treatment for symptomatic patients

EBRT: External beam radiation therapy, TURP: Transurethral resection of the prostate
questions.learning: Active surveillance — The given clinical vignette of a 75-year-old man, with a low PSA ( 70 years) Intermediate Risk Radical prostatectomy and/or Radical radiotherapy(EBRT) ( 70 years) High Risk Early androgen ablation + Radiotherapy + Surgical treatment…

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A female patient comes with complaints of swelling and pain in her great toe. Her uric acid level is found to be high. A drug which reduces uric acid levels is prescribed. Which of the following enzyme should the drug inhibit?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Xanthine oxidase

Allopurinol is a purine antimetabolite and an inhibitor of the xanthine oxidase enzyme.

Allopurinol is used to treat hyperuricemia in patients with gout. It also prevents the occurrence of gout in those with haematological malignancies about to undergo chemotherapy.

Allopurinol and its primary metabolite, oxypurinol (alloxanthine), reduce urate production by inhibiting xanthine oxidase. This prevents the conversion of hypoxanthine to xanthine, and xanthine to uric acid, thereby reducing plasma uric acid levels. Allopurinol is also a substrate for xanthine oxidase.

Febuxostat is a nonpurine inhibitor of uric acid synthesis. It is not an analogue of hypoxanthine. It acts by inhibiting the enzyme xanthine oxidase and it is indicated in gout management.

Other options:

Option A: Acetohydroxamic acid is used for the treatment of struvite stone. It is a urease inhibitor (urease generates ammonia from urea that elevates the pH of the urine that can lead to formation of triple phosphate stones).

Option B: Alkaptonuria is a disorder of tyrosine metabolism, that develops due to the defect in homogentisate oxidase, which oxidizes homogentisate to maleylacetoacetate.

Option C: Menkes disease is caused by defective lysyl oxidase enzyme.

Pearl PF0240: Some Examples of Suicidal Inhibitors

Suicidal Inhibitors

Enzyme

Allopurinol

Xanthine oxidase

Aspirin

Cyclooxygenase

5-Flurouracil

questions.learning: Xanthine oxidase Allopurinol is a purine antimetabolite and an inhibitor of the xanthine oxidase enzyme. Allopurinol is used to treat hyperuricemia in patients with gout.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: By the action of the enzyme aromatase, testosterone is converted into estradiol (an estrogen).
questions.explanation: The enzyme aromatase (part of the cytochrome P450 superfamily) plays a pivotal role in steroidogenesis by catalyzing the "aromatization" of androgens into estrogens. Specifically, it transforms testosterone into estradiol (Option B) and androstenedione into estrone. This process occurs in various tissues, including the granulosa cells of the ovary, adipose tissue, and the brain. Option A refers to a dihydrotestosterone-like metabolite, but it is not the product of aromatase. Cortisol (Option C) and Cortisone (Option D) are glucocorticoids synthesized in the adrenal cortex through different enzymatic pathways involving 21-hydroxylase and 11-beta-hydroxylase. Understanding the aromatase pathway is clinically significant in both reproductive health and oncology, as aromatase inhibitors are used to treat hormone-receptor-positive breast cancer by reducing the peripheral production of estradiol. Therefore, estradiol is the definitive metabolic product of testosterone aromatization
questions.learning: The enzyme aromatase (part of the cytochrome P450 superfamily) plays a pivotal role in steroidogenesis by catalyzing the "aromatization" of androgens into estrogens.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: The best way to plot trends in the incidence of diarrheal disease in a given area is by?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Line graph

Line graphs or line diagrams are the best way to plot trends in the incidence of a disease in a given area.

Pearl PF0302: Graphical Representation of Data

1. Histogram

* A histogram, by definition, is a graphical representation of frequency distribution that contains rectangles and shows the underlying frequency of a set of continuous, quantitative data.

* The X or horizontal axis is called the abscissa which usually has the group scores or class intervals of the variables/data and the Y or vertical axis is called the ordinate which usually shows the frequencies at which these variables appear.

* The following is a histogram of cholesterol levels from the Framingham Heart Study.

2. Bar Chart

* It is also called a bar graph.

* It is used mainly for nominal or ordinal scale data as they are not quantitative and usually qualitative.

* The difference between a bar graph and a histogram is that the rectangles are separated by spaces representing data that forms discrete categories instead of continuous groups.

* Bar graphs can be simple, multiple or component bar graphs.

3. Pie Charts

* Pie charts are also used for nominal or ordinal data.

* The categorical data are represented as segments of a circle.

4. Frequency polygons

* Frequency polygons are used for mainly ratio and interval scale data.

* In a frequency polygon, the mid-points of each class interval are joined together by straight lines.

5. Ogive

* A frequency polygon which is drawn to represent cumulative frequency distributions form a typical S-shaped curve which is called an ogive. It referred to as a cumulative frequency diagram.

6. Line chart

* It is also called a line diagram or line graph.

* Its best use is to show the trend of events or change over passage of time.
questions.learning: Line graph Line graphs or line diagrams are the best way to plot trends in the incidence of a disease in a given area. Pearl PF0302: Graphical Representation of Data 1.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Given below are statements regarding panophthalmitis. All are true except:
options: Untreated cases can progress to cavernous sinus thrombosis
It involves all three coats of the eyeball.
Enucleation is the treatment of choice.
Presents with painful limitation of movements.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Enucleation is the treatment of choice.

Panophthalmitis is a severe, suppurative inflammation involving all layers of the eyeball (sclera, choroid, retina) along with intraocular contents and surrounding orbital tissues. It usually results from severe ocular infection following trauma, surgery, corneal ulcer, or endogenous spread.

Clinical features include:

• Severe ocular pain
• Marked redness and swelling
• Proptosis
• Painful restriction of extraocular movements
• Loss of vision

Complications:

• Orbital cellulitis
• Cavernous sinus thrombosis
• Intracranial spread of infection

Management:

• Intensive systemic and intravitreal antibiotics
• Evisceration is generally preferred in severe uncontrolled infection
• Enucleation is usually avoided initially because it may increase the risk of spread through the optic nerve sheath.
questions.learning: Enucleation is the treatment of choice. Panophthalmitis is a severe, suppurative inflammation involving all layers of the eyeball (sclera, choroid, retina) along with intraocular contents and surrounding orbital tissues.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: A 60-year-old patient came with a puncture wound on the left chest wall. Radiological investigations confirmed pneumothorax. Which of the following is correct regarding this condition?
options: Lung volume increases, thoracic volume increases
Lung volume decreases, thoracic volume increases
Lung volume increases, thoracic volume decreases
lung volume decreases, thoracic volume decreases
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Lung volume decreases, thoracic volume increases

In pneumothorax, lung volume is decreased and thoracic volume is increased.

Both lungs and the chest wall (thoracic cage) are elastic structures. Under normal conditions, the elastic tendency of the lungs to collapse is exactly balanced by the elastic tendency of the chest wall to expand.

In pneumothorax, air is introduced into the pleural space, so the pleural pressure, which is normally subatmospheric, becomes equal to atmospheric pressure. The chest wall springs outward and the lungs collapse. This increases the thoracic volume and decreases the lung volume.
questions.learning: Lung volume decreases, thoracic volume increases — In pneumothorax, lung volume is decreased and thoracic volume is increased. Both lungs and the chest wall (thoracic cage) are elastic structures.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: During the assessment of an elderly man with multiple comorbidities including chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, hypertension, and diabetes, which prescribing criteria should be used to systematically review and optimize his medications?
questions.explanation: The Beers Criteria (American Geriatrics Society Beers Criteria) is the standard clinical guide used for medication review in elderly patients. It identifies "potentially inappropriate medications" (PIMs) that should be avoided or used with caution in the geriatric population due to an increased risk of adverse events, drug-drug interactions, or lack of efficacy. This is particularly relevant for a patient with multiple comorbidities like COPD, hypertension, and diabetes, who is likely on multiple medications (polypharmacy). Duke's criteria (Option A) are used for diagnosing infective endocarditis. Light’s criteria (Option B) are used to differentiate exudative from transudative pleural effusions. Jones criteria (Option D) are used for the diagnosis of acute rheumatic fever. Utilizing the Beers criteria helps physicians optimize drug therapy for the elderly, reducing the incidence of falls, cognitive impairment, and GI bleeding. It provides a structured framework for de-prescribing unnecessary or high-risk medications, thereby improving the overall safety and quality of care for older adults

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient developed a lesion as shown below after 6 months of a heart surgery. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Keloid scar

The given image shows a keloid scar.

Keloid scars are associated with elevated levels of growth factors.

A keloid scar is defined as excessive scar tissue that extends beyond the boundaries of the original incision or wound. Its etiology is unknown, but is associated with elevated levels of growth factor, deeply pigmented skin, and inherited tendency and certain areas of the body (triangle whose points are the xiphisternum and each shoulder tip).

The histology of keloid scars shows excess collagen with hypervascularity, and there is disorganized type 1 and type 3 collagen.

Keloid scars do not improve spontaneously with time and excision of the keloid scar has a high rate of recurrence.

Treatment:

* Pressure - local molds or elastic garments.

* Silicone gel sheeting.

* Intralesional triamcinolone injection

* Excision and steroid injections

* Excision and postoperative radiation (external beam or brachytherapy)

* Intralesional excision.

* Laser to reduce redness

* Vitamin E and palm oil massage
questions.learning: Keloid scar — The given image shows a keloid scar. Keloid scars are associated with elevated levels of growth factors.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following agents cause hydrops fetalis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Parvovirus

Parvovirus B19 is the most common infectious cause of nonimmune hydrops fetalis. Parvovirus B19 infects fetal erythroid progenitor cells and causes anemia. Severe anemia leads to high-output cardiac failure and nonimmune hydrops fetalis.

Hydrops is diagnosed by identifying two or more fetal effusions, such as pleural, pericardial, or ascitic effusions, or the presence of one effusion along with anasarca. Hydrops can be seen in association with red cell auto immunization, which is termed immune hydrops. Otherwise, it is nonimmune.

Nonimmune hydrops is more common than immune hydrops. Causes of nonimmune hydrops include cardiac pathology (Ebstein anomaly), chromosomal (Turner's syndrome), hematological (hemoglobinopathies), lymphatic abnormalities (cystic hygroma), and thoracic abnormalities.

Infectious causes of nonimmune hydrops are parvovirus B19 (most common), syphilis, cytomegalovirus, toxoplasmosis, rubella, enterovirus, varicella, herpes simplex, coxsackievirus, listeriosis, leptospirosis, Chagas disease, and Lyme disease.

The following image shows a stillborn baby with hydrops fetalis:
questions.learning: Parvovirus Parvovirus B19 is the most common infectious cause of nonimmune hydrops fetalis. Parvovirus B19 infects fetal erythroid progenitor cells and causes anemia.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: On your morning walk in the park, you notice an unconscious man lying on the ground. Which of the following options would be the next best step?
options: Check carotid pulse, start CPR, and call for help; Defibrillate if no pulse.
Call for help, check pulse, do CPR, defibrillate if no pulse
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Call for help, check pulse, do CPR, defibrillate if no pulse

The next best step is to Call for help, check pulse, do CPR, defibrillate If no pulse.

Steps in basic life support:

First step – Assess safety of the surroundings.

Second step - Assess for responsiveness

Third step – Proceed if the patient is unresponsive. Shout for help.

If the patient is unresponsive, assess for breathing and carotid pulse simultaneously for no more than 10 seconds.

In the given scenario, it is already mentioned that you are in a park (scene safety has been assessed), and that the person is unconscious (responsiveness has been assessed). So, the immediate next step is to call for help, and start CPR.

questions.text: All tissues are correctly matched to their stem cell location, except:
options: Intestine – Paneth cells near base of crypt
Skin – Bulge region of hair follicle
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Cornea – Ciliary body

Adult stem cells reside in specific tissue niches responsible for regeneration and repair.

Correct stem cell locations:

• Intestine: Stem cells located at the base of crypts of Lieberkühn, closely associated with Paneth cells.
• Skin: Stem cells present in the bulge region of hair follicles.
• Liver: Hepatic progenitor cells (oval cells) located in the Canal of Hering.

Incorrect match:

• Cornea – Ciliary body: Corneal stem cells are actually located in the limbus (limbal stem cells) at the junction of cornea and sclera, not the ciliary body.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: All are true about renal tubular acidosis in children except
options: Type 4 is due to defective ammoniagenesis and aldosterone resistance
Type 2 is Fanconi and hypophosphatemic rickets
Type 4 with paradoxical aciduria and hypokalemia
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Type 4 with paradoxical aciduria and hypokalemia

Hyperkalemia and metabolic acidosis are features of type 4 renal tubular acidosis

Type IV (hyperkalemic) renal tubular acidosis: Hyperkalemia with distal RTA occurring due to aldosterone resistance or deficiency is termed type 4 RT A. Aldosterone directly stimulates the proton pump, increases Na+ absorption resulting in negative intrahibular potential and increases urinary K+ losses and stimulates basolateral Na+ /K+ ATPase. Hence, aldosterone deficiency or resistance is expected to cause hyperkalemia and acidosis.

The clinical features seen in Type IV RTA are as follows:

• Hyperkalemia: Hypoaldosteronism results in an increase in potassium concentration.
• Metabolic acidosis: The important buffers in urine are ammonia and phosphate. Hyperkalemia impairs ammonia production in the proximal tubule, which reduces the buffering of hydrogen ions. This results in decreased hydrogen ion excretion.
• Urinary pH<5.5: Due to the decreased production of ammonia in the proximal tubule, excess protons are excreted in the renal tubules, thus decreasing the urinary pH.

RTA type I (distal RTA) is seen in autoimmune diseases like Sjogren's syndrome, systemic lupus erythematosus, systemic sclerosis, medullary sponge kidney disease, cirrhosis, drugs like amphotericin B, lithium, etc. The patients develop hypokalemia and metabolic acidosis with alkaline urine (urinary pH >5.5).

RTA type II (proximal RTA) is seen in Fanconi syndrome, Wilson's disease, heavy metals ingestion, etc., The patients develop hypokalemia and metabolic acidosis with acidic urine (urinary pH <5.5). It occurs due to generalized proximal tubule dysfunction. Defective HCO3- resorption is the primary dysfunctional mechanism causing metabolic acidosis and is also associated with glycosuria, aminoaciduria, and phosphaturia. Rickets is rare in isolated proximal RTA but common in Fanconi syndrome.

RTA type III (mixed RTA) is seen in inherited mutations of carbonic anhydrase II. A combined pathology of type I and type II RTA is seen in this type. It results in hypokalemia and metabolic acidosis.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 35-year-old non-pregnant woman presents with persistent intermenstrual spotting for the past several months. Her serum β-hCG is negative. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Endometrial polyp

Endometrial polyps are the most common cause of persistent intermenstrual (between-period) bleeding in reproductive-aged women after pregnancy has been excluded (β-hCG negative). They are localized overgrowths of endometrial glands and stroma that bleed irregularly.

• Best initial imaging: Transvaginal ultrasonography (TVS).
• Most sensitive test: Saline infusion sonography (SIS).
• Gold standard for diagnosis and treatment: Hysteroscopy with polypectomy.

Why the Other Options Are Incorrect

• A. PCOS: Typically causes oligomenorrhea/amenorrhea with irregular heavy bleeding due to anovulation, not persistent intermenstrual spotting.
• C. Endometrial hyperplasia: Usually presents with abnormal heavy or prolonged uterine bleeding, especially in women with chronic unopposed estrogen exposure.
• D. Submucosal fibroid: Commonly causes heavy menstrual bleeding (menorrhagia) and may cause intermenstrual bleeding, but persistent spotting is more characteristic of an endometrial polyp.
questions.learning: Endometrial polyp Endometrial polyps are the most common cause of persistent intermenstrual (between-period) bleeding in reproductive-aged women after pregnancy has been excluded (β-hCG negative).

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A patient hailing from Delhi presents with fever, arthralgia, and extensive petechial rash for 3 days. Lab investigations revealed a hemoglobin of 9 g/dL, a white blood cell count of 9000 cells/mm3, a platelet count of 20000 cells/mm3, and a prolonged bleeding time. The clotting time was normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Dengue

The given clinical vignette is suggestive of dengue fever.

Dengue is an acute febrile disease caused by the mosquito-borne dengue viruses (DENVs), consisting of four serotypes (DENV 1 to 4), that are members of the Flaviviridae family, genus Flavivirus.

Dengue virus is transmitted from person to person by Aedes aegypti mosquitoes.

After an incubation period of 3–15 days, classical dengue fever begins with an abrupt onset of high fever. The condition is self-limiting though debilitating with headache, retro-orbital pain, myalgia, arthralgia, petechiae rash, and leucopenia. A macular-papular recovery rash appears 3–4 days after the onset of fever, and it usually starts on the trunk before spreading peripherally. The rash in dengue appears as 'white islands in a red sea' due to erythema with petechiae.

Shown below is an image of the rash in dengue:

Dengue fever is sometimes referred to as ‘break bone fever’ due to associated severe muscle and joint pain or ‘seven-day fever’ since the symptoms usually persist for 7 days.

The diseases range in severity from undifferentiated acute febrile illness, classical dengue fever (DF), to the life-threatening conditions dengue hemorrhagic fever (DHF)/dengue shock syndrome (DSS).

DHF is associated with:

* plasma leakage and hemoconcentration

* hemorrhagic tendencies

* Increased vascular permeability

* Thrombocytopenia

DSS is distinguished from DHF by the presence of cardiovascular compromise, which occurs when plasma leakage into the interstitial spaces results in shock. DSS is a fatal condition. Common clinical warning signs for DSS include a rapidly increasing hematocrit, severe abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, and a narrowing or absence of blood pressure.

Other options:

Option B: Malaria is a protozoal disease caused by Plasmodium species. It is transmitted by the female anopheles mosquito. Here, the definitive host is the anopheles mosquito and humans are the intermediate hosts. Clinical features are periodic bouts of fever with chills and rigors, followed by anemia, splenomegaly, and hepatomegaly.

Option C: Scrub typhus is caused by Orientia tsutsugamushi and transmitted by trombiculid mites. The incubation period is 1-3 weeks. The patient typically develops a characteristic eschar which is a punched-out ulcer covered with a blackened scab at the site of the mite bite, with regional lymphadenopathy and maculopapular rash. Here is a picture of the eschar.

Option D: Typhoid (enteric) fever is a systemic disease manifested by fever and abdominal pain caused by Salmonella typhi or Salmonella paratyphi.

Clinical features include fever, abdominal pain, headache, chills, myalgia, malaise, diarrhea, sweating, nausea, and vomiting. Rose spots are the classic cutaneous manifestation of typhoid fever, which presents as pink macules on the abdomen and the chest. Hepatosplenomegaly and relative bradycardia might be seen. The WBC count may be normal or low.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 65-year-old man with a history of chronic smoking came with complaints of ulcerative lesions on his lower lip for a year. On examination, there is a presence of a palpable ipsilateral submental node approximately 5*5 cm. Biopsy from the lesion was suggestive of squamous cell cancer. What is the next step in the management of this patient? MRND-Modified radical neck dissection
options: Resection of primary lesion with lip reconstruction and MRND
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Resection of primary lesion with lip reconstruction and MRND

The given patient has a squamous cell carcinoma of the lip with a primary lesion on the lower lip with ipsilateral lymph node metastasis to the submental node. This patient will need resection of the primary lesion with reconstruction and modified radical neck dissection (MRND).

Lip cancer most commonly occurs in men from 50 to 70 years old but can be seen in younger patients. Risk factors include sunlight exposure, smoking, and tobacco use. Squamous cell carcinoma is the most common type of lip cancer. But commonly occurring cancer in the upper lip is basal cell carcinoma.

Most lip cancers occur in the lower lip followed by the upper lip and commissure. The most common site is the vermilion border of the lower lip. Ulcerative lesion on the vermilion border of the lower lip is the most common clinical manifestation. Mass can extend and fix on the underlying bone. Loss of sensation over the chin indicates mental nerve involvement. The most frequently involved nodes are the submental and submandibular nodes.

Surgical resection (wide local excision with negative margins) is the preferred treatment modality. The typical lip length is 6 to 7 cm. For defects of <1/3rd of the lip, resection with primary closure is the preferred treatment.

For defects of more than 1/3rd of the lip, require local flaps for reconstruction after resection:

* Johansen step technique- local flap for large central defects

* Lip-switch (Abbe-Estlander) flap- based on the sublabial or superior labial artery. When the defect involves only the commissure, the Estlander flap is used, and the Abbé flap is used for midline defects. Abbe-Estlander Flap is used for mixed defects. The markings of the Abbe-Estlander flap are shown below.

* Karapandzic flap - circumoral advancement flap. It is a neuromuscular flap that includes the remaining orbicularis oris muscle with its innervation.

In the presence of neck metastasis, neck dissection is indicated. Postoperative radiation is administered to patients with positive margins, lymph node metastases, tumor thickness >4mm, or perineural invasion. If the mandible is involved, mandibulectomy and free flap reconstruction is required.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 5 year old with gradually progressive hoarseness of voice over three months and respiratory distress for 2 weeks. Diagnosis is
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Respiratory papillomatosis

The given clinical scenario of a child presenting with chronic hoarseness (3 months) of voice and respiratory distress for 2 weeks suggests the diagnosis of respiratory papillomatosis (juvenile papillomatosis).

Croup (Option A) and acute epiglottitis (Option D), which cause acute upper respiratory tract obstruction, are ruled out due to the chronic nature of the symptoms. In croup, the upper airway obstruction becomes apparent after 1 to 3 days of low-grade fever, rhinorrhea, and pharyngitis. On the other hand, in epiglottitis, a child experiences respiratory distress within hours of developing a fever.

Vocal nodules (Option C) are not typically associated with respiratory distress.

Respiratory papillomatosis is the most common respiratory tract neoplasm in children. They are simple warts (benign tumors) caused by human papillomavirus types 6 and 11 commonly seen in children aged 3 to 5 years.

The course involves remissions and exacerbations of recurrent papillomas, mostly affecting the glottic area (vocal cords), and supraglottis. The patient presents with progressively worsening hoarseness, sleep-disordered breathing, dyspnea, stridor, and severe airway obstruction if left untreated.

Diagnosis confirmed by direct laryngoscopy, which shows grape-like projections (shown below), and biopsy. Treatment consists of micro laryngoscopy and CO2 laser excision. Antivirals like interferon alpha2a, ribavirin, cidofovir, and acyclovir are used as adjunct therapies.

Other options:

Option A: Croup (laryngotracheobronchitis) is caused by the parainfluenza virus. The patient initially presents with an upper respiratory tract infection (rhinorrhea, pharyngitis, cough, low-grade fever) followed by a characteristic barking cough, hoarseness, and inspiratory stridor.

Option C: Vocal nodule (singer’s or screamer's nodule) occurs as a result of chronic vocal abuse. They appear symmetrically at the junction of the anterior one-third and posterior two third of the vocal cord. The patient presents with chronic hoarseness and voice fatigue.

The image below shows symmetric vocal nodules:

Option D: Acute epiglottitis is caused by streptococcus pyogenes, pneumococci, Hemophilus influenzae, and staphylococcus aureus. It is characterized by an acute rapidly progressive course of high-grade fever, dyspnea, and stridor.
questions.learning: Respiratory papillomatosis — The given clinical scenario of a child presenting with chronic hoarseness (3 months) of voice and respiratory distress for 2 weeks suggests the diagnosis of respiratory papillomatosis (juvenile papillomatosis).

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A baby is brought to the OPD with complaints of lethargy and poor feeding. On examination, it is noted that the urine had a smell of burnt sugar. A defect in which of the following enzymes causes this disease?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Branched-chain ketoacid dehydrogenase

The diagnosis, in this case, is that of maple syrup urine disease (MSUD). This disease occurs due to a defect of the enzyme branched-chain keto acid dehydrogenase.

MSUD is an autosomal recessive disorder that occurs due to a deficiency of branched-chain ketoacid dehydrogenase complex. This impairs the metabolism of branched-chain amino acids valine, leucine, isoleucine, and alloisoleucine. These amino acids, particularly leucine and its metabolite accumulate in the blood, causing toxic effects on the brain.

The affected child develops poor feeding and vomiting a few days after birth. There is a period of hypertonicity with a period of flaccidity in between. These appear as repetitive boxing and bicycling movements. The babies may also have hypoglycemia, but this is not corrected by the administration of glucose. The urine, sweat, and cerumen of the baby have a sweetish maple syrup-like odor.

Laboratory investigations will show increased levels of branched-chain amino acids in the plasma and urine. Leucine levels are usually higher than isoleucine, valine, and alloisoleucine. Since the patient excretes ketone bodies in the urine, the urine will be positive for the dinitrophenylhydrazine test.

Treatment involves controlled intake of branched-chain amino acids using commercially available formulas and judicious supplementation of isoleucine and valine. Very high levels of leucine are removed by hemodialysis.
questions.learning: Branched-chain ketoacid dehydrogenase — The diagnosis, in this case, is that of maple syrup urine disease (MSUD). This disease occurs due to a defect of the enzyme branched-chain keto acid dehydrogenase.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: You are the intern posted in the emergency department. You came across an ABG report given below. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Metabolic acidosis

The given ABG report shows decreased blood arterial pH(Normal range: 7.35-7.45), and decreased HCO3 levels(Normal: 22-28 mEq/L) indicating metabolic acidosis.

Metabolic disorders

Conditions
Features
Etiology

Metabolic acidosis

There is decreased blood arterial pH because of an increase in endogenous acid production (Example: Diabetic ketoacidosis, increased lactate in sepsis), loss of HCO3- (Example: diarrhea), or low excretion of net acid by kidneys (Example: chronic kidney disease). Respiratory compensation (alveolar hyperventilation) occurs causing a decrease in PaCO2.

High anionic metabolic acidosis

• Methanol
• Uremia
• Diabetic ketoacidosis
• Propylene glycol
• Iron tablets
• Lactic acidosis
• Ethylene glycol
• Salicylates (Late)

Normal anionic gap metabolic acidosis

• Hyperalimentation
• Addison's disease
• Renal tubular acidosis
• Diarrhea
• Acetazolamide
• Spironolactone
• Saline infusion

Metabolic alkalosis

There is increased blood arterial pH, as a result of a net gain of HCO3- or a loss of nonvolatile acid from the extracellular fluid. Compensatory alveolar hypoventilation occurs and causes an increase in PaCO2.

Loss of hydrogen:

• Gastrointestinal loss

• Removal of gastric secretions- vomiting or nasogastric suction
• Chloride-losing diarrhea
• Gastrocolic fistula
• Villous adenoma
• Antacid therapy, particularly if combined with cation exchange resin

• Renal loss

• Loop or thiazide diuretics
• Mineralocorticoid excess (primary aldosteronism, Cushing's, steroids, licorice)
• Posthypercapnic states
• Hypercalcemia, including the milk-alkali syndrome

• H+ movement into cells

• Hypokalemia

Exogenous Alkali:

• Administration of NaHCO3, sodium citrate/gluconate/acetate/antacids
• Massive blood transfusion
• Antacids- Milk alkali syndrome

Contraction alkalosis (loss of ECF volume):

• Loop or thiazide-type diuretics
• Sweat losses in cystic fibrosis
• Gastric losses in achlorhydria

Miscellaneous:

• Bartter's syndrome
• Gitelman's syndrome

Respiratory acidosis

There is decreased blood arterial pH as a result of an increase in PaCO2 following alveolar hypoventilation.

• Central: Stroke, infection
• Airway: Obstruction, Asthma
• Lung Parenchyma: Emphysema, Pneumoconiosis, Bronchitis
• Neuromuscular: Muscular dystrophies, Myasthenia
• Obesity
• Hypoventilation

Respiratory alkalosis

There is an increase in blood arterial pH due to a decrease in PaCO2 due to alveolar hyperventilation.

Hyperventilation

• Anxiety/panic attack
• Hypoxemia( eg: High altitude)
• Salicylates (Early)
• Pulmonary embolism
• Tumor

Pearl PF1719: Interpretation of Acid-Base Disorders

pH<7.35 is acidosis

pH>7.45 is alkalosis

A primary change in HCO3- is termed metabolic

If the change in HCO3- is in keeping with the pH (i.e. if there are acidosis and HCO3- is decreased) the problem is metabolic.

If the change in HCO3- is opposite with the pH (i.e. if there is acidosis and HCO3- is increased or normal) the problem is compensatory metabolic.

A primary change in CO2 is termed as respiratory

If the change in CO2 keeping in line with the pH (if in acidosis CO2 is raised) the problem is termed respiratory

If the change in CO2 is in the opposite direction of that of the pH (i.e. if there are acidosis and CO2 is decreased or normal ) the problem is termed compensatory respiratory
