questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: A and B in the graph below represent which of the following ions, in terms of permeability for action potential generation?
options: A is Na+, B is K+
A is Na+, B is Ca2+
A is K+, B is Ca2+
A is Ca2+, B is K+
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. A is Na+, B is K+

In the given graph, showing action potential generation in terms of ion permeability, wave A represents Na+ and B represents K+.

The sequence of events during the action potential occurs in 7 steps as described below.

1. Resting-state - Both channels are closed

2. Na+ channels open in response to depolarizing stimulus. Sodium enters the cell. The membrane reaches threshold potential.

3. The sodium influx causes the opening of more Na+ channels through a positive feedback mechanism. Rapid depolarization occurs.

4. Sodium conductance decreases.

5. Na+ channels close and K+ channels open. Repolarization occurs.

6. Sodium channels are reset, and are ready to respond to another depolarizing stimulus (relative refractory period). During this phase, the potassium channels remain open and slowly return to closed state causing after-hyperpolarization.

7. Both channels are closed. The membrane returns to RMP.
questions.learning: A is Na+, B is K+ — In the given graph, showing action potential generation in terms of ion permeability, wave A represents Na+ and B represents K+. The sequence of events during the action potential occurs in 7 steps as described below.

Though the data seems to be expressed in numbers, it is actually a qualitative or nominal variable as we assess the proportion of children who are affected by the disease and those who are not affected by the disease.
• The chi-square test can be used to compare two or more groups.

questions.text: Identify the type of cartilage shown in the image below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Elastic cartilage

The above image shows an elastic cartilage.

The elastic cartilage, like the hyaline cartilage, contains individual or small groups of chondrocytes that are surrounded by type II collagen fibrils. However, it differs from hyaline cartilage in that, much of the interterritorial matrix consists of fine yellow elastic fibres containing elastin protein.

On microscopy, elastic cartilage consists of:

• Chondrocytes within lacunae
• Elastic fibres in the matrix

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following is an inhibitor of DNA synthesis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 6-mercaptopurine

6-Mercaptopurine is an inhibitor of DNA synthesis.

6-Mercaptopurine is inactive in its parent form. It must be metabolized by hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyltransferase to form monophosphate nucleotide 6-thioinosinic acid. This inhibits several enzymes of de novo purine nucleotide synthesis.

Option B- Mitomycin acts as an alkylating agent and crosslinks DNA. It also generates free radicals which damage DNA.

Option C- Actinomycin causes single-strand breaks in DNA. It blocks RNA transcription as well.

Option D- L-Asparaginase causes the breakdown of asparagine and thus interferes with protein synthesis.
questions.learning: 6-mercaptopurine 6-Mercaptopurine is an inhibitor of DNA synthesis. 6-Mercaptopurine is inactive in its parent form.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text:
The steps in the management of snake bite include:

1. Loose tourniquet
2. Debride to avoid the spread
3. Kill the snake
4. Hospitalize for anti-venom administration
5. Immobilization
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 4 and 5

The management of snakebites includes immobilization and administration of anti-snake venom (ASV) after hospitalization.

Immobilization is done to minimize the spread of the venom. Hospitalization, followed by ASV administration is the definitive management of snake bites.

Measures that can be taken in the case of snakebite:

• Apply firm pressure over the bitten area, which delays the absorption of venom
• Pressure immobilization is recommended for elapid and sea-snake bites, but not for viper bites as it may cause local necrosis
• Immediately apply a broad firm bandage (Sutherland wrap) on the bitten area and around the limb. As much of the limb should be bandaged as possible. It should be tight enough to occlude the superficial venous and lymphatic return, but not the arterial or deep venous flow. A pressure of 50 to 70 mm Hg is maintained.
• In bites on the trunk, head, or neck, apply firm pressure over the bitten area
• Immobilize the limb, as movement can accelerate the spread of venom
• Make the patient lie on one side in the recovery position so that the airway is clear, in case of vomiting or fainting.

Measures contraindicated in the case of snakebite:

• Suction and incision of the wound
• Electric shock treatment of wound site
• Application of tourniquets because they obstruct arterial flow and cause ischemia
• Ice water immersion of the bitten limb
• Do not attempt to kill or catch the snake as it may be dangerous.
• Administration of ASV locally at the wound site.
• Herbal/local remedies
questions.learning: 4 and 5 The management of snakebites includes immobilization and administration of anti-snake venom (ASV) after hospitalization. Immobilization is done to minimize the spread of the venom.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 22-year-old woman presents with a large right ovarian mass. Histopathology shows the tumor contains elements from all three germ layers. What is the most likely type of ovarian tumor?
questions.explanation: A tumor that contains tissues derived from all three germ layers (ectoderm, mesoderm, and endoderm)—such as hair, teeth, bone, and nervous tissue—is definitively a teratoma (Option B) . In young women, the most common type is the benign mature cystic teratoma, also known as a dermoid cyst. Dysgerminoma (Option A) is a germ cell tumor composed of uniform, undifferentiated cells and does not contain differentiated tissues from the three layers. Thecoma (Option C) is a solid, sex-cord stromal tumor that secretes estrogen. Theca lutein cysts (Option D) are functional cysts usually associated with high hCG levels (e.g., in molar pregnancies) rather than true neoplastic growths. Because the "three germ layer" origin is the pathognomonic histological definition of this tumor, teratoma is the correct diagnosis. Most teratomas are benign, but they are prone to ovarian torsion due to their heavy, asymmetrical weight
questions.learning: A tumor that contains tissues derived from all three germ layers (ectoderm, mesoderm, and endoderm)—such as hair, teeth, bone, and nervous tissue—is definitively a teratoma (Option B) .

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following molecular analysis methods is used to detect monkeypox virus?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Real time PCR

Real-time PCR is used to detect monkeypox virus which contains enveloped double-stranded DNA.

Real-time PCR helps quantify the PCR and gives an estimate of the pathogen DNA load in the specimen. It uses fluorescent dyes or specific DNA probes. It is also known as qPCR (Quantitative PCR)

Other types of PCR:

* Reverse transcriptase PCR: The enzyme reverse transcriptase (RT) is used to synthesize a complementary copy of DNA (cDNA) from RNA and this cDNA is then used as a template for PCR.

* Multiplex PCR: Primers to more than one pathogen are used simultaneously and hence multiple products are obtained.

* Nested PCR: It involves the sequential use of two primer sets. The first primer set is used for amplification and the amplicon obtained is then used as a target sequence for second amplification. This ensures specificity.

Other options

Option A: Sanger's technique was the first technique used to determine the sequence of proteins. The first protein to be sequenced by this method was insulin. Sanger’s reagent is 1- Flouro 2,4 Dinitro benzene. Only dipeptides and tripeptides can be sequenced by this method.

Option B:  Western blot, also called immunoblots, is a technique used to study protein molecules. The proteins undergo electrophoresis and then are transferred to a membrane. These proteins are then tagged with the specific antibodies and visualized.

Option C: ELISA (Enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay) involves the use of an immunosorbent, which is an absorbing material that is specific for one of the components of the reaction, either the antigen or antibody.
questions.learning: Real time PCR Real-time PCR is used to detect monkeypox virus which contains enveloped double-stranded DNA. Real-time PCR helps quantify the PCR and gives an estimate of the pathogen DNA load in the specimen.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A young patient presents with unexplained hair loss and persistent abdominal discomfort. During surgery, a mass is retrieved from the stomach (as shown in the image). What is the most probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The clinical combination of unexplained hair loss (alopecia due to trichotillomania) and persistent abdominal discomfort in a young patient is highly suggestive of a Trichobezoar. A bezoar is a mass of trapped, undigested material in the stomach, and a trichobezoar is specifically composed of ingested hair. Over time, the hair forms a large, solid cast that takes the shape of the entire stomach, as shown in the provided surgical image. Splenic rupture (Option B) presents with acute hemoperitoneum and shock. Pancreatic necrosis (Option C) is a complication of severe acute pancreatitis. Carcinoma of the stomach (Option D) is rare in young patients and does not explain the alopecia. A large trichobezoar that extends into the small intestine is known as "Rapunzel syndrome." Diagnosis is often made via ultrasound or endoscopy. Management typically requires surgical removal via gastrotomy, as these masses are usually too large and dense for endoscopic retrieval. Psychiatric referral for the underlying hair-pulling and eating behaviors is essential to prevent recurrence
questions.learning: The clinical combination of unexplained hair loss (alopecia due to trichotillomania) and persistent abdominal discomfort in a young patient is highly suggestive of a Trichobezoar.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: What is the causative organism for the condition shown in the image below?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Echinococcus granulosus

The given image shows a hydatid cyst in the liver. It is caused by Echinococcus granulosus.

Echinococcus granulosus is the most common causative agent in hydatid cysts, while Echinococcus multilocularis and Echinococcus ligartus account for a small number of cases.

Dogs are the definitive hosts of E. granulosus. Sheep are the usual intermediate hosts, but humans are accidental intermediate hosts. Humans are end-stage hosts of the parasite since there is no human to human transmission.

Approximately 75% of hydatid cysts are located in the right lobe of the liver and are solitary. The clinical presentation of a hydatid cyst is largely asymptomatic until complications occur. The most common presenting symptoms are abdominal pain, dyspepsia, and vomiting. The most frequent sign is hepatomegaly.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: What are the components to establish the diagnosis of Brain Death? I. Absent brain stem reflexes II. Apnoea in presence of elevated PCO₂ III. Hypothermia IV. Irreversible and unresponsive coma Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. I, II and IV

Brain death is defined as the irreversible cessation of all functions of the entire brain, including the brainstem. It is a clinical diagnosis that requires demonstration of irreversible coma, absence of all brainstem reflexes, and apnea despite adequate stimulation by elevated carbon dioxide (CO₂) after excluding reversible causes.

• I. Absent brainstem reflexes ✔

• Essential for the diagnosis.
• Includes absent:

• Pupillary light reflex
• Corneal reflex
• Oculocephalic reflex (doll’s eye)
• Oculovestibular reflex (caloric test)
• Gag reflex
• Cough reflex

• II. Apnea in the presence of elevated PCO₂ ✔

• Demonstrated by the apnea test.
• Absence of spontaneous respiratory effort despite PaCO₂ ≥60 mmHg or an increase of ≥20 mmHg above baseline confirms loss of medullary respiratory drive.

• III. Hypothermia ✘

• Hypothermia is not a criterion for brain death.
• In fact, hypothermia must be excluded before testing because it can suppress brain function.
• Core temperature should generally be ≥36°C before assessment.

• IV. Irreversible and unresponsive coma ✔

• The patient must be in a known irreversible coma with no response to painful stimuli.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text:
Which of the following statements are true about the internal capsule?

1. Charcot's artery supplies the posterior limb.
2. Retrolenticular part of the internal capsule contains optic radiation.
3. Anterior limb of the capsule contains corticospinal tract fibers of the upper limb and face.
4. Internal capsule has projection fibers.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 1, 2, 4

Statements 1, 2, and 4 are true about the internal capsule.

The charcot’s artery of hemorrhage is a larger lenticulostriate or lateral striate artery. Lateral striate arteries supply the anterior limb, genu and the posterior limb of the internal capsule. These arteries are also commonly involved in ischemic and hemorrhagic strokes.

The retrolentiform part of the internal capsule carries fibers mainly from optic radiation. A lesion here produces homonymous hemianopia, superior quadrantanopia, or inferior quadrantanopia.

The anterior limb of the internal capsule carries fronto-pontine fibers. A lesion here produces confusion, impaired attention, agitation, and dysarthria.

The posterior limb of the internal capsule carries cortico-spinal motor fibers in the anterior part and the lesion here produces contralateral hemiparesis. The posterior part of the posterior limb of the internal capsule carries sensory fibers and lesions here may produce contralateral hemi-sensory deficits.

The internal capsule predominantly contains projection fibers, not commissural fibers. Projection fibers are the fibers that project from higher to lower centers or vice versa in CNS.
questions.learning: 1, 2, 4 Statements 1, 2, and 4 are true about the internal capsule. The charcot’s artery of hemorrhage is a larger lenticulostriate or lateral striate artery.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Under the Anemia Mukt Bharat (AMB) initiative, mild to moderate anemia in pregnant women at less than 34 weeks of gestation is treated with:

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 30-year-old woman presents with a unilateral throbbing headache that worsens with exposure to bright light. She occasionally skips breakfast. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The patient's symptoms are classic for migraine: a unilateral, throbbing headache associated with photophobia (light sensitivity). Migraines are significantly more common in women and are often triggered by factors such as skipping meals (fasting) or stress. While hunger can trigger a headache (Option A), the specific throbbing nature and photophobia point toward migraine. Tension headaches (Option C) are typically "band-like," bilateral, and not associated with severe photophobia. Cluster headaches (Option D) are excruciating, unilateral, and located around the eye, but they occur in "clusters" of multiple short attacks per day and are much more common in men. Migraine management involves avoiding known triggers, acute treatment with triptans or NSAIDs, and potentially prophylactic medications if attacks are frequent. This 30-year-old woman is the "typical" patient profile for this neurological disorder
questions.learning: The patient's symptoms are classic for migraine: a unilateral, throbbing headache associated with photophobia (light sensitivity). Migraines are significantly more common in women and are often triggered by factors such as skipping meals (fasting) or stress.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Identify the type of pelvis in the given image below
questions.explanation: The pelvis in the given image shows a heart-shaped (triangular) pelvic inlet, which is the hallmark feature of an android pelvis. The anterior segment is narrow, and the side walls appear convergent, giving the inlet a more constricted appearance. Additionally, the subpubic angle is relatively narrow, and the sacrum is more prominent and directed forward, all of which are characteristic of the android type. The android pelvis resembles the typical male pelvis and is considered less favorable for childbirth due to its reduced space and narrower outlet. These features match the structure shown in the image, confirming option (C). Why Other Options Are Wrong (A) Platypelloid pelvis: Shows a flat, wide inlet (transverse > AP), not heart-shaped. (B) Anthropoid pelvis: Has an elongated oval inlet (AP > transverse), not triangular. (D) Gynecoid pelvis: Has a rounded, spacious inlet, which is not seen here

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 24-year-old male who is a known case of bronchial asthma presented for a routine follow-up. PFT was done earlier—his FEV1 was 70%, which improved to 83% after bronchodilator nebulization. He was already on MDI Albuterol daily. On questioning, it seems like he is being symptomatic for at least 2 times per week and is waking up in the nights due to symptoms at least once per week. On examination, there are scattered rhonchi. What should be done?
options: Add Fluticasone MDI two times a day
Shift to MDI Salmeterol two times a day
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Add Fluticasone MDI two times a day

Symptoms ≥2 times/week with nighttime awakening indicate persistent asthma, despite SABA use.

PFT shows reversibility, confirming asthma with inadequate anti-inflammatory control.

The correct step-up is adding an inhaled corticosteroid (fluticasone) to treat airway inflammation.

| Severity | Symptoms | Treatment

| -------- | -------- | ---------

| Intermittent | <2/week | SABA

| Mild persistent | ≥2/week | Low-dose ICS

| Moderate persistent | Daily symptoms | ICS + LABA

| Severe | Continuous | High-dose ICS + LABA

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: What is the most common complication associated with the following abnormality?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Exposure keratopathy

The given image shows a coloboma of the upper eyelid. The most common complication associated with this condition is exposure keratopathy since the defect leaves the cornea exposed. If left untreated, it can lead to corneal ulceration.

Coloboma of the eyelid is a partial or full-thickness eyelid defect. It usually occurs near the nasal side. It more frequently involves the upper lid than the lower lid. It occurs when eyelid development is incomplete, due to failure of migration of lid ectoderm to fuse with the lid folds.

Small defects can be managed by primary closure, while large defects require skin grafts and rotation flaps.

Upper lid colobomas occur at the junction of the middle and inner thirds. It has a relatively strong association with cryptophthalmos, facial abnormalities, and Goldenhar syndrome. Cryptophthalmos is a congenital anomaly in which the eyelids are absent, replaced by a continuous layer of skin.

Lower lid colobomas occur at the junction of the middle and outer thirds and are frequently associated with systemic conditions.

Treacher Collins syndrome (mandibulofacial dysostosis) is a genetically heterogeneous condition. It is characterized by mandibular and ear anomalies. lower eyelid coloboma, slanted palpebral apertures, cataract, microphthalmos, and lacrimal atresia.
questions.learning: Exposure keratopathy — The given image shows a coloboma of the upper eyelid. The most common complication associated with this condition is exposure keratopathy since the defect leaves the cornea exposed.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which organization plays a role in intersectoral coordination under the Integrated Child Development Services (ICDS) program?
questions.explanation: The Integrated Child Development Services (ICDS) scheme requires extensive intersectoral coordination between the Ministry of Women and Child Development and various health initiatives to provide holistic care for children and mothers. The National Health Mission (NHM) is the primary organization that collaborates with ICDS to provide essential health services, including immunization, health check-ups, and referral services at the village level. NACO (Option B) focuses on AIDS control. NLEP (Option C) is dedicated to leprosy elimination. UNDP (Option D) is an international developmental agency and is not a core part of the domestic intersectoral coordination framework for ICDS. Coordination between NHM and ICDS occurs primarily through the collaboration of Anganwadi Workers and ASHAs. This partnership ensures that nutrition, health education, and medical care are integrated to reduce infant mortality and improve childhood development outcomes. Therefore, NHM is the correct coordinating organization for health-related ICDS goals
questions.learning: The Integrated Child Development Services (ICDS) scheme requires extensive intersectoral coordination between the Ministry of Women and Child Development and various health initiatives to provide holistic care for children and mothers.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A patient presents with ureteric colic. Examination is normal. What is the best imaging to diagnose?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. NCCT KUB

Non‑contrast CT KUB is the gold standard for detecting urinary stones, highly sensitive and specific. NCCT KUB shows-

• Stone = hyperdense focus
• Exact location (PUJ, mid-ureter, VUJ)
• Size & number (guides management)
• Hydroureter / hydronephrosis
• Alternative diagnoses (appendicitis, diverticulitis) if no stone

| CT Finding | Meaning

| ---------- | -------

| Hyperdense dot in ureter | Calculus

| Perinephric stranding | Inflammation from obstruction

| Dilated pelvis/ureter | Upstream obstruction

| “Soft tissue rim sign” | Ureteral wall edema around stone

MRI is poor for stones, ureteroscopy is therapeutic, and CECT is unnecessary for stone detection.

| Modality | Role | Limitations

| -------- | ---- | -----------

| NCCT KUB | Gold standard, detects all stones | Radiation

| USG KUB | Screening, pregnancy | Misses ureteric stones

| CECT KUB | Tumors/vascular | Masks stones

| MRI | Rare role | Poor for stones

| Ureteroscopy | Diagnostic + therapeutic | Invasive, not first-line

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 27-year-old female patient was found to have uterus didelphys. Which of the following is not likely to be a complication of this uterine anomaly?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Transverse lie

Among the given options, transverse lie is not a likely complication of uterus didelphys. A transverse lie is more likely to be seen with an arcuate or sub-septate uterus.

A uterus didelphys is a Mullerian defect characterized by two separate uterine horns, each with an endometrial cavity and uterine cervix. It occurs due to the failure of fusion of the Müllerian ducts.

It is usually asymptomatic but can rarely present with dyspareunia, dysmenorrhea, hematocolpos, and hematometra. Rarely, endometriosis (option B) and genital neoplasms may be associated with uterus didelphys.

Pregnancy is possible with uterus didelphys, however, there is an increased risk of the following complications:

• Spontaneous abortion (option A)
• Preterm labor (option C)
• Breech presentation
• Cesarean delivery
• Intrauterine growth restriction
• Low birth weight (<2.5kg)
• Perinatal death

Uterus didelphys can be diagnosed with ultrasound or hysterosalpingography, but MRI provides the most accurate diagnosis.
questions.learning: Transverse lie Among the given options, transverse lie is not a likely complication of uterus didelphys. A transverse lie is more likely to be seen with an arcuate or sub-septate uterus.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: What is the most common cause of chronic pancreatitis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Alcohol

Alcohol consumption is the most common cause of chronic pancreatitis, accounting for 60–70% of the cases. Smoking increases the risk of alcohol-induced chronic pancreatitis.

Cystic fibrosis is the most common cause of chronic pancreatitis in the pediatric age group.

Other causes of chronic pancreatitis include:

• Pancreatic divisum
• Annular pancreas
• Hyperlipidemia
• Hypercalcemia
• Hyperparathyroidism
• Chronic duct obstruction
• Autoimmune pancreatitis
• Cystic fibrosis
• Tropical pancreatitis
• Hereditary pancreatitis
questions.learning: Alcohol Alcohol consumption is the most common cause of chronic pancreatitis, accounting for 60–70% of the cases. Smoking increases the risk of alcohol-induced chronic pancreatitis.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: During a routine thyroid examination, a 45-year- old woman is found to have a palpable thyroid nodule, and fine-needle aspiration cytology confirms papillary thyroid carcinoma. Which of the following statements regarding papillary thyroid cancer is NOT true?
options: It often presents with cervical lymph node metastases
It is the most common type of thyroid cancer.
questions.explanation: Papillary thyroid cancer is derived from the follicular cells of the thyroid, not the parafollicular C-cells. Parafollicular C-cells give rise to medullary thyroid cancer, which secretes calcitonin. The other statements are correct: it is indeed the most common type of thyroid cancer (Option B), accounting for over 80% of cases. It is known for its slow growth and frequent spread to cervical lymph nodes (Option A), although this does not significantly worsen the generally excellent prognosis. Most well-differentiated thyroid cancers, including papillary, are TSH dependent (Option D), meaning that suppressing TSH levels with levothyroxine is a key part of post-operative management to prevent recurrence. Histologically, it is recognized by characteristic features such as "Orphan Annie eye" nuclei and psammoma bodies. Understanding these distinctions is vital for the correct diagnosis and staging of thyroid malignancies
questions.learning: Papillary thyroid cancer is derived from the follicular cells of the thyroid, not the parafollicular C-cells. Parafollicular C-cells give rise to medullary thyroid cancer, which secretes calcitonin.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following receives venous drainage from the left atrium and both ventricles?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Great cardiac vein

The great cardiac vein receives venous drainage from the left atrium and both ventricles.

The great cardiac vein begins at the apex of the heart. It ascends in the anterior interventricular sulcus. At the coronary sulcus, the great cardiac vein turns to the left and lies at the base of the heart. Here, it is associated with the circumflex branch of the left coronary artery. In the coronary sulcus, the great cardiac vein enlarges to form the coronary sinus.

The middle cardiac vein begins near the apex of the heart and ascends in the posterior interventricular sulcus. It is associated with the posterior interventricular branch of the right or the left coronary artery.

The small cardiac vein begins in the anterior section of the coronary sulcus between the right atrium and the right ventricle. It continues in this groove onto the base of the heart and then enters the coronary sinus. It accompanies the right coronary artery in its course and may receive the right marginal vein.

The posterior cardiac vein lies on the posterior surface of the left ventricle just to the left of the middle cardiac vein. Anterior veins of the right ventricle drain the anterior portion of the right ventricle and enter the right atrium directly.

Venae cordis minimae, or veins of Thebasius, drain directly into the cardiac chambers and are mainly associated with the right atrium and right ventricle.
questions.learning: Great cardiac vein — The great cardiac vein receives venous drainage from the left atrium and both ventricles. The great cardiac vein begins at the apex of the heart.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which among the following hormones, in a lactating mother, is responsible for the growth of breast tissue?
questions.explanation: In a lactating mother, prolactin is the primary hormone responsible for stimulating the growth, development, and maintenance of the milk-producing lobuloalveolar tissue in the breast. It acts on lactotrophs to promote the hyperplasia of mammary glands necessary for milk synthesis. Oxytocin (Option A) is responsible for the milk ejection reflex (let-down) but does not cause tissue growth. Estrogen (Option B) stimulates ductal growth and overall breast enlargement during puberty and pregnancy but is not the specific driver of the alveolar milk-producing tissue growth during established lactation. Progesterone (Option D) supports alveolar development in preparation for milk production during pregnancy but its levels drop significantly after delivery to allow for the full action of prolactin. Therefore, prolactin is the essential hormone for both the development of productive breast tissue and actual milk synthesis in the postnatal period
questions.learning: In a lactating mother, prolactin is the primary hormone responsible for stimulating the growth, development, and maintenance of the milk-producing lobuloalveolar tissue in the breast.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A patient presents with photosensitivity, purpura, and blistering lesions on sun-exposed skin. Biochemical analysis reveals impaired conversion of uroporphyrinogen III to coproporphyrinogen III within the heme biosynthesis pathway. Which of the following enzyme is deficient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase

Porphyria cutanea tarda (PCT) is the most common porphyria and results from uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase (UROD) deficiency. Defective conversion of uroporphyrinogen III to coproporphyrinogen III leads to the accumulation of uroporphyrins, which are photosensitizing compounds. Exposure to sunlight generates reactive oxygen species, causing photosensitivity, skin fragility, blistering lesions, hyperpigmentation, and purpura on sun-exposed areas.

Why not the other options?

• A. Coproporphyrinogen oxidase deficiency: Causes Hereditary coproporphyria, characterized by acute neurovisceral attacks with or without photosensitivity.
• C. Ferrochelatase deficiency: Causes Erythropoietic protoporphyria, presenting with painful photosensitivity without blistering due to protoporphyrin accumulation.
• D. Porphobilinogen deaminase deficiency: Causes Acute intermittent porphyria (AIP), which presents with abdominal pain, neuropsychiatric symptoms, and neuropathy, without photosensitivity.
questions.learning: Uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase Porphyria cutanea tarda (PCT) is the most common porphyria and results from uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase (UROD) deficiency.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A young male patient presents with ptosis which reportedly worsens in the evening and improves in the morning. He also complains of excessive fatiguability towards the end of the day which improves with rest. Placing an ice pack over his eyes significantly decreases the ptosis. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Myasthenia gravis

From the given clinical picture, myasthenia gravis is the most likely diagnosis. This patient has symptoms of ptosis, progressive weakness, and excessive fatiguability which improves with rest.

Myasthenia gravis is an autoimmune neuromuscular junction disorder that is characterized by weakness and fatigability of skeletal muscles. It is due to the autoantibody-mediated destruction of the acetylcholine receptors (AChRs) at the post-synaptic membrane. This consequentially leads to a decreased transmission at the neuromuscular junction. Failure of transmission results in muscle weakness.

Females are more commonly affected than males and the disease tends to occur in middle age.

Clinical features of myasthenia gravis:

* Muscle weakness and fatiguability increase with repeated use or during late in the day and may improve following rest or sleep. Limb weakness is proximal and asymmetrical

* Cranial muscles particularly the lids and extraocular muscles are involved early in the course - diplopia, ptosis

* Facial weakness - snarling expression on smiling

* Weakness in chewing

* Speech with nasal timbre due to the weakness of palate and tongue

* Difficulty in swallowing

* Deep tendon reflexes are intact

* Myasthenic crisis - acute exacerbation of muscle weakness especially intercostal and diaphragmatic muscles resulting in ventilatory failure. It is most commonly due to infection and anticholinesterase medication overuse.

Myasthenia gravis is associated with thymoma and other autoimmune diseases such as Hashimoto's thyroiditis, Grave's disease, neuromyelitis optics, systemic lupus erythematosus, etc.

Diagnosis:

* Ice-pack test - application of ice pack over the eyes improves ptosis (decreases activity of acetylcholinesterase, this increases the amount of acetylcholine in the synaptic cleft and increases transmission)

* Antibodies associated with myasthenia gravis: Anti-AChR antibodies, Anti-MuSK antibodies, Anti-LRP4 antibodies

* Repetitive nerve stimulation test shows a decremental response.

* Edrophonium chloride or Tensilon test - improvement of symptoms occurs on injecting edrophonium. Edrophonium is an acetylcholinesterase inhibitor. This increases the amount of acetylcholine in the synaptic cleft and improves transmission.

Treatment:

* Anticholinesterase drugs - Pyridostigmine.

* Thymectomy.

* Immunosuppression therapy with glucocorticoids, azathioprine, tacrolimus, rituximab, etc.

* Plasmapheresis and intravenous immunoglobulin.
questions.learning: Myasthenia gravis From the given clinical picture, myasthenia gravis is the most likely diagnosis. This patient has symptoms of ptosis, progressive weakness, and excessive fatiguability which improves with rest.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: In which type of hanging does the weight of the head act as a constricting force?
questions.explanation: Hanging is defined as a form of ligature strangulation where the force is provided by the weight of the body. In "complete hanging," the entire body is suspended and the feet do not touch the ground. In "partial hanging," some part of the body (feet, knees, or even the buttocks) remains in contact with the ground or a supporting surface. In these instances, the full weight of the body is not used; instead, only the weight of the head or the upper torso acts as the constricting force on the ligature around the neck. "Typical hanging" (Option C) refers to the knot being at the occiput. "Atypical hanging" (Option D) refers to the knot being at any other position. Partial hanging is frequently seen in suicidal cases, where individuals use low points of attachment like door handles or bedposts. Forensic examiners must be aware that even a small force (about 2-5 kg) is sufficient to compress the jugular veins and carotid arteries, leading to death
questions.learning: Hanging is defined as a form of ligature strangulation where the force is provided by the weight of the body. In "complete hanging," the entire body is suspended and the feet do not touch the ground.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 50-year-old man presents with anemia, fever, and recurrent epistaxis, along with hepatosplenomegaly on examination. Laboratory investigations reveal severe anemia (Hb 6 g/dL), marked leukocytosis (TLC 40,000/cu.mm) with 10% blasts, and profound thrombocytopenia (12,000/cu.mm). Cytogenetic analysis of the blasts shows a t(8;21) translocation. What is the most likely diagnosis in this patient?
questions.explanation: The patient presents with signs of bone marrow failure (anemia, recurrent nosebleeds from thrombocytopenia) and an acute proliferative process (fever, high WBC, organomegaly). The definitive diagnostic hallmark provided is the presence of the t(8;21) chromosomal translocation in the blasts. According to the WHO classification, the presence of specific genetic abnormalities like t(8;21) allows for a diagnosis of Acute Myeloblastic Leukemia (AML) regardless of the blast percentage (although this patient has a significant 10% in the blood). This specific translocation corresponds to the FAB M2 subtype and is generally associated with a favorable prognosis. ALL (Option A) would show lymphoblasts and different translocations. Preleukemia (Option C) refers to MDS, which lacks high blast counts or specific AML-defining translocations. Aleukemic leukemia (Option D) occurs when blasts are present in the marrow but the blood count is low, unlike the count seen here
questions.learning: The patient presents with signs of bone marrow failure (anemia, recurrent nosebleeds from thrombocytopenia) and an acute proliferative process (fever, high WBC, organomegaly).

questions.text: A 14-year-old rape victim is 22 weeks pregnant and she would like to terminate her pregnancy. Which of the following is done under the MTP Act?
options: Opinion of 1 doctor is enough upto 24 weeks
Termination allowed between 20-24 weeks only if detrimental to mother's life
Can terminate pregnancy upto 24 weeks for sexual assault
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Can terminate pregnancy upto 24 weeks for sexual assault

According to the MTP Act with 2021 amendments, pregnancy can be terminated upto 24 weeks of gestation in victims of rape and incest, fetal anomalies, or congenital malformations.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 55-year-old man presents with a lump in the left testis and is diagnosed with left testicular carcinoma following imaging and biopsy. Which lymph node group is most commonly involved first in the spread of this malignancy?
questions.explanation: The lymphatic drainage of the testes follows their embryological path of descent. The testes originate in the high posterior abdominal wall near the kidneys and descend into the scrotum during development, carrying their blood supply and lymphatic vessels with them. Therefore, lymphatic drainage from the testes bypasses the superficial lymph nodes and goes directly to the "para-aortic" (lumbar) lymph nodes at the level of the renal vessels (L1-L2). For the left testicle, the primary drainage is specifically to the left para-aortic nodes. The inguinal lymph nodes (Option A) drain the scrotum and the skin of the penis, but not the testicle itself; they only become involved in testicular cancer if the tumor invades the scrotal skin. The iliac (Option C) and precaval (Option D) nodes are further downstream or lateral to the primary drainage site. Understanding this "leapfrog" drainage pattern is crucial for the staging and surgical management (like Retroperitoneal Lymph Node Dissection) of testicular malignancies

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Match the following: 1. Leprosy 2. Tinea capitis 3. Contact dermatitis 4. Lupus vulgaris a. Biopsy b. Patch test c. KOH mount d. Slit smear
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 1-d, 2-c, 3-b, 4-a

Match the Following:

A. Leprosy → D. Split skin smear

• Caused by Mycobacterium leprae
• Diagnosis depends on demonstrating bacilli

Split Skin Smear

• Taken from ear lobes, lesions, or cooler areas
• Stained with Ziehl–Neelsen (modified)
• Shows acid-fast bacilli (AFB)
• Helps calculate Bacillary Index (BI) → classification (PB vs MB)

B. Tinea capitis → C. KOH Wet Mount

• Fungal infection of scalp (dermatophytes: Trichophyton, Microsporum)

KOH Preparation

• Hair/skin scrapings + 10–20% KOH
• KOH dissolves keratin → leaves fungal elements
• Shows:

• Hyphae
• Spores (endothrix/ectothrix)

C. Contact Dermatitis → B. Patch Test

• Type IV hypersensitivity reaction (delayed)

Patch Test

• Standard allergens applied on back for 48 hours
• Reading at 48–72 hours
• Identifies specific allergen

D. Lupus vulgaris → A. Biopsy

• Cutaneous tuberculosis (paucibacillary)

Biopsy Findings

• Granulomas with epithelioid cells + Langhans giant cells
• Caseation may be minimal
• AFB often not easily seen

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 5-year-old girl presents with pubic and axillary hair growth, as observed by her mother. Which of the following conditions is least likely to explain these signs?
questions.explanation: In a 5-year-old girl, the appearance of pubic and axillary hair growth (precocious adrenarche/pseudopuberty) indicates an excess of androgens. Congenital adrenal hyperplasia (CAH) variants like 21-hydroxylase deficiency (Option B), 11 -hydroxylase deficiency (Option C), and 3 -hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase deficiency (Option D) all cause a "shunting" of precursors toward the androgen pathway, leading to virilization and hair growth . In contrast, 17-hydroxylase deficiency (Option A) is characterized by a complete block in the production of both cortisol and androgens. This results in an excess of mineralocorticoids (causing hypertension) and a profound lack of androgens. Therefore, a child with 17-hydroxylase deficiency would NEVER present with pubic or axillary hair; they would instead experience delayed puberty. Thus, 17-hydroxylase deficiency is the definitive "least likely" (or impossible) diagnosis for the described virilizing signs. Understanding the steroidogenic pathway is essential for differentiating these complex adrenal disorders

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: In which of the following conditions is Gelle's test negative?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Otosclerosis

Gelle’s test is negative when the ossicular chain is fixed as in cases of otosclerosis.

Gelle’s test is a test of bone conduction and examines the effect of increased air pressure in the ear canal on hearing. In normal individuals, due to the increased intralabrynthine pressure applied by the Seigel's speculum, there is immobility of the basilar membrane, as the tympanic membrane and the ossicles are pushed inwards (medially). This results in decreased hearing. But, in diseased individuals, where the ossicular chain and the tympanic membrane are fixed or disconnected, no change in hearing is observed.

Gelle’s test is positive in normal persons and in those with sensorineural hearing loss.

Note: This test was commonly used for the diagnosis of otosclerosis, but has since been replaced by tympanometry.
questions.learning: Otosclerosis Gelle’s test is negative when the ossicular chain is fixed as in cases of otosclerosis. Gelle’s test is a test of bone conduction and examines the effect of increased air pressure in the ear canal on hearing.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The hard palate contains ________
options: Keratinised epithelium, submucosa, minor salivary glands
Keratinised epithelium, absent submucosa, no salivary glands
Non-keratinised epithelium, submucosa, minor salivary glands
Non-keratinised epithelium , absent submucosa, minor salivary glands
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Keratinised epithelium, submucosa, minor salivary glands

The hard palate contains keratinised stratified squamous epithelium, has a submucosa, and contains minor salivary gland. This keratinised stratified squamous epithelium has regional variations and may be orthokeratinised or parakeratinised(found in hard palate and gingiva).

The bony structure of the hard palate is covered by a firmly attached mucosa in the central part. In the lateral parts, the hard palate also has a submucosal layer containing blood vessels. There are minor mucous type salivary glands in the submucosa in the posterior part of the hard palate.

(Note: In the orthokeratinized epithelium the cell nuclei disappear in the keratinized layer, whereas in the parakeratinized epithelium flattened, highly condensed nuclei remain in the cell cytoplasm of the keratinized layer until exfoliation)
questions.learning: Keratinised epithelium, submucosa, minor salivary glands The hard palate contains keratinised stratified squamous epithelium, has a submucosa, and contains minor salivary gland.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following arteries is being palpated in the given image?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Posterior tibial artery

The given image shows the physician's fingertips between the medial malleolus and the calcaneal tendon, and the artery being palpated here is the posterior tibial artery.

Dorsalis pedis artery:

Popliteal artery:

Anterior Tibial Artery -

* Anteriorly midway between the medial and lateral malleoli, lateral to the EHL tendon, against the lower end of the tibia

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following is the gold standard treatment for the condition shown in the image?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Endothermal ablation

The gold standard for the treatment of varicose veins is endothermal ablation. The given image shows tortuous dilated veins suggestive of varicose veins.

The management of varicose veins is as follows:

Incompetence
Management

Great saphenous vein (GSV) and saphenofemoral (SFJ)

• Endothermal ablation (gold standard treatment for varicose veins). It includes:

• Endovenous laser ablation (EVLA)
• Radiofrequency ablation (RFA)

• Trendelenburg procedure (Flush Ligation of Saphenofemoral Junction (SFJ) after ligation of 6 tributaries) ± stripping (retrogradely up to the knee, to prevent saphenous nerve injury.)

Short saphenous vein (SSJ) and saphenopopliteal (SPJ)

• Flush ligation of SPJ
• Endothermal ablation

• Endovenous laser ablation (EVLA)
• Radiofrequency ablation (RFA)

Perforator

• Dodd and Crockett surgery - Multiple subfascial ligations
• Subfascial endoscopic perforator surgery (SEPS) - smaller incision, so cosmetically better
• Endothermal ablation:

• Endovenous laser ablation (EVLA)
• Radiofrequency ablation (RFA)

New treatment modalities:

* Foam sclerotherapy - The Tessari method is a widely used method to prepare foam for sclerotherapy. Sclerosant: air ratio taken is 1:3 or 1:4

* Endovenous glue therapy - endoluminal application of cyanoacrylate adhesive

* Transilluminated powered phlebectomy

Option B: Injection sclerotherapy: In this technique, a detergent is injected directly into the veins.

* Most commonly used sclerosant is Sodium tetradecyl sulfate.

* The detergent causes endothelial damage leading to thrombosis, fibrosis, and obliteration (sclerosis) of veins.

* Injection sclerotherapy alone can be successful in varicose veins <3 mm in diameter and in telangiectatic vessels.

* Complications from sclerotherapy include allergic reaction, local hyperpigmentation, air embolism, stroke and pain at the site of injection.

Option C: Phlebectomy -Small stab incisions are made to revert the reflux by occluding the refluxing tributaries of the veins.

Option D: Saphenous vein ligation and stripping is the preferred therapy for patients with GSVs of very large diameter (>2 cm).

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A 40-year-old woman with multidrug-resistant tuberculosis presents with fatigue, constipation, weight gain, and neck swelling. Which of the following drugs is implicated in this case?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Ethionamide

The given clinical features are suggestive of hypothyroidism with goiter, which is a known adverse effect of ethionamide.

Mutidrug-resistant tuberculosis (MDR-TB) is treated with 2nd line agents that include ethionamide (ETH). ETH is not a first-line agent due to its gastrointestinal side effects. Ethionamide inhibits activity of the InhA gene product, resulting in inhibition of mycolic acid synthesis. It is structurally related to thionamides (propylthiouracil and methimazole) and therefore causes hypothyroidism by preventing organification of iodine in thyroid hormone synthesis. Another antitubercular drug that can cause hypothyroidism is Para-amino salicylic acid (PAS).

ETH/PAS-induced hypothyroidism should be treated with thyroxine replacement therapy, instead of changing the regimen. Thyroid function usually optimizes within 2 months after completing MDR therapy.
Ethionamide also causes hepatotoxicity and neurological adverse effects and may require pyridoxine supplementation.

MDR-TB is when there is resistance to atleast isoniazid and rifampicin which are the most potent first-line drugs. The treatment of MDR-TB is curated with drugs grouped into different classes by the world health organization (WHO).

Group A: Levofloxacin, bedaquiline, linezolid
Group B: Clofazimine, cycloserine
Group C: Ethambutol, pyrazinamide, delamanid, ethionamide
In patients treated previously or with additional drug resistance, a longer MDR-TB regimen of 18-20 months is recommended. Drugs belonging to group A are preferred along with one drug from group B whenever possible. A shorter regimen of 6 months including bedaquiline with other drugs can be used in patients not treated before and without extensive disease. In pregnant women with MRD-TB, drugs such as bedaquiline and delamanid should be avoided.

Other options :
Option A : Pyrazinamide inhibits fatty acid synthase-I leading to inhibition of cell membrane synthesis. Pyrazinamide causes hyperuricemia and hepatotoxicity.
Option C : Adverse effects of cycloserine are mainly neurological. Half of the patients on cycloserine (1g/day) experience neuropsychiatric symptoms. It ranges from headaches to psychosis, seizures, and suicidal ideas.

Option D : Streptomycin is an aminoglycoside which binds to the 30S ribosomal subunit and interferes with the initiation of protein synthesis.  It is a second-line agent for the treatment of active tuberculosis. Streptomycin produces ototoxicity, vestibulotoxicity, optic nerve dysfunction, including scotomas, and peripheral neuritis.
questions.learning: Ethionamide — The given clinical features are suggestive of hypothyroidism with goiter, which is a known adverse effect of ethionamide. Mutidrug-resistant tuberculosis (MDR-TB) is treated with 2nd line agents that include ethionamide (ETH).

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which constituent is the major determinant of serum osmolality among the given options?
questions.explanation: Sodium is the predominant cation in the extracellular fluid and the primary determinant of serum osmolality. This is evident from the standard clinical formula for estimated serum osmolality: Sodium is multiplied by two to account for its accompanying anions (mainly chloride and bicarbonate), demonstrating that it contributes the largest share to total osmolality. Potassium (Option A) is mainly an intracellular cation and is present in low serum concentrations, so its osmotic contribution is minimal. Bicarbonate (Option C) acts as a buffer but is present in much lower concentrations than sodium. Hydrogen ions (Option D) regulate pH and exist in extremely low concentrations, making their osmotic effect negligible. Therefore, sodium is the principal regulator of serum osmolality and water balance, and disturbances in serum sodium directly lead to osmotic shifts causing cerebral edema or dehydration

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: A patient planned for elective hip surgery is currently on aspirin, enalapril, a multivitamin, and metoprolol. The procedure is scheduled to take place in five days. What is the most appropriate perioperative management of these medications?
options: Stop aspirin to minimize perioperative bleeding risk
Stop metoprolol to increase cardiac output
Increase aspirin dosage for additional analgesic benefit
questions.explanation: ACE inhibitors like enalapril should typically be discontinued 24 hours prior to elective surgery to prevent clinically significant intraoperative hypotension. Orthopedic procedures, such as the hip surgery mentioned, generally allow the continuation of aspirin (Option B) because the cardiovascular risks of stopping it often outweigh the modest bleeding risk. Beta-blockers like metoprolol (Option C) must always be continued perioperatively; abrupt withdrawal can lead to dangerous sympathetic hyperactivity, tachycardia, hypertension, myocardial ischemia, or mortality. Increasing the aspirin dosage (Option D) has no proven analgesic benefit in this context and only serves to increase the surgical bleeding risk unnecessarily. Standard preoperative management usually involves continuing most chronic medications, such as antiepileptics, antidepressants, and calcium channel blockers, while specifically stopping ACE inhibitors and certain hypoglycemics. Therefore, the most appropriate step for this patient is to discontinue the enalapril one day before the procedure to ensure hemodynamic stability during anesthesia
questions.learning: ACE inhibitors like enalapril should typically be discontinued 24 hours prior to elective surgery to prevent clinically significant intraoperative hypotension.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: The following device shown attached to the baby is used in all except :
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Measure central cyanosis

The image shows a pulse oximeter. It cannot be reliably used to measure central cyanosis.

A pulse oximeter employs spectrophotometry to measure the percentage saturation of oxygen at a peripheral site. In cases of markedly deranged hemoglobin (Hb) levels and abnormal Hb, pulse oximetry doesn't correlate with central cyanosis, which depends on the absolute value of reduced Hb.

A pulse oximeter can be used for assessing response to resuscitation, titrating oxygen therapy in newborns, monitoring apnea (bradycardia and desaturation), confirming endotracheal tube placement, evaluating the effectiveness of bag and mask ventilation, and monitoring for hypoxia during suction and laryngoscopy.

Cyanosis is characterized by a bluish discoloration of the skin and mucous membranes due to elevated levels of reduced Hb (more than 4 g/dL) or Hb derivatives. It is examined in the nail beds and mucous membranes, earlobes, lips, and fingers. It can be classified into central and peripheral types.

Central cyanosis can be due to reduced oxygen saturation or the presence of abnormal Hb derivatives. Causes include high altitudes, impaired pulmonary function, anatomic shunts, and abnormal Hb. Both the mucous membranes and skin will be affected.

The absolute amount of reduced Hb rather than its relative quantity is significant in cyanosis. In severe anemia, even with marked arterial desaturation, cyanosis may not be present. Conversely, polycythemia patients are prone to cyanosis even at higher oxygen saturation levels.

The presence of abnormal Hb species may lead to errors in SpO2 readings. In a patient with methemoglobinemia, the SpO2 will be 80% to 85%, irrespective of arterial saturation (SaO2). A patient with carbon monoxide poisoning will have a falsely elevated SpO2 level. A co-oximeter is a better device to measure abnormal hemoglobins.

Carbon monoxide poisoning does not lead to true cyanosis. It causes cherry red discoloration.

Peripheral cyanosis occurs due to decreased blood flow and excessive oxygen extraction from normally saturated arterial blood. The mucous membranes of the oral cavity and sublingual mucosa are spared. The causes include reduced cardiac output, cold exposure, and arterial and venous obstruction. Here, the degree of cyanosis will generally correspond to SpO2 readings. However, the SpO2 levels may be falsely low despite normal SaO2.
questions.learning: Measure central cyanosis — The image shows a pulse oximeter. It cannot be reliably used to measure central cyanosis.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: The addition of Vitamin A to butter is an example of which of the following public health interventions?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Food fortification

Food fortification is the deliberate addition of essential micronutrients to commonly consumed foods to prevent or correct nutrient deficiencies in the population. Addition of vitamin A to butter is an example of food fortification.

Why not the other options?

• A. Food adulteration: Addition of inferior or harmful substances to food, reducing its quality or safety.
• C. Food enrichment: Restoration of nutrients lost during food processing to their original levels (e.g., adding B vitamins to refined flour).
• D. Food addition: Not a recognized public health nutrition intervention.
questions.learning: Food fortification Food fortification is the deliberate addition of essential micronutrients to commonly consumed foods to prevent or correct nutrient deficiencies in the population.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A 25-year-old male presented to the emergency department with pain and swelling of the right knee. Radiograph shows the following finding. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Patellar fracture

The radiograph shows the displaced patellar fracture.

A patellar fracture can either occur via a direct injury to the knee or because of a violent contraction of the quadriceps.

The fracture may be undisplaced either because of the pre-patellar expansion of the quadriceps tendon which holds the fragments together or because of the patellar retinaculae on the sides.

Patellar fracture results in the disruption of the extensor apparatus (not the flexor apparatus).

Due to the disruption of the extensor apparatus, the patient will not be able to lift his leg with the knee in full extension; it remains in a position short of full extension (extensor lag). Clinically, it can be tested using the Active Straight leg raising (SLR) test, which the patient will not be able to perform.

The extensor apparatus of the knee includes the Quadriceps femoris muscle with its tendon, the patella bone and, the ligamentum patellae with its insertion into the tibial tuberosity.

An un-displaced fracture of the patella is treated with a plaster cast extending from the groin to just above the malleoli, with the knee in full extension. This is called as a cylinder cast and is usually left in place for a period of at least 3 weeks.

A two part fracture (Displaced transverse fracture) of the patella must be reduced, and the fragments are fixed with tension band wiring using K wires and the extensor retinaculae is repaired

Other treatment options which are available for patellar fracture are:

* Undisplaced patellar fractures with minimal joint incongruity and intact extensor retinaculum can be treated by cylinder cast.

* Displaced patellar fractures are usually treated by tension band wiring.

* Severely comminuted fractures where the reduction of the fragments is difficult are treated by patellectomy.

Pearl PF1177: Tension band wiring

A tension band wire is a form of internal fixation used to convert distraction forces into compression forces, promoting bone healing.

It is used in:

* Fracture patella

* Fracture olecranon

* Fracture lateral malleolus

* Fracture greater trochanter
questions.learning: Patellar fracture — The radiograph shows the displaced patellar fracture. A patellar fracture can either occur via a direct injury to the knee or because of a violent contraction of the quadriceps.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: A 28-year-old man has recurrent episodes of mania and depression and is diagnosed with bipolar disorder. He is currently stable and requires long-term therapy to prevent future mood episodes. Which is the drug of choice for maintenance treatment?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Lithium

Lithium is the drug of choice for long-term maintenance treatment of bipolar disorder. It is effective in preventing both manic and depressive episodes, reducing relapse rates, and lowering the risk of suicide. Lithium is considered the gold standard mood stabilizer for maintenance therapy in patients with bipolar disorder.

Why not the other options?

• B. Diazepam: A benzodiazepine used for acute agitation, anxiety, or insomnia; it has no role in long-term mood stabilization.
• C. Fluoxetine: An SSRI antidepressant that may precipitate mania if used alone in bipolar disorder; it is not used as monotherapy for maintenance.
• D. Haloperidol: A typical antipsychotic used for acute manic episodes, but not the drug of choice for long-term maintenance due to extrapyramidal side effects.
questions.learning: Lithium Lithium is the drug of choice for long-term maintenance treatment of bipolar disorder. It is effective in preventing both manic and depressive episodes, reducing relapse rates, and lowering the risk of suicide.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: In a gunshot injury where autopsy findings show an entry wound with inverted margins and surrounding tattooing, but no blackening or singeing of hair, what is the most probable range from which the firearm was discharged?
questions.explanation: Forensic determination of the firing range is based on artifacts found on the skin. Tattooing (peppering) is caused by unburnt gunpowder particles embedding in the skin and is the hallmark of a Close shot (typically within a range of 1 to 3 feet for handguns). In this case, the absence of blackening (smoke deposit) and singeing of hair suggests the weapon was far enough away that the heat and smoke didn't reach the skin, but close enough for gunpowder particles to leave their mark. A Contact shot (Option A) would show a muzzle mark, "star-shaped" tearing, and internal soot. A Near shot (Option B) would definitely include blackening and singeing. A Distant shot (Option D) would show only the entry hole (abrasion collar) without any tattooing, blackening, or singeing. Therefore, the combination of tattooing without smoke deposits is the classic forensic indicator for a "Close range" gunshot

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: What is the best position for a conscious patient to be in during the insertion of a Ryle's tube?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Sitting with neck flexion

The best position for a conscious patient to be in during the insertion of Ryle's tube (RT) is sitting with neck flexion. The described position helps in directing the RT towards the esophagus and also prevents it from coiling in the oropharynx or entering the trachea.

RT, also known as nasogastric (NG) tube, measures 120-125 cm. It has 4 markings at 40cm (cardia), 50cm (body), 60cm (pylorus), and 70 cm (duodenum) to indicate the approximate position after the placement.

Indications for NG tube:

• Feeding in patients with dysphagia, decreased appetite, or those who are nil per os (NPO) for medical or surgical reasons.
• Aspiration of gastric fluid
• Gastric decompression in cases of intestinal obstruction and paralytic ileus.
• Zollinger-Ellison syndrome
• Bowel irrigation

The absolute contraindications for an NG tube are severe midface trauma, recent nasal surgery, and basilar skull fractures

Steps for the correct insertion of RT in an adult:

1. Examination of the patient’s nostril for any anatomical abnormalities and then instillation with 10 ml of 1% lignocaine
2. NEX method is used to measure the length of the RT:  Place the exit port of the tube at the tip of the nose. Extend the tube to the earlobe, and then to the xiphisternum.
3. The patient is asked to sit upright with partial neck flexion. The tip of the Ryle’s tube is lubricated and passed along the floor of the nasal passage until a resistance is felt(corresponds to nasopharynx)
4. The patient is subsequently asked to swallow water to guide the tube through the esophagus into the stomach until the marked length (based on the NEX method).
5. NG tube is finally taped to secure it in place.

Confirmation of the correct position is done by:

1. Auscultation in the epigastric area while injecting a bolus of air
2. X-ray chest to locate the lead markers
3. Aspiration of contents and subsequently confirming gastric origin (pH <6 indicates gastric placement)

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 55-year-old shipbuilding worker with a 25- year occupational history presents with dyspnea. Which specific malignancy is most likely associated with his occupational exposure?
questions.explanation: The patient’s 25-year history of working in the shipbuilding industry is a classic occupational risk factor for asbestos exposure. While asbestos exposure increases the risk of many lung cancers, Malignant Mesothelioma (Option B) is the most specific malignancy associated with it. Mesothelioma is an aggressive cancer of the pleural or peritoneal lining and is almost exclusively linked to prior asbestos inhalation. Bronchogenic carcinoma (Option A), including small cell (Option C) and squamous cell (Option D) types, are more common overall in the general population and are primarily driven by smoking, although their risk is significantly multiplied in asbestos workers. However, the term "most specific" refers to the cancer that is pathognomonic for the exposure. Therefore, given the long-term shipyard history, Malignant Mesothelioma is the expected definitive diagnosis. Diagnosis is usually confirmed by pleural biopsy and imaging showing diffuse pleural thickening

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: Which of the following is the mechanism of action of Local anesthetics?
questions.explanation: Local anesthetics (such as lidocaine or bupivacaine) work by preventing the generation and conduction of nerve impulses. Their primary mechanism of action is to reversibly block voltage-gated sodium (Na+) channels on the neuronal cell membrane. By binding to the internal portion of the channel, they prevent the influx of sodium ions required for depolarization, thus halting the propagation of an action potential along the nerve fiber. They do not function by stimulating calcium channels (Option B), blocking chloride channels (Option C), or stimulating potassium channels (Option D). Local anesthetics preferentially block smaller, unmyelinated fibers (carrying pain and temperature sensations) before larger, myelinated motor fibers. This selective blockage allows for "differential blockade," where pain can be eliminated while some motor function is preserved. Toxicity can occur if the anesthetic is injected intravascularly, leading to cardiovascular and central nervous system effects
questions.learning: Local anesthetics (such as lidocaine or bupivacaine) work by preventing the generation and conduction of nerve impulses. Their primary mechanism of action is to reversibly block voltage-gated sodium (Na+) channels on the neuronal cell membrane.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A couple brings their 4-year-old child to the outpatient department due to self-mutilating behavior and poor growth. Which condition and associated enzyme deficiency could explain these symptoms?
questions.explanation: Self-mutilation (such as biting lips and fingers) combined with poor growth and neurological symptoms like dystonia is the hallmark of Lesch-Nyhan syndrome. This X-linked recessive disorder is caused by a near-complete deficiency of the enzyme Hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyltransferase (HGPRT). HGPRT is essential for the purine salvage pathway; its absence leads to massive overproduction of uric acid. This results in hyperuricemia, gouty arthritis, and severe neurological dysfunction. Homogentisic Aciduria (Option B) is Alkaptonuria, which causes dark urine and joint cartilage damage but not self-mutilation. Phenylalanine Hydroxylase deficiency (Option C) causes Phenylketonuria (PKU), leading to intellectual disability and a "mousy" odor, but not the specific aggressive self-harm seen in Lesch-Nyhan. Benzoyl Acidase deficiency (Option D) is not a standard clinical metabolic disorder associated with these symptoms. Therefore, HGPRT deficiency is the definitive enzymatic diagnosis for a child presenting with this unique behavioral phenotype
questions.learning: Self-mutilation (such as biting lips and fingers) combined with poor growth and neurological symptoms like dystonia is the hallmark of Lesch-Nyhan syndrome.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: According to the American Heart Association (AHA), what is the 6th link added to the chain of survival?
questions.explanation: The American Heart Association (AHA) expanded the Chain of Survival concept by adding a sixth link: recovery and rehabilitation. This addition reflects the growing recognition that survival extends far beyond the immediate resuscitation period. The complete AHA Chain of Survival now includes early recognition and activation of emergency response, high-quality CPR, rapid defibrillation, advanced life support, post-cardiac arrest care, and finally, recovery and rehabilitation. Rapid defibrillation (Option A) is already included as the critical third link. High-quality CPR (Option C) constitutes the second link, emphasizing proper depth and rate. Advanced airway management (Option D) is part of the fourth link (advanced life support) but should never interfere with or delay chest compressions and defibrillation. Therefore, the newly introduced sixth link acknowledges the long-term support needed for survivors
questions.learning: The American Heart Association (AHA) expanded the Chain of Survival concept by adding a sixth link: recovery and rehabilitation. This addition reflects the growing recognition that survival extends far beyond the immediate resuscitation period.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text:
A 6-year-old girl born out of nonconsanguineous marriage presented with rachitic changes in limbs since 1½ years of age for which she has received multiple courses of vitamin D. Investigations showed the following. What is the most likely diagnosis?

Parameter
Lab determined value

Calcium
9.5 mg/dl

Phosphate
1.6 mg/dl

Alkaline Phosphatase (ALP)
814 IU

Serum Parathyroid hormone (PTH)
Normal levels

Serum electrolytes
Within Normal Limits (WNL)

Serum creatinine
Within Normal Limits (WNL)

Arterial Blood Gas analysis (ABG)
Within Normal Limits (WNL)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Hypophosphatemic rickets

A history of resistant rickets with normal levels of calcium (9 to 11 mg/dL), parathyroid hormone (PTH), arterial blood gas (ABG), with decreased phosphate (normal - 2.5 to 4.3 mg/dL), and elevated levels of alkaline phosphatase (ALP) (normal, 33 to 96 U/L) in a child is suggestive of hypophosphatemic rickets.

Hypophosphatemic rickets:

X-linked dominant hypophosphatemic rickets (XLH) is the most common genetic cause of rickets while the most common, overall is nutritional vitamin D deficiency. Mutations in the PHEX gene (phosphate-regulating endopeptidase on x chromosome) leads to increased FGF-23 (phosphatonin), which inhibits phosphate reabsorption in the proximal tubule levels and hence, causes increased excretion of phosphate. It also inhibits renal 1-alpha hydroxylase leading to reduced 1,25 dihydroxy vitamin D.

Causes of hypophosphatemic rickets include familial vitamin D resistance, autosomal dominant hypophosphatemic rickets, autosomal recessive hypophosphatemic rickets, tumor-induced rickets, McCune Albright syndrome, epidermal nevus syndrome, and neurofibromatosis.

In X-linked dominant hypophosphatemic rickets lower extremity abnormalities, short stature, poor growth, delayed dentition, and tooth abscesses are common.

The chart attached below summarizes the evaluation of hypophosphatemic rickets.

Patients with hypophosphatemic rickets respond well to oral phosphorus and 1,25-D (calcitriol). Phosphorus supplementation is usually given in 1-3 g elemental phosphorus divided into 4–5 doses. Frequent dosing reduces diarrhea, which is a complication of high-dose oral phosphorus.

Calcitriol is administered 30–70 ng/kg/day divided into 2 doses. Burosumab, a monoclonal antibody to FGF-23 can be used in children > 1 year of age with XLH rickets.

Further, Joulie's solution is also useful in the treatment of familial hypophosphatemic rickets. Joulie's solution includes contains 30.4 mg of phosphate/mL. The most common side effect is diarrhea.

Other options:

Option A: Vitamin D-dependent rickets type 1A is due to mutation in the gene coding for 1α-hydroxylase leading to reduced calcitriol levels (1,25-D). Type 1B is due to a mutation in the gene for 25-hydroxylase leading to reduced calcidiol (25-D). Type 2A have mutations in the gene coding for vitamin D receptor. Type 2B is due to the over-expression of a hormone response element-binding protein that interferes with the actions of 1,25-D. All of them have normal to low calcium levels, low phosphorus, elevated PTH and ALP levels.

Option B: Hypoparathyroidism will present with features of hypocalcemia. There will be a decrease in serum PTH levels and calcium levels.

Option C: In chronic renal failure, 1α-hydroxylase activity is reduced leading to reduced 1,25-D. They have normal to low calcium levels and elevated PTH and ALP levels. They have hyperphosphatemia due to decreased renal excretion of phosphate.

The image below summarizes the common features of rickets in children.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: In the history of public health, as a part of modern medicine, the following four distinct phases can be demarcated: 1. Health for All phase 2. Health promotional phase 3. Disease control phase 4. Social engineering phase Which one of the following represents the correct sequence of the phases in chronological order (from the oldest to the newest)?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 3 → 2 → 4 → 1

The historical evolution of public health can be broadly divided into four phases:

1. Disease control phase — Oldest

• Focused primarily on controlling communicable diseases through sanitation, vaccination, isolation and other disease-specific measures.

2. Health promotional phase

• Shifted emphasis toward health education, lifestyle modification and promotion of healthy behaviours.

3. Social engineering phase

• Recognized that health is strongly influenced by social, economic, environmental and political determinants.

4. Health for All phase — Newest

• Emphasized equity, primary health care and universal access to essential health services, particularly following the Alma-Ata Declaration.

Therefore:

Disease control → Health promotional → Social engineering → Health for All

3 → 2 → 4 → 1 → C.
