questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient presents with joint pain, fatigue, and abnormal liver function tests. Genetic testing is performed due to these symptoms and a relevant family history. Which gene mutation is most commonly associated with hemochromatosis?
questions.explanation: Hereditary Hemochromatosis is an autosomal recessive iron-overload disorder. It results from a mutation in the HFE gene (most commonly the C282Y mutation), which leads to excessive intestinal iron absorption. This excess iron is deposited in organs, particularly the liver, heart, and joints, causing the described symptoms of fatigue, joint pain (arthropathy), and liver dysfunction (cirrhosis). PTEN (Option B) is a tumor suppressor gene associated with Cowden syndrome and various cancers. The ATP7B gene (Option C) mutation is responsible for Wilson's disease, which involves copper overload. The MRP2 protein (Option D) is involved in bilirubin transport and is defective in Dubin-Johnson syndrome. Therefore, the HFE gene is the definitive genetic marker for hereditary hemochromatosis. Early diagnosis is critical, as the condition can be effectively managed with regular therapeutic phlebotomy to prevent permanent organ damage
questions.learning: Hereditary Hemochromatosis is an autosomal recessive iron-overload disorder. It results from a mutation in the HFE gene (most commonly the C282Y mutation), which leads to excessive intestinal iron absorption.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: What is the probable diagnosis based on the image of the scan given below?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Craniopharyngioma

The given MRI of the brain demonstrates a craniopharyngioma, which is a suprasellar tumour that arises from remnants of Rathke's pouch.

The two variants of craniopharyngioma are:

• Adamantinomatous type (common in children):  Predominantly solid with cystic components. Diagnostic features include compact lamellar keratin ("wet keratin") and areas of dystrophic calcification.
• Papillary type (common in adults): Contains both solid sheets and papillae lined by well-differentiated non-keratinized squamous epithelium.

These tumours are usually large and heterogeneous, displaying solid and cystic components. The cysts contain a cholesterol-rich, thick brownish-yellow fluid that is compared to 'machine oil'.

Clinical features include headaches (most common), visual abnormalities - decreased acuity and bitemporal hemianopia, GH deficiency, growth failure, delayed sexual maturation due to pituitary hypofunction, and polyuria (central diabetes insipidus).

Radiologically:

• CT may show calcifications associated with the solid and cystic wall components
• MRI is the imaging modality of choice which shows:

Cysts

T1
Iso to hyperintense to the brain (due to high protein content "machinery oil cysts")

T2
Mostly hyperintense

Solid component

T1
Vivid enhancement

T2
Variable or mixed

Craniopharyngiomas tend not to expand the pituitary fossa unless they become huge, which is a differentiating feature from pituitary macroadenomas.

Other options:

Option A: Pituitary apoplexy is an acute clinical condition associated with the rapid expansion of the pituitary gland, which is evident on an MRI as enhancement around a non-enhancing infarcted centre.
Option B: Pituitary macroadenoma (with cystic degeneration or necrosis) shows indentation at the diaphragma sellae, giving rise to a snowman/figure of eight appearance/cottage loaf. Calcification is often absent. The image below shows the snowman appearance:

Option C: Rathke cleft cyst shows no solid or enhancing component. Calcification is rare. It is unilocular and the majority are completely or mostly intrasellar.
questions.learning: Craniopharyngioma — The given MRI of the brain demonstrates a craniopharyngioma, which is a suprasellar tumour that arises from remnants of Rathke's pouch.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following DMARD use requires regular monitoring of visual acuity and fundus examination?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Hydroxychloroquine

Hydroxychloroquine toxicity causes bull’s eye maculopathy. Hence, ophthalmic monitoring every 12 months is necessary.

Hydroxychloroquine is generally used for the treatment of rheumatoid arthritis and malaria. Chloroquine binds to melanin in the retinal pigment epithelium, causing cytotoxic effects. RPE atrophy occurs in the macula, resulting in dark areas on the autofluorescence image.

Fundus image of bull’s eye maculopathy is shown below

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 55-year-old man presents with hematuria and a mass in the left kidney on a CECT scan, as shown below. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Renal cell carcinoma

The history of an elderly male presenting with painless hematuria, renal mass, and an axial renal cortical phase CECT image showing renal lesions with irregular enhancement is suggestive of renal cell carcinoma (RCC).

Renal cell carcinoma (RCC) is the most common malignant tumor of the kidney. It usually occurs in the age group 50–70 years and macroscopic hematuria is seen in about 60% of the cases. It usually presents with painless gross hematuria, flank pain, or painless flank mass.

Contrast-enhanced CT is the investigation of choice for RCC. On CT, small lesions enhance homogeneously, whereas larger lesions have irregular enhancement due to areas of necrosis. The clear cell subtype may show much stronger enhancement is a differential for angiomyolipoma. Still, it is essential to note that macroscopic fat is almost always associated with ossification or calcification.

T1-weighted MRI is often heterogeneous due to necrosis, hemorrhage, and solid components. T2-weighted MRI is hyperdense for clear cell RCC and hypodense for papillary RCC. Thus, a T2-weighted MRI can be used for histological diagnosis. Contrast-enhanced MRI is the investigation of choice for detecting vascular invasion of RCC.

Other options:

Renal angiomyolipoma: Angiomyolipomas are benign tumors that occur sporadically or in association with tuberous sclerosis. The mean age of presentation is 43 years, and there is a female predilection. CT findings show cortical lesions that demonstrate macroscopic fat (less than -20 HU) and absence of ossification or calcification.

Renal oncocytoma: They are relatively benign in nature and usually present in the 6th to 7th decade. An important point regarding this tumor is its similarity with RCC, and hence, it is very difficult to differentiate between them preoperatively. A sharp central stellate scar may be seen in one-third of the cases. But RCC may also show this stellate scar appearance in some cases.

Renal cyst: It is a broader term that includes the cystic lesions of the kidney. They can be simple cysts that are benign. Complex or complicated cystic lesions needs evaluation and can be malignant. Bosniak classification of renal cysts is given above.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 32 year old female nearing her due date has been admitted following regular contractions. The resident doctor did an examination and told the intern that the head is at +1 station. Where is the exact position of head?
options: High up in the false pelvis
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Just below ischial spine

The station is just below the ischial spine.

Station of the head is in relation to ischial spines as spines are the most prominent bony projections felt on internal examination.

The level of ischial spines is the halfway between the pelvic inlet and outlet. This level is known as station zero (0).

The levels above and below the spines are divided into fifths to represent centimeters. The station is said to be “O” if the presenting part is at the level of the spines. The station is stated in minus figures, if it is above the spines (–1 cm, –2 cm, –3 cm, –4 cm and –5 cm) and in plus figures if it is below the spines (+1 cm, +2 cm, +3 cm, +4 cm and +5 cm).

Stations of the presenting part
questions.learning: Just below ischial spine — The station is just below the ischial spine. Station of the head is in relation to ischial spines as spines are the most prominent bony projections felt on internal examination.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Re-infection with which of the following pathogens can cause severe or catastrophic symptoms despite the presence of existing antibodies?
questions.explanation: Dengue virus infection exhibits a unique immunological phenomenon known as Antibody-Dependent Enhancement (ADE). There are four distinct serotypes of the Dengue virus. When an individual is re-infected with a different serotype than the initial infection, the pre-existing antibodies from the first infection do not neutralize the new virus. Instead, they bind to it and facilitate its entry into macrophages via Fc receptors. This leads to a significantly higher viral load and a massive release of cytokines, resulting in "catastrophic" symptoms such as Dengue Hemorrhagic Fever (DHF) or Dengue Shock Syndrome (DSS). Yellow fever (Option B), Japanese encephalitis (Option C), and Zika (Option D) typically provide solid, neutralizing immunity after a single infection or vaccination. Therefore, because pre-existing antibodies paradoxically increase the severity of subsequent Dengue infections, it is the correct answer
questions.learning: Dengue virus infection exhibits a unique immunological phenomenon known as Antibody-Dependent Enhancement (ADE). There are four distinct serotypes of the Dengue virus.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: In the quadruple marker test, a 33-year-old G2P1L1 at 18 weeks of gestation was found to be at a high risk of neural tube defects and low risk of trisomy 21. What is the next investigation to be done?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Anomaly Scan

For a female with a quadruple test showing a low risk of trisomy 21, the next investigation to be done is an anomaly scan, as part of routine antenatal care.

Prenatal genetic counseling involves screening and diagnostic methods. The various screening methods are as follows

Dual test (1st trimester)
Triple test (2nd trimester)
Quadruple test
(2nd trimester)

1. Beta HCG

2. PAPPA (Pregnancy-associated plasma protein A)

This can be combined with nuchal translucency by USG

1. Beta HCG

2. Unconjugated estriol

3. MSAFP

1. Beta HCG

2. Unconjugated estriol

3. MSAFP

4. Serum inhibin A

The values of the parameters in trisomy 21 are as follows :

PAPP-A - low, MSAFP - low, unconjugated estriol - low,  NT - increased, Beta hCG - high, inhibin A - high.

If the screening tests report a high risk of aneuploidy, then the confirmatory diagnostic test is performed, depending on the trimester.

• Chorionic villus sampling - Transcervical - 10-13 weeks, transabdominal - 10 weeks to term
• Amniocentesis - After 15 weeks
• Cordocentesis - 18-20 weeks

Since the screening test report in the question mentions a low risk of trisomy 21, the female should be followed up with an anomaly scan, which is performed as a part of the antenatal care at 18-20 weeks. It gives a detailed survey of fetal anatomy, placental localization and the integrity of the cervical canal.

Other options :

Option A - Amniocentesis is a confirmatory karyotyping test performed if the initial screening test reveals a high risk of aneuploidy.

Option B - Chorionic villus sampling (CVS) is also a confirmatory test, hence done if there is a high risk of aneuploidy. Moreover, CVS is not performed at 18 weeks.

Option C - Non-invasive prenatal testing utilizes cell-free fetal DNA in the maternal blood. However, it is a screening test. Since the female here has already undergone a screening test, there is no benefit is subjecting her to a second screening test.
questions.learning: Anomaly Scan For a female with a quadruple test showing a low risk of trisomy 21, the next investigation to be done is an anomaly scan, as part of routine antenatal care.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: What is meant by using a split-thickness skin graft for wound closure on the thigh?
options: Epidermis and variable part of the dermis
questions.explanation: A split-thickness skin graft (STSG) is a surgical graft that includes the entire epidermis and a variable portion of the underlying dermis. It is "split" because it leaves the deep dermal layers and skin appendages (like sweat glands and hair follicles) at the donor site, allowing the donor area to heal spontaneously. Option A describes a Full-Thickness Skin Graft (FTSG), which includes the entire dermis. Option C is incorrect, as a graft consisting of only epidermis would not survive or provide adequate coverage. Option D refers to a composite graft or skin-flap, as grafts never include fat because they require a vascular bed to take. STSGs are preferred for covering large areas, such as the thigh, because they have a higher "take" rate compared to thicker grafts. Therefore, the inclusion of the epidermis and a partial thickness of the dermis is the definitive anatomical description of an STSG

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following is the best investigation to establish a diagnosis of GERD?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 24-hour ambulatory pH monitoring

24-hour ambulatory pH monitoring is the ‘gold standard’ to establish a diagnosis of GERD.

* Transient lower esophageal sphincter relaxations are the most important manometric findings in GERD.

24-hour ambulatory pH monitoring in GERD:

* In the proximal esophagus (15 cm above the LES), acid exposure normally occurs less than 1% of the time.

* In the distal esophagus (5 cm above the LES), it normally occurs less than 4% of the time.

De Meester score

* An overall score is obtained with the use of a formula that assigns a weight to each item according to its capacity to cause esophageal injury.

* A value greater than 14.7 indicates reflux.
questions.learning: 24-hour ambulatory pH monitoring 24-hour ambulatory pH monitoring is the ‘gold standard’ to establish a diagnosis of GERD. * Transient lower esophageal sphincter relaxations are the most important manometric findings in GERD.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A patient presents with hypotension associated with marked bradycardia (low heart rate). Which of the following is the most appropriate drug to increase both blood pressure and heart rate?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Dopamine

Dopamine is the preferred vasopressor in a patient with hypotension associated with marked bradycardia because it produces dose-dependent stimulation of β₁-adrenergic receptors, increasing heart rate (positive chronotropy), myocardial contractility (positive inotropy), and cardiac output, while α₁-mediated vasoconstriction at higher doses increases blood pressure.

Why not the other options?

• B. Adrenaline (Epinephrine): Increases both heart rate and blood pressure, but is primarily reserved for cardiac arrest, anaphylaxis, and refractory shock, not as the first choice for hypotension with bradycardia.
• C. Noradrenaline (Norepinephrine): Potent α₁ agonist causing vasoconstriction and increased blood pressure. It may cause reflex bradycardia and is preferred in septic shock, not in patients with significant bradycardia.
• D. Phenylephrine: Pure α₁ agonist that increases blood pressure but often causes reflex bradycardia, making it unsuitable when the heart rate is already low.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which mental functions are examined in the Mental State Examination (100-7)?
questions.explanation: In a Mental State Examination (MSE), the specific test of asking a patient to perform "100-7" (serial subtractions of 7 starting from 100) is used to evaluate the patient's Concentration and sustained attention. This task requires the patient to hold a number in their memory while performing a calculation, making it a sensitive indicator of cognitive focus. Judgment (Option A) is assessed by asking the patient how they would react to a social scenario (e.g., finding a stamped letter). Orientation (Option C) is assessed by checking the patient's knowledge of time, place, and person. Language (Option B) is evaluated through general conversation, naming objects, and comprehension tasks. Impairment in the "serial 7s" task is commonly seen in patients with delirium, dementia, or severe depression (pseudo-dementia). It is a standard component of the Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE). Accurately identifying which cognitive domain is being tested allows the psychiatrist to localize the mental dysfunction during the clinical evaluation. AAns AAns AAns AAns
questions.learning: In a Mental State Examination (MSE), the specific test of asking a patient to perform "100-7" (serial subtractions of 7 starting from 100) is used to evaluate the patient's Concentration and sustained attention.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A young woman presents with recurrent headaches, easy bruising, and episodes of visual blurring. Laboratory tests show an elevated platelet count, while red blood cell and white blood cell counts are normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: This clinical scenario describes Essential Thrombocytosis (ET), a myeloproliferative neoplasm characterized by a sustained elevation in the platelet count and a tendency for both thrombotic and hemorrhagic complications. The patient's symptoms of recurrent headaches and visual blurring are common manifestations of microvascular occlusion caused by excessive platelets. Easy bruising occurs despite high platelet counts because the platelets may be functionally defective or cause acquired von Willebrand syndrome. In ET, the red blood cell and white blood cell counts typically remain within normal limits, which distinguishes it from other myeloproliferative disorders like Polycythemia Vera, where red cells are elevated, or Chronic Myeloid Leukemia, where white cells are markedly increased. Diagnosis often requires identifying characteristic mutations in JAK2, CALR, or MPL genes. Management focuses on reducing the risk of thrombosis using antiplatelet agents like aspirin or cytoreductive therapy in high-risk patients
questions.learning: This clinical scenario describes Essential Thrombocytosis (ET), a myeloproliferative neoplasm characterized by a sustained elevation in the platelet count and a tendency for both thrombotic and hemorrhagic complications.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 35-year-old female patient presents to you with fever, breathlessness, and cough with expectoration. A CT scan was done which is shown below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Consolidation with air bronchogram

The given history and the CT scan image are highly suggestive of pneumonia in which, consolidation with an air bronchogram can be seen.

A patient presenting with fever, breathlessness, and cough with expectoration is most likely suffering from pneumonia. Other symptoms include nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, fatigue, headache, myalgias, arthralgias, etc. The CT image shows a sharply demarcated homogenous consolidation that crosses segmental boundaries and involves only a single lobe. It is suggestive of lobar pneumonia.

In lobar pneumonia, the infection develops within the distal airspaces. It spreads via the collateral air drift and produces homogenous opacification of complete or partial lung segments. The airways remain patent as they are not primarily involved. Patent bronchi may be seen within the area of consolidation called air bronchograms. Total resolution of the opacification occurs within 4-6 weeks.

The most common organism implicated in community-acquired adult bacterial pneumonia is Streptococcus pneumoniae. Some of the predisposing factors include:

• Chronic illness
• Splenectomy
• Alcoholism
• Sickle cell disease

Other options:

Option B: A mediastinal mass can be in one of the three mediastinal compartments namely the anterior, middle, or posterior compartment. CT scan is the only imaging modality that should be done for the evaluation in most instances. Barium studies are indicated in patients with posterior mediastinal masses. Given below is a CT image of a large mass in the left anterior mediastinum, most likely a thymoma.

Option C: Pleural effusion is the accumulation of fluid within the pleural space. It can be either transudative (seen in cardiac failure) or exudative (seen in malignancies, infections, pulmonary embolism, etc.). On a CT image, pleural effusion appears as a dependent sickle-shaped opacity of low attenuation. The image below shows a CT image of right-sided pleural effusion.

Option D: Diaphragmatic hernia occurs due to intrathoracic movement of the abdominal contents through a diaphragmatic defect. The types include:

• Bochdalek hernia (posterior): Most common type. Herniation occurs through the pleuroperitoneal foramen.
• Morgagni hernia (anterior): Herniation occurs through the foramen of Morgagni.

Given below is a CT image showing Bochdalek hernia.

The child's parents mention that the pain has been increasing over the past few hours. On examination, the child appears distressed and has abdominal tenderness. An X-ray is ordered, and it reveals a gasless abdomen. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Acute pancreatitis

None

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which one of the following statements is correct regarding foetal physiology?
options: Haematopoiesis is demonstrated first in the yolk sac by 14th day
Breathing movements are identified at 26 weeks
Foetal pancreas secretes insulin as early as 20 weeks
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Haematopoiesis is demonstrated first in the yolk sac by 14th day

The yolk sac is the first site of hematopoiesis, beginning around the 3rd week (day 17–18) of embryonic life. Many examination texts simplify this as around the 14th day, making this the best answer.

Why are the other options incorrect?

• B. Meconium appears at 16 weeks: Meconium begins to accumulate by approximately 12 weeks of gestation, not 16 weeks.
• C. Breathing movements are identified at 26 weeks: Fetal breathing movements begin much earlier, around 10–12 weeks, and can be detected by ultrasound by the late first to early second trimester.
• D. Foetal pancreas secretes insulin as early as 20 weeks: Fetal insulin secretion begins by 10–12 weeks of gestation, well before 20 weeks.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which of the following is not helpful for differentiating between necrosis and apoptosis?
options: Internal organelle disintegration with lipid change
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Altered cell shape

Both necrosis and apoptosis show altered cell shape (Necrosis-cell enlarges; apoptosis-cell shrinks), making it non-discriminatory.

| Option | Necrosis | Apoptosis | Discriminates?

| ------ | -------- | --------- | --------------

| A. Intact cell organelle | Organelles disintegrate | Organelles preserved (esp. early) | Yes → points to apoptosis

| B. Altered cell shape | Cell swelling (oncosis) | Cell shrinkage + apoptotic bodies | No — shape changes in both

| C. Caspase-mediated degradation | Lysosomal hydrolases (auto-/heterolysis) | Caspases + endonucleases | Yes → points to apoptosis

| D. Internal organelle disintegration with lipid change | Yes — myelin figures | No | Yes → points to necrosis

Why B is the answer: Both processes distort cell morphology — necrosis via swelling, apoptosis via shrinkage. The mere presence of an altered shape tells you a cell is dying but not by which mechanism, so it has no discriminatory value.

• Mnemonic — Apoptosis = "A SHRINK": ATP-dependent, Shrinkage, Hyperchromatic (chromatin condensation), Regulated (caspases), Intact membrane, No inflammation, Karyorrhexis into apoptotic bodies.
• Nucleus: pyknosis → karyorrhexis → karyolysis is the necrosis sequence; apoptosis stops at fragmentation into membrane-bound bodies.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A 30-year-old man is brought after a road traffic accident with deformity of the left lower limb. The limb is positioned in flexion, abduction, and external rotation, with apparent lengthening. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The specific posture of the affected limb is the key to differentiating hip dislocations. An anterior hip dislocation (Option B) classically presents with the leg held in abduction, external rotation, and flexion, which results in "apparent lengthening" of the limb. This is much rarer than a posterior dislocation (Option A), which presents with the opposite posture: adduction, internal rotation, and flexion, with apparent shortening. Intertrochanteric (Option C) and femoral neck fractures (Option D) also cause external rotation but would present with true shortening and no abduction . Anterior dislocations can be "obturator" (more flexion) or "pubic" (more extension). Management requires urgent closed reduction under general anesthesia to prevent avascular necrosis of the femoral head. Because the patient demonstrates the unique "abducted and externally rotated" posture, anterior dislocation is the only accurate diagnosis

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A hospital has reported an outbreak of MRSA infection. On investigation, it was found out that a staff nurse had nasal carriage of MRSA. Which of the following drugs helps in the removal of colonization of bacteria?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Topical mupirocin

Topical mupirocin is the preferred agent for the elimination of nasal carriers of MRSA.

As Mupirocin has no structural similarities with existing systemic antibiotics that might lead to the development of cross-resistance and has minimal toxicity in its topical form, it is approved for the prevention of MRSA outbreaks

Mixed therapy with systemic agents is not preferred as it would cause unnecessary antibiotic exposure potentially paving way for drug resistance.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Stapedial reflex is dependent on the integrity of which cranial nerve for its motor response?
questions.explanation: The stapedial reflex (acoustic reflex) is a protective mechanism where loud sounds trigger the contraction of the stapedius muscle to dampen ossicular movement. The motor (efferent) limb of this reflex is provided by the facial nerve (CN VII), which innervates the stapedius muscle. The trigeminal nerve (CN V) (Option A) provides motor supply to the muscles of mastication and is involved in the separate tensor tympani reflex. The glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) (Option C) and the vagus nerve (CN X) (Option D) have no direct role in the motor limb of the stapedial reflex. Clinically, a lesion of the facial nerve proximal to the stapedius branch will result in an absent stapedial reflex, often causing hyperacusis (increased sensitivity to sound)

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Identify the given drain.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Closed suction drain

The Romo Vac drain, depicted in the image, is a closed suction drain commonly used after mastectomy.

Drains are placed at surgical sites to freely collect the air or fluids that may accumulate. This enhances wound healing by preventing the formation of unnecessary cavities. Drains are prophylactic in elective surgeries and therapeutic in emergency surgeries. Drains can be -

• Open - They are based on the principle of gravity
• Semi-open - Their action is based on capillary effect
• Closed - They carry out their actions through suction

Suction drains are commonly used in chest, breast, abdominal, thyroid, and plastic surgeries. They remove intraperitoneal secretions, anastomotic leaks, and blood from hemorrhage at the surgical site. Romo Vac drain is a negative suction drain closed drain kept in the subcutaneous tissue. Romo Vac drain is indicated in modified radical mastectomy, subcutaneous swelling excision, and amputations.

Special types of drains:

• Chest drains (option A) are connected to an underwater seal to aid the exit of air from the pleural cavity. They are used in pneumothorax, pleural effusion, and hemothorax.
• After surgical exploration of the bile duct, the sphincter of Oddi goes into spasm. To facilitate drainage of bile, a T tube may be used.

Drain insertion site care: The site of insertion of the drain is kept clean by drying and patting the drain insertion site with a clean towel after bath. The dressing is changed daily with folded gauze pieces placed below and above the drain site.

Removal of drains: The catheter at the site is milked for residual collections. It is then clamped and the suture holding the catheter is cut. The tube is then gently pulled out and any clots at the perforation end are removed. The time of removal of drains for various conditions is given below.

• Drains used in surgeries like thyroidectomy are usually removed within 24 hours. Their main purpose is to cover postoperative bleeding.
• In a mastectomy, a drain is placed for 5 days to collect serous collections.
• Drains used to cover the colorectal anastomoses are placed for 5-7 days.
• Common bile duct T-tube drains are usually placed for 10 days.
• Drains for infections are removed when the infection subsides or when the content of the drain is minimal.

After the drain is removed, a folded gauze is placed over the drain insertion area. The dressing can be removed after 24 hours. The patient may be given an antibiotic ointment to apply over the area for a week.

Other options:

Option A: The following image shows an underwater seal drain.

Option C: A Penrose drain is a flexible, soft, latex tube used to drain fluid from a surgical site after surgery. It's a type of passive drain.

Option D: Nelaton drain/catheter is commonly used as an intermittent urinary catheter. Like other intermittent catheters, it is also attached temporarily for draining the bladder and then removed.
questions.learning: Closed suction drain — The Romo Vac drain, depicted in the image, is a closed suction drain commonly used after mastectomy. Drains are placed at surgical sites to freely collect the air or fluids that may accumulate.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following is not an indication for parathyroidectomy in a patient?
options: Serum calcium >1 mg/dL above the upper limits of normal
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Creatinine clearance < 90 ml

Creatinine clearance <90 mL/min is not an indication of parathyroidectomy in primary hyperparathyroidism.

Indications for parathyroidectomy in asymptomatic primary hyperparathyroidism:

* Serum calcium >1 mg/dL above the upper limits of the normal level.

* GFR < 60mL/ min, 24-hour urine calcium >400 mg/dL and increased risk of or the presence of nephrolithiasis or nephrocalcinosis

* Decreased bone mineral density at the lumbar spine, total hip, femoral neck, or distal radius (>2.5 SD below peak bone mass, T score below −2.5; vertebral fracture)

* Age <50 years

* Long-term medical surveillance not desired or possible

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: According to NACO guidelines, when an HIV-positive patient receives counseling and screening for tuberculosis at an ICTC clinic, which level of prevention is being implemented?
questions.explanation: According to NACO guidelines, HIV care includes both preventive counseling and active screening for opportunistic infections like tuberculosis (TB). Primary prevention is represented by counseling, where the patient is educated about TB symptoms, transmission, adherence to treatment, and risk reduction. Since HIV patients are at high risk of developing TB, this counseling helps prevent occurrence or worsening of disease, thus falling under primary prevention. Secondary prevention is represented by screening for TB, which aims at early detection and prompt treatment. Identifying TB at an early stage in HIV-positive individuals reduces complications, transmission, and mortality. Why other options are incomplete: (A) Primordial → Deals with prevention of risk factors before they appear (B) Primary → Only covers counseling, not screening (C) Secondary → Only covers screening, ignores counseling component

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which adverse effect of bleomycin can be worsened by radiation therapy?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Pulmonary fibrosis

Pulmonary fibrosis, a known side-effect of Bleomycin can be exacerbated by radiation therapy.

Bleomycin is an anticancer antibiotic. It acts by generating free radicals by binding with a reducing agent (iron) in the presence of oxygen. This metal-drug complex cleaves the DNA of the tumor cell. It is used as a component in the treatment regimens of Hodgkin's lymphoma and testicular cancer.

It is a cell-cycle-specific drug that acts during the G2 phase of the cell cycle.

Bleomycin has a bone marrow–sparing effect. The major adverse events include flagellate dermatitis and pulmonary toxicity, which may progress to pulmonary fibrosis.

Flagellate dermatitis starts as bands of pruritic, flagellate, and erythematous lesions over the trunk and extremities. These rashes heal with persistent flagellate hyperpigmentation. No treatment is necessary since the lesions usually disappear on the stoppage of the drug. These lesions respond to topical corticosteroids.

The image given below shows flagellate dermatitis.

Other agents causing flagellate dermatitis are docetaxel, bendamustine, and peplomycin.

Drugs causing pulmonary fibrosis - Mnemonic "BITMAP":

* Bleomycin (chemotherapy)

* Infliximab (and other TNF inhibitors)

* Tocilizumab (IL-6 inhibitor)

* Methotrexate (immunosuppressant)

* Amiodarone (antiarrhythmic)

* Paraquat (herbicide, though not a medication)
questions.learning: Pulmonary fibrosis Pulmonary fibrosis, a known side-effect of Bleomycin can be exacerbated by radiation therapy. Bleomycin is an anticancer antibiotic.

Correct answer: A. Ito cells

Vitamin A is stored in the liver perisinusoidal stellate (Ito) cells as retinyl ester (retinol palmitate).

Kupffer cells, also known as stellate macrophages and Kupffer-Borowicz cells; are specialized macrophages located in the liver that form part of the mononuclear phagocyte system. These are present, lining the walls of the sinusoids, not the perisinusoidal space (Space of Disse).

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: A man is found 100 km away from home, confused about identity and travel, after an earthquake. No head injury or substance use. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Dissociative fugue

Dissociative fugue involves sudden travel, amnesia for the period, and identity confusion, often triggered by trauma. Dissociative amnesia lacks travel, DID involves multiple identities, and schizophrenia presents differently.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: Two girls in the same class are diagnosed with meningococcal meningitis. Their 12-year old friend from the same school is afraid of contracting the disease. What advice should be given to the exposed students?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Antibiotic prophylaxis

Antibiotic prophylaxis is provided to the close contacts of persons with confirmed meningococcal disease.

Close contacts of individuals with confirmed meningococcal disease are at an increased risk of developing the illness. Prophylaxis is also offered to individuals with direct and prolonged contact with a case of meningococcal disease. Antibiotics are effective in preventing additional cases by eradicating the carriage of the invasive strain.

Treatment is provided to the contacts within 24 hours of identification of the index case. The antibiotics effective include rifampicin, ciprofloxacin, ceftriaxone, and azithromycin.

Prophylaxis is not generally recommended for medical personnel, except in cases where there is exposure to aerosols of respiratory secretions, such as during mouth-to-mouth resuscitation, intubation, or suctioning. This recommendation applies within 24 hours before or after the initiation of antibiotic therapy in the index case.

For the treatment of cases, penicillin is the preferred drug, but ceftriaxone or other third-generation cephalosporins are recommended for patients with penicillin allergy. Droplet infection control precautions should be followed for hospitalized patients for 24 hours after effective therapy has been initiated.

Offering quadrivalent meningococcal A, C, W, Y conjugate vaccines in addition to antimicrobial prophylaxis can further reduce the risk of disease among close contacts of cases caused by vaccine capsular groups.

Meningococcal vaccines are available in two forms: polysaccharide vaccines and polysaccharide-protein conjugate vaccines. Polysaccharide vaccines can be given as a single dose to individuals aged 2 years and older. They are offered in bivalent (A, C), trivalent (A, C, W135), and quadrivalent (A, C, W135, Y) formulations.

Meningococcal conjugate vaccines are available as monovalent (A or C) or quadrivalent (A, C, W135, Y) formulations. Conjugate vaccines, which offer increased immunogenicity and potential for herd protection, are preferred over polysaccharide vaccines, especially in children under 2 years of age. Both types of vaccines are safe to use during pregnancy.
questions.learning: Antibiotic prophylaxis Antibiotic prophylaxis is provided to the close contacts of persons with confirmed meningococcal disease. Close contacts of individuals with confirmed meningococcal disease are at an increased risk of developing the illness.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Serum thyroglobulin level is an important tumor marker for:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Papillary carcinoma thyroid

Note: Serum thyroglobulin (Tg) is a tumor marker for differentiated thyroid cancers (both papillary and follicular carcinoma). Since follicular carcinoma is not among the options, the best answer is papillary carcinoma thyroid.

Thyroglobulin (Tg) is a glycoprotein produced by normal thyroid follicular cells and differentiated thyroid cancers. It is not used for diagnosis but is an excellent tumor marker for postoperative surveillance after total thyroidectomy and radioactive iodine ablation.

Why not other options?

• A. Medullary carcinoma thyroid:

• Arises from parafollicular C. cells.
• Tumor marker: Calcitonin (± CEA).

• C. Anaplastic carcinoma thyroid:

• Highly undifferentiated tumor.
• Does not produce thyroglobulin reliably, so Tg is not a useful marker.

• D. Thyroid lymphoma:

• Usually associated with Hashimoto thyroiditis.
• No role for thyroglobulin as a tumor marker.
questions.learning: Papillary carcinoma thyroid Note: Serum thyroglobulin (Tg) is a tumor marker for differentiated thyroid cancers (both papillary and follicular carcinoma).

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: What is the level of termination of the spinal cord in infants?
questions.explanation: In human anatomy, the level at which the spinal cord (medullary cone) ends varies with age due to the differential growth rates of the spinal cord and the vertebral column. In infants, the spinal cord typically terminates at the level of the L3 vertebra (Option C) . As the child grows, the vertebral column lengthens more than the spinal cord, causing the cord to "ascend" relatively. In an adult, the spinal cord usually ends at the lower border of L1 or the upper border of L2 (Options A and B). This anatomical difference is of critical clinical importance when performing a lumbar puncture in a neonate or infant; the needle must be inserted at a lower level (usually the L4-L5 space) to avoid direct injury to the spinal cord. Therefore, L3 is the definitive anatomical standard for infants
questions.learning: In human anatomy, the level at which the spinal cord (medullary cone) ends varies with age due to the differential growth rates of the spinal cord and the vertebral column.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A woman with a previous cesarean section presents in labor with contractions occurring three times in ten minutes. The membranes are intact, and there are no signs of fetal distress. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Perform artificial rupture of membranes (ARM) and monitor
questions.explanation: In a patient with a prior cesarean undergoing a Trial of Labor After Cesarean (TOLAC), the goal is to allow natural progress while minimizing risks. Since the patient is stable with regular contractions and no fetal distress, performing an Artificial Rupture of Membranes (ARM) is an appropriate next step to stimulate endogenous prostaglandins and enhance labor naturally. Oxytocin (Option A) should be used with extreme caution in TOLAC due to the increased risk of uterine rupture. Instrumental delivery (Option C) is only indicated during the second stage of labor, not the first. A repeat cesarean (Option D) is not currently indicated as there is no evidence of labor arrest or fetal compromise. Thus, ARM provides a safe method of labor augmentation

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A hypertensive pregnant woman presented with abdominal pain, bleeding per vagina, and loss of fetal movements. What is the most probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Abruptio placenta

The given clinical picture with abdominal pain, bleeding per vagina, and loss of fetal movements in a hypertensive pregnant woman points to the diagnosis of placental abruption.

Abruptio placenta is the partial/total separation of a normally implanted placenta before delivery.

The bleeding may be either

* Revealed - Blood dissects downwards between membranes and uterine wall to escape through the cervix. Or,

* Concealed -Blood accumulates between the detached placenta and uterus. Or,

* Mixed

Risk factors for abruption placenta include prior abruption history, preterm premature rupture of membranes, and pregnancy-associated hypertension. The haemorrhage into decidua basalis causes separation and compression of the placenta. This compromises fetal circulation leading to fetal distress.

Depending upon the degree of placental abruption and its clinical effects, the cases are graded as follows:

Grade 1
Grade 2
Grade 3

Vaginal bleeding is slight
Vaginal bleeding mild to moderate
Bleeding is moderate to severe or concealed.

Uterus irritable, minimal tenderness

Uterine tenderness is always present
Uterine tenderness is marked.

Maternal BP and fibrinogen unaffected
Maternal pulse increased, BP maintained
Shock is pronounced

FHS good
Fetal distress present
Fetal death is the rule

Maternal shock absent
Maternal shock absent
Associated coagulation defect or anuria may complicate

Placenta previa occurs when the placenta is implanted in the lower uterine segment over or very close to the cervical os. Vaginal bleeding is usually painless in this condition. Fetal condition is generally good until bleeding is severe which occurs in later stages. High-risk factors include multiparty, previous cesarean, or myomectomy scar in the uterus.

In preterm labour, fetal movements are not compromised. Hydramnios does not present with bleeding PV.
questions.learning: Abruptio placenta — The given clinical picture with abdominal pain, bleeding per vagina, and loss of fetal movements in a hypertensive pregnant woman points to the diagnosis of placental abruption.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: Choose the true statement regarding CF (Cystic Fibrosis) :
options: Chloride secretion is decreased in sweat and increased in pancreatic fluid
Chloride secretion is increased in sweat and decreased in pancreatic fluid
Chloride secretion is decreased in both sweat and pancreatic fluid
Chloride secretion is increased in both sweat and pancreatic fluid
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Chloride secretion is increased in sweat and decreased in pancreatic fluid

Cystic fibrosis is caused by CFTR channel dysfunction leading to abnormal chloride transport in different tissues, producing opposite effects in sweat glands and exocrine organs.

• In sweat glands: defective reabsorption of chloride → increased chloride in sweat (basis of sweat chloride test)
• In pancreas and other exocrine glands: decreased chloride secretion → thick, viscous secretions causing ductal obstruction

Clinical correlation:

• High sweat chloride is diagnostic
• Pancreatic insufficiency leads to malabsorption and failure to thrive

questions.text: All of the following are growth promoting proto-oncogenes except?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. TGF beta

TGF-β is growth-inhibitory, not growth-promoting.

Proto-oncogenes encode growth factors that stimulate cell proliferation and survival.

FGF, PDGF, and TGF-α act as mitogenic signals promoting cell cycle progression.

Growth factors (FGF, PDGF, TGF-α)

↓

Receptor activation

↓

RAS/MAPK pathway

↓

Cell proliferation

TGF-β, in contrast, inhibits epithelial cell proliferation by inducing cell cycle arrest via SMAD signalling. Loss of TGF-β signalling contributes to oncogenesis, but the gene itself functions as a tumor suppressor.

| ------ | -------- | --------------

| FGF | Proliferation, angiogenesis | Oncogenic

| PDGF | Cell growth | Oncogenic

| TGF-α | EGFR activation | Oncogenic

| TGF-β
“Beta” = brake 🛑 | Growth inhibition | Tumor suppressor

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A previously healthy 3-month-old girl is brought to the physician because of fever, irritability, and rash for 3 days. The rash started around the mouth before spreading to the trunk and extremities. Her temperature is 38.6°C (101.5°F). Examination shows a diffuse erythematous rash with flaccid bullae on the neck, flexural creases, and buttocks. Gentle pressure across the trunk with a gloved finger creates a blister. Oropharyngeal examination shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most likely underlying mechanism of these skin findings?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Toxin-induced cleavage of desmoglein-1

This infant has staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome (SSSS), suggested by fever, irritability, diffuse erythema, flaccid bullae, and a positive Nikolsky sign, with no mucosal involvement. SSSS is caused by exfoliative toxins (ETA, ETB) from Staphylococcus aureus that cleave desmoglein-1, a desmosomal protein in the superficial epidermis (stratum granulosum). Loss of cell adhesion leads to superficial blistering and skin desquamation.

Why the other options are incorrect:

B. Bacterial production of erythrogenic toxin – Causes scarlet fever (sandpaper rash), not bullae or Nikolsky positivity.

C. Bacterial invasion of the epidermis – Seen in bullous impetigo; lesions are localized and contain bacteria.

D.Autoantibody deposition in stratum spinosum – Describes pemphigus vulgaris (anti-desmoglein-3) with mucosal involvement.
questions.learning: Toxin-induced cleavage of desmoglein-1 — This infant has staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome (SSSS), suggested by fever, irritability, diffuse erythema, flaccid bullae, and a positive Nikolsky sign, with no mucosal involvement.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A 60-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes mellitus develops vaginal candidiasis. Which antidiabetic (hypoglycemic) agent should be avoided in this patient?
questions.explanation: Gliflozins (SGLT2 inhibitors), such as canagliflozin or empagliflozin, work by inhibiting glucose reabsorption in the proximal tubules of the kidney, leading to glycosuria (glucose in the urine). While effective for blood sugar control and providing cardiovascular benefits, the increased urinary glucose concentration promotes the growth of fungi. Therefore, a major and common side effect of Gliflozins is an increased risk of genitourinary infections, particularly vaginal candidiasis and urinary tract infections. In a patient already suffering from candidiasis, these drugs should be avoided as they will likely exacerbate the infection. Acarbose (Option A), Metformin (Option B), and Linagliptin (Option D) do not cause glycosuria and are not associated with an increased risk of fungal infections. Clinical management requires weighing the significant renal and cardiac benefits of SGLT2 inhibitors against the risk of recurrent infections, often necessitating counseling on proper hygiene and prompt treatment of any symptomatic episodes
questions.learning: Gliflozins (SGLT2 inhibitors), such as canagliflozin or empagliflozin, work by inhibiting glucose reabsorption in the proximal tubules of the kidney, leading to glycosuria (glucose in the urine).

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 62-year-old man presents with gradually worsening difficulty rising from a chair and climbing stairs. His muscle strength transiently improves with repeated activity but later deteriorates, causing frequent falls. A chest scan shows a hilar mass. Which type of lung cancer is most likely associated with this presentation?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Small cell carcinoma

The patient most likely has Lambert–Eaton myasthenic syndrome (LEMS), a paraneoplastic syndrome strongly associated with small cell lung carcinoma (SCLC). LEMS is caused by autoantibodies against presynaptic P/Q-type voltage-gated calcium channels (VGCCs) at the neuromuscular junction, resulting in decreased acetylcholine release. A characteristic feature is proximal muscle weakness that temporarily improves with repeated muscle use (facilitation), distinguishing it from myasthenia gravis. The patient has:

• Proximal muscle weakness (difficulty rising from a chair, climbing stairs)
• Transient improvement with repeated activity
• Hilar lung mass
• Frequent falls

These findings are classic for Lambert–Eaton myasthenic syndrome, which is most commonly associated with small cell lung carcinoma.

Why not the other options?

• A. Squamous cell carcinoma: Commonly associated with PTHrP secretion, causing hypercalcemia, not Lambert–Eaton syndrome.
• B. Large cell carcinoma: May produce β-hCG, causing gynecomastia, but is not typically associated with LEMS.
• D. Adenocarcinoma: The most common lung cancer overall, especially in nonsmokers, but has no strong association with Lambert–Eaton syndrome.
questions.learning: Small cell carcinoma — The patient most likely has Lambert–Eaton myasthenic syndrome (LEMS), a paraneoplastic syndrome strongly associated with small cell lung carcinoma (SCLC).

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Which muscle pairs are responsible for levo depression?
questions.explanation: Levo depression means depression of both eyes when looking to the left (levoversion). In left gaze, the left eye is abducted and the right eye is adducted. 1. The left eye (abducted) is depressed mainly by the Left Inferior Rectus (LIR). 2. The right eye (adducted) is depressed mainly by the Right Superior Oblique (RSO). Thus, the correct muscle pair is RSO (right superior oblique) and LIR (left inferior rectus). Why other options are wrong: (A) LSO and RIR: These muscles produce depression in the opposite gaze combination (not levo depression). (C) RIO and LIR: Inferior oblique elevates the eye, not depresses it. (D) LIO and RIR: Inferior oblique again causes elevation, and the pairing does not match left gaze depression
questions.learning: Levo depression means depression of both eyes when looking to the left (levoversion). In left gaze, the left eye is abducted and the right eye is adducted.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: From which amino acid is nitric oxide synthesized?
questions.explanation: Nitric oxide (NO), a potent vasodilator and signaling molecule, is synthesized from the amino acid Arginine. The reaction is catalyzed by the enzyme Nitric Oxide Synthase (NOS), which converts L-arginine into L-citrulline and NO in the presence of oxygen and NADPH. NO plays a critical role in regulating blood pressure, inhibiting platelet aggregation, and acting as a neurotransmitter. Tryptophan (Option A) is the precursor for serotonin and melatonin. Lysine (Option B) is an essential amino acid involved in protein synthesis and collagen cross-linking. Tyrosine (Option D) is the precursor for catecholamines, thyroid hormones, and melanin. Because of its vasodilatory properties, pharmacological agents that increase NO (like nitroglycerin) are used to treat angina. Understanding the arginine-NO pathway is fundamental to cardiovascular physiology and pharmacology. Thus, arginine serves as the unique and indispensable nitrogen source for the production of this essential gaseous mediator

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text:
In FFA, the microaneurysms appear as:

FFA- Fundus Fluorescein Angiography
options: Hyperfluorescent branching-like structures in the vessel
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Hyperfluorescent dots

In Fundus Fluorescein Angiography (FFA), microaneurysms (a hallmark of diabetic retinopathy) appear as hyperfluorescent dots due to the accumulation of fluorescein dye in the localized dilations of retinal capillaries.

Other options:

Option A: Hypofluorescent dots indicate blocked fluorescence, often due to hemorrhage or ischemia.

Option C: Hypofluorescent line might occur in cases of vascular occlusion.

Option D: Hyperfluorescent branching-like structure in the vessel suggests leakage from neovascularization or vascular abnormalities.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient with diabetes develops a UTI, which gets complicated with hypotension that is resistant to IV fluids. Which of the following antibiotics can be used?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Piperacillin-Tazobactam

A diabetic patient with a urinary tract infection, now presenting with hypotension unresponsive to IV fluids is suggestive of urosepsis (septic shock). Hence, the patient should be treated with Piperacillin-Tazobactam. In septic shock, there is peripheral vasodilation due to toxins from the infectious agent causing endothelial injury and fluid leak, leading to hypotension which can be refractory to fluid therapy in the early stages.

Urinary tract infections (UTIs) are more common in diabetic patients due to poor metabolic control, altered immune status, poor bladder control and incomplete voiding. E.coli is the most common organism to cause urinary tract infections. Other organisms causing infections include Klebsiella spp, Proteus spp, Enterobacter spp and Enterococci. They are more prone to resistance to common antibiotics used in uncomplicated urinary tract infections. UTIs can range from asymptomatic bacteriuria, cystitis, pyelonephritis and complicated urosepsis.

Other options:

Option B: Amoxiclav is used for the treatment of upper respiratory tract infections and skin and soft tissue infections. Though most cases of UTI are caused by E.coli, due to increased resistance (ESBL-producing strains), it can be challenging to treat with oral beta-lactams and generally, they have lower cure rates compared to other classes of drugs such as fluoroquinolones or trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole.

Option C: When a patient with uncomplicated pyelonephritis is treated with trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole and organism susceptibility is unknown, ceftriaxone 1 gram IV can be used initially.

Option D: Nitrofurantoin is used for the treatment of uncomplicated cystitis.

Factors that suggest a complicated urinary tract infection:

• Functional or anatomic abnormality of the urinary tract
• Male gender
• Diabetes
• Elderly
• Immunosuppression
• Childhood urinary tract infection
• Recent antimicrobial usage
• Indwelling urinary catheter
• Urinary tract instrumentation
• Hospital-acquired infection
• Symptoms more than 7 days at presentation.
questions.learning: Piperacillin-Tazobactam — A diabetic patient with a urinary tract infection, now presenting with hypotension unresponsive to IV fluids is suggestive of urosepsis (septic shock).

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: What is the most likely diagnosis in a 20-year-old male presenting with right flank pain, fever with chills, and pain on passive extension of the right hip, along with leukocytosis and characteristic findings on CT scan?
questions.explanation: The clinical presentation of fever, flank pain, and the classic "psoas sign" (pain on passive extension of the hip) is highly suggestive of a psoas abscess. The psoas muscle is located deep in the retroperitoneum, and its proximity to the hip joint causes inflammation there to manifest as pain when the muscle is stretched. While acute appendicitis (Option C), especially with a retrocecal appendix, can also cause a psoas sign, the primary location of the pain in the "flank" often shifts the differential toward an abscess or renal pathology. Pyelonephritis (Option A) causes flank pain and fever but typically does not produce a positive psoas sign. Torsion of an undescended testis (Option D) can cause lower abdominal or groin pain but would not typically involve the psoas sign and would show a missing testis in the scrotum. Therefore, the inflammatory symptoms localized to the psoas muscle confirm a psoas abscess diagnosis
questions.learning: The clinical presentation of fever, flank pain, and the classic "psoas sign" (pain on passive extension of the hip) is highly suggestive of a psoas abscess.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 4-year-old-boy was brought to emergency department with complaints of acute radiating pain in right iliac region and during surgery the following structure was found. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Meckel’s Diverticulum

The clinical history and the image are both suggestive of Meckel's Diverticulum.

Meckel’s diverticulum is a true diverticulum, which extends from the antimesenteric side of the small bowel. The diverticula which contain all the layers of the intestine are called true diverticula. It is caused by a failure of normal regression of the vitelline duct that develops during weeks 5-7 of gestation.

The rule of 2's (Mnemonic for Meckel’s diverticulum) :

* 2 types of heterotopic mucosa (gastric & pancreatic)(Option d).

* 2% incidence

* located within 2 feet of the ileocecal valve

* approximately 2 inches in length

* Usually symptomatic by 2 years of age

The most common presentation is painless, massive, lower GI bleed in children younger than 5 years. Meckel's diverticulum can be the lead point for ileoileal or ileocolic intussusception.

A bleeding Meckel's diverticulum may be confirmed by a 99 mTc-pertechnetate isotope scan to detect ectopic gastric mucosa.

Surgical treatment is the definitive therapy for Meckel’s diverticulum. A simple V-shaped diverticulectomy with transverse closure of the ileum is the ideal surgical approach.

Other Options:

Option A: The most common tumor of the appendix is the well-differentiated neuroendocrine (carcinoid) tumor. This neoplasm, which is almost always benign, most frequently forms a solid bulbous swelling at the distal tip of the appendix.

Option B: Adenocarinoma of  the appendix is very rare, accounting for 0.5% of all gastrointestinal cancers. They are detected in 0.08 to 0.1% of appendectomy specimens. Mucinous is a subtype of the adenocarinoma of  the appendix.

Option D: In bowel loop obstruction, the obstructed bowel loops are centrally located and lie transversely. In cases of jejunal obstruction, valvulae conniventes, which are mucosal folds that span the entire diameter of the bowel, create a ladder effect. Additionally, a distended cecum may exhibit a gas shadow in the right iliac fossa.
